body.text:
I bought the persimmon soap the internet keeps telling women my age to buy.
I used it every day for 3 weeks, morning and night, the whole bar.
My husband is still sleeping in the spare room.

I am 61. Ron and I have been married 34 years. He retired last September after 38 years at the county.

He was still in our room at Christmas. I want to be accurate about that, because I have gone over the order of it more times than I can tell you.

This is what happened in between, and what it cost me to find out.

By January he had stopped coming into our bedroom.

He would stand in the doorway with his coffee and tell me about the gutters from there. Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold like a man delivering something.

In March he moved his pillow into the spare room. He said it was his back, and that the mattress in there was firmer, and that he was sorry, and he was sorry the way you are sorry when you have already decided.

I bought him a mattress topper in April. The expensive one, the one the man in the store said was for people with backs.

In June I went in there for the window fan and I found it behind the door. Still in the plastic. The tape had not been broken.

I stood there holding a mattress topper for a long time.

He had not been sleeping badly. He had been sleeping somewhere else, and he had found a reason for it that I could not argue with, because you cannot argue with a man's back.

Kate is our daughter. She is 33 and she is 40 minutes away, and she is the kind of daughter who calls on the drive home.

She had been putting the window down in my car since about February. Two inches. Then she would say something about the heat, in February, in Ohio.

In May she drove us both to my sister's and she had the air on the whole way with the windows cracked, and when I asked her she said she gets carsick if it is stuffy. She has never been carsick in her life.

In April, at my own table, she suggested we eat out on the porch. It was 48 degrees. We ate out on the porch, all of us, in coats, and everybody said what a lovely idea.

I want to be fair to them. Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not once. Not one word.

They just kept finding reasons, and the reasons were all good ones, and there were a lot of them.

The night I found the topper I sat up until 2 in the morning with my phone, typing things into it I would not have said out loud in an empty house.

I will not write out what I typed. Any woman my age who has done it knows what I typed.

I found women saying the same 3 words to each other on a page I will not name. Persimmon soap. That was all of it. Nobody said why it was persimmon and I did not care why.

I ordered a persimmon soap that night. 9 dollars, an orange bar, persimmons all over the box, a bit of Japanese on the front. It came on the Thursday.

I used it every day for 3 weeks.

I want to tell you exactly how careful I was, because I need you to understand what it did to me when nothing happened. Every morning. Every night. The whole bar.

Ron stayed in the spare room.

Kate put the window down in July.

And I stopped, because there is only one thing left to think when the answer does not work. It is not the answer that is wrong. It is you. And you are not fixable.

I put the wrapper in the bin and I did not tell one living person I had bought it.

In August I went into the pharmacy on Harrison for Ron's back. That is the part I still cannot get over. I was in there buying a heat patch for the back he does not have a problem with.

Maggie has been behind that counter 17 years. She did my mother's blister packs for the last 2 years of her life and she never once made me feel like I was asking too much.

She rang up the heat patches and she said, "How is he doing?"

And I said, "He's fine," and then I stood there and did not move away from the counter.

There was nobody behind me. She waited.

"Maggie, can I ask you something that isn't about him."

She put the patches in the bag and left the bag on the counter.

"Is there something about me. A smell. I have thought about it every day since March and I cannot ask anybody in my own house."

She did not look surprised, which was the first kind thing that happened to me all year.

"There's something," she said. "You're not imagining it. But it isn't what you think it is."

"I shower every day. I have showered every day of my life."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"I've stood here 17 years. Things change for women our age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She leaned on the counter.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"That can't be right."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I put my hand on the counter.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

"Persimmon. The tannins take it apart. It doesn't cover it."

And I heard myself say it out loud in a pharmacy at 20 past 4 in the afternoon.

"I bought that. I bought a persimmon soap in June. I used it for 3 weeks and nothing happened, so I stopped."

She did not say anything for a second.

Then she said, "Have you still got the box?"

I said it was in the bin in June.

"Then buy another one and bring me the box before you use it. Any of them. Whichever one you like the look of."

I did. I brought it in the following Tuesday in my purse.

She turned it over on the counter and put her finger on the list on the back and read it to me out loud, the way she reads a label to somebody's mother.

Water. Palm oil. Glycerin. Fragrance. A color, with a number on it.

She got to the bottom of the list and stopped.

"Now find me the persimmon."

It was on the front of the box 4 times. It was in the name of the product. There was a photograph of one on it.

It was not in the list at all.

"That's what you bought in June," she said. "You didn't try persimmon soap. You tried an orange soap that had been told to look like one."

I stood in that pharmacy and my eyes went, which I had not done in front of anybody all year, including in the spare room doorway in March.

"So it was never me."

"It was never you. And it wasn't even your judgment. It was one line on a label that nobody has ever told you to read."

She reached under the counter for her handbag, which is a thing I had never seen her do, and she took out a small parcel wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon orange. Characters on the front I could not read.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"I can't take yours."

"I buy 3 at a time. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone, so I've learned."

"Does it work?"

"I've used it 6 years. One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped standing a bit back from people. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. I can't sell it to you. That is more or less the point of it."

I used it that night. It is a bar of soap. I did not expect anything, because I had already been here in June.

The first week I could not tell.

The second week Kate drove me to my sister's again and we had the windows up the whole way and she talked about her job the entire time and I do not think she noticed she was doing it.

At the end of August, Ron came into our bedroom to get a book off his own shelf, which he had been doing from the doorway since January.

He came in. He sat on the end of the bed while he found his place in it. He stayed about 20 minutes.

He did not say anything and neither did I. I have learned something about what does not get said in that house.

In September a woman waiting for her prescription behind me at Maggie's counter said, "I'm sorry, what is that? It's citrus. It's lovely."

I said it was a bar of soap.

Maggie did not look up from her computer. She said, "Isn't it."

Ron came back into our room on the 4th of October. He carried his own pillow in and put it down and said, "I've been sleeping badly in there."

I said, "Have you."

That is as close as either of us is going to get, and after 34 years I find I do not need the rest of it.

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

I was right in June. I had the right idea in the middle of the night on my own phone, and I paid 9 dollars for it, and it did nothing, and I decided that meant there was something wrong with me that could not be fixed.

It was the bar. It was only ever the bar.

Maggie texted me last week. Kaori is back on the website. She has ordered 3, because that is what she does.

Kate is driving us both to my sister's for her birthday on the 2nd.

She has already asked if I am bringing the good pie. I told her yes.

If your husband has found a reason he can live with and moved down the hall.

If somebody has started opening a window in your car and telling you it is the heat.

If you have already tried the thing that was supposed to work, and stopped, and quietly decided the problem is you.

You do not need to be fixed.

You need to find out what you actually bought.

Get the soap. Take the shower. Turn the box over first.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

It was never me.

It was never going to be me.

Your move.

cards.body:
I lost my granddaughter at 66 because I can't smell. She told her mom my house makes her sick. I can't smell a thing. But that I heard.

I was in the kitchen. She was in the hallway with her mom. She didn't know I was there.

"Mommy I don't want to go to grandma's house. It makes me sick."

My sweet girl. The one who used to fall asleep on my chest every Sunday. That girl just told her mother that being near me makes her sick.

I stood there holding the counter and I couldn't breathe. Makes her sick. What makes her sick? What is she talking about?

I lost my sense of smell a year before Covid hit. It never came back. Not even a little. I can't smell my food, my clothes, my house, my own skin. Nothing. So when my granddaughter says something makes her sick, I can't just sniff it out like a normal person. I'm blind.

That night I didn't sleep.

I crawled through every room on my hands and knees trying to understand what she meant. Pressed my face into the couch cushions. Nothing. Held my curtains against my nose. Nothing. Put my face flat on the carpet. Nothing.

What is it, baby? What are you smelling? I was begging my house to give me an answer my nose couldn't.

I cleaned everything. Every surface, every fabric, every corner. Had the pipes checked. Had someone look for mold. Opened every window for days in the middle of winter. None of it mattered. Because I couldn't tell if any of it helped. I was fixing things in the dark.

And the whole time there was one place I never thought to check.

Something in the back of my mind was already whispering it. I just wasn't ready to hear it.

Then I started remembering things I had been too afraid to connect.

My granddaughter pulling away from me. Not all at once. Slowly. First she stopped sitting in my lap. Then she stopped hugging me. Then she started staying on the other side of the room.

I told myself she was just growing up. Kids do that.

But then I thought about my son. Last time he hugged me at the door, he held his breath. I felt his chest lock up against mine. Just for a second. He thought I wouldn't notice. But when you lose your smell, you start feeling things other people miss. Your whole body pays attention in ways it never did before. I felt him stop breathing.

After the hug he opened both windows in the guest room. It was November.

Then I thought about my neighbor. Every Tuesday we have coffee. And every Tuesday for six months her chair moved a little further from mine. One week she said let's sit outside. It was 45 degrees.

Then my book club. How Carol opens a window when I arrive. How Janet switched seats last month. How nobody says a word but something shifts every time I walk in.

Nobody told me. Not one person. But every single one of them did something.

Standing alone in my hallway at 1 AM, all of it hit me at once. The windows. The chairs. The held breath. The distance. My granddaughter's words.

They could all smell something I couldn't.

It was never the pipes. Never mold. Never the house.

It might be me.

That thought almost broke me.

I stopped inviting people over. Birthdays became phone calls. I quit book club. I couldn't sit in Carol's living room for two hours wondering if everyone was waiting for me to leave.

You want to know the loneliest feeling in the world? Sitting in your own living room afraid to answer the door because you have no idea what hits people when they walk in. And you can't fix it because you can't smell it. And you can't ask because you're terrified of the answer.

I showered twice a day. Bought the most expensive body wash I could find. Scrubbed until my skin turned red. Stayed up past 2 AM searching things I was ashamed to type. "Why do old people smell." "Can you stink and not know it." Found women my age asking the same questions. All of them doing everything right. Not one had figured it out.

I closed my laptop and sat in the dark. This is my life now. A grandmother who makes her own granddaughter sick. And I can't even smell why.

Then Margaret showed up.

No call. No text. She just appeared at my kitchen door on a Thursday with a paper bag. Put it on the table. Sat down. Took both my hands.

And said three words nobody had said to me in years.

You smell, Linda.

I broke down. Not from shame. From relief. Finally someone loved me enough to say what everyone else was too polite to say.

And then she told me something that changed everything.

Margaret worked in elder care for 30 years. Thousands of older people. And she told me something no doctor, no family member, no friend ever did.

She said our bodies start making a compound as we age. Called Nonenal. It comes out through the skin. Musty. Stale. Sour. The kind of smell that gets into furniture, blankets, walls.

And here's what made my jaw drop. Every person she ever cared for who had this smell was clean. Bathed. Groomed. It didn't matter. Because Nonenal is not dirt. It's not sweat. It comes from inside the skin. And regular soap, no matter how expensive, no matter how hard you scrub, cannot touch it.

Every shower. Every body wash. Every time I scrubbed my arms raw. None of it could have worked. Not because I wasn't trying hard enough. Because soap was never built to fight what was actually on my skin.

Margaret said her staff tried everything for 30 years. Air fresheners. Essential oils. Special detergent. Organic soap. Nothing worked. Because nothing was going after the actual cause.

Until one day a nurse brought in a soap made with Japanese persimmon. Persimmon has something that grabs onto Nonenal and breaks it apart. Not covers it up. Not hides it. Breaks it down. Gone.

Within days the staff saw the difference. Not air freshener fighting something underneath. Just clean.

Then she opened the paper bag. Inside was a bar of Kaori soap. She put it in my hands like it was medicine.

"I already ordered it for you. Two more bars are coming next week. This is the one we use. Has been for years. The concentration is right, it actually works, and it's made with real Japanese persimmon. Not some watered down version. The real thing."

She paused.

"Just so you know, they sell out. A lot. So when you get low, don't wait."

She squeezed my hands, got up, and went home.

I used it that night. Didn't expect anything. First thing I noticed was my skin. Softer. Like something that had been sitting on it for years was gone. A layer I didn't know was there.

But I couldn't smell it. I still can't. So I had to wait and watch the people around me.

Week one. My daughter sat right next to me on the couch. Arm against arm. She hadn't done that in a very long time.

Week two. Margaret came by and didn't say a word about any smell.

Week three. My son hugged me at the door. His chest opened up. He breathed in. Full breath. Face near my neck. Like it was nothing. Like I was just his mom again.

Week four.

I stood there holding the counter and I couldn't breathe. Makes her sick. What makes her sick? What is she talking about?

That night I didn't sleep.

I crawled through every room on my hands and knees trying to understand what she meant. Pressed my face into the couch cushions. Nothing. Held my curtains against my nose. Nothing. Put my face flat on the carpet. Nothing.

What is it, baby? What are you smelling? I was begging my house to give me an answer my nose couldn't.

I cleaned everything. Every surface, every fabric, every corner. Had the pipes checked. Had someone look for mold. Opened every window for days in the middle of winter. None of it mattered. Because I couldn't tell if any of it helped. I was fixing things in the dark.

body.text:
My husband told me I smell like a "nursing home" at 63. Then he showed up uninvited to my girls trip in Tulum. He's been sleeping on our couch ever since.

Mark and I have been married for 26 years.

We met when I was 36. He was 40. Both working in tech in Phoenix.

We got married a year later. Had two kids -- Emma and Jake. Both grown now. Emma's in Seattle, Jake's in Denver.

For the first nineteen years, things were good.

We traveled. We hiked. We went to concerts.

Then Mark retired early. Two years ago. Sold his company. Made enough that we're comfortable.

And I'll tell you, that's when things changed.

He started playin' golf five days a week. Long lunches with his buddies from work. His whole life became tee times and the clubhouse.

Most of his golf friends are divorced. Remarried to younger women.

Dave's wife is 38.

Tom's girlfriend is 41.

Steve's wife is 35.

And Mark started comparing.

Never directly to me. Just ... mentioned. Constantly.

"Dave's wife wears that perfume from Italy. The whole house smells incredible."

"Tom's girlfriend has that fresh, just-out-of-the-shower thing all day."

"Steve's wife always smells like jasmine. Even at the gym."

I told myself he was just observing. I told myself a lot of things.

Then the comments started.

At Thanksgiving last year, my sister hugged me a long time at the door. Longer than usual. Then she went into the kitchen with Mark and said something quiet to him. I didn't hear it.

That night, in our bedroom, Mark turned to me and said: "You smell different than you used to, Becca. Maybe just ... older. It's not a big deal."

It's not a big deal.

A few weeks later, he was making coffee in the kitchen. I came up behind him to grab a mug. He stepped to the side without looking up.

"Sorry," he said. "Just hot."

The coffee wasn't ready yet.

Then at our neighbor's barbecue last summer, I sat down next to him on the wicker couch. After a minute he stood up. "Gonna grab another beer." He didn't sit back down with me when he came back.

By January, honey, he was stopping in the doorway when he came into our bedroom. Not crossing in. Just talkin' from the threshold.

"Becca, you've gotten a little ... stale. I don't know how else to put it. Maybe look into something. For yourself."

For yourself.

He smiled like it was a joke. Like he was being thoughtful.

I didn't laugh.

In February I got a text from some old college friends.

Four women I went to University of Arizona with. We'd stayed close for over 30 years.

"Girls trip. Tulum. Five days. March. Who's in?"

I said yes immediately.

When I told Mark over dinner, he put down his fork.

"Five days? In Mexico?"

"Yes."

"Becca, you sure that's a good idea?"

"Why wouldn't it be?"

He looked at me carefully. "Just ... five days in close quarters with four other women. Heat. Sun all day. I'm just thinkin' about you."

I'm just thinking about you.

"I'm going."

"Of course. Just pack accordingly. Bring whatever you usually use. Maybe more of it."

I left the table before I said somethin' I'd regret.

The next day I called my friend Carol.

Carol and I have known each other since the kids were in middle school. She's 69. Retired nurse -- twenty-eight years on a geriatric ward. Lives ten minutes from me.

I told her everything. About the threshold. About the wicker couch. About "getting a little stale."

She was quiet for a long time.

Then: "Becca. Come over. I want to give you somethin'."

I drove to her house that afternoon. She had a small bar of soap on her kitchen island. Wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon-orange wrapper. Japanese characters.

"It's called Kaori," she said. "I used to keep these in the locker on the ward. For after long shifts."

"What is it?"

She smiled. "Japanese soap. My patients used to swear by it. I bought a stack about eight months ago when they announced they were pausing production. I've been waiting to give you one."

I held the bar.

"You knew."

"Honey. I'm a nurse. I notice things. I've been waiting for you to ask ... or for someone to be cruel enough that I had to step in."

I drove home with the bar in my purse.

That night I showered with it.

The next morning I caught myself standing in front of the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just ... standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

Two weeks before the flight I was packing. Mark came into the bedroom. Stopped at the threshold like always.

"That's all you're bringin'?"

"That's all I need."

"You sure? You should bring extra stuff. For the heat. You know how you get."

I zipped the bag.

"I'm sure."

The morning of the flight I called an Uber. Mark was making coffee.

"You sure you don't want me to drive you?"

"I'm fine."

"Alright. Have fun. Try not to overdo it."

I left.

The Uber dropped me at the airport.

I walked into the terminal.

And I saw him.

Mark.

Standing at the check-in counter. With two suitcases.

He turned and saw me.

"Surprise," he said.

I just stared.

"What are you doing here?"

"I couldn't stop thinkin' about it. You going all that way alone. I got worried."

"Mark. I'm going with my friends."

"I know. But still. I just want to make sure you're okay. I booked the same flight. I'll stay at a different resort. Do my own thing. Just be nearby in case."

He said it like he was doin' me a favor.

"You booked the same flight without telling me."

"I wanted it to be a surprise."

The check-in agent was watching us.

Both his bags came out overweight. $75 each. He paid $150 in fees while I walked to the next counter.

"Just the one bag?"

"Just the one."

At security, Mark got pulled aside. Shoes. Belt. Watch.

I went through and walked to the gate.

We landed in Tulum. I met my friends at the rideshare pickup.

"Is he really here?"

"He's really here."

"What is he thinkin'?"

"He thinks I need supervision."

I checked into the resort. Unpacked in five minutes. Showered with the bar.

When I came out into the suite, my college roommate Maya was sitting on the bed.

She tilted her head slightly.

"You smell incredible. What is that?"

"Soap."

"From where?"

"A friend gave it to me."

She kept her eyes on me a second too long. Then she smiled. "Send me the link when you get home."

I changed into my swimsuit and met my friends at the pool.

An hour later, Mark showed up. At our resort.

He was sunburned already. Forgot sunscreen. Wearing the same shirt from the plane.

"There you are," he said. "I checked into my place down the road. Just wanted to make sure you got here okay."

My friends stared.

"I'm fine, Mark."

He stood there. Awkward.

That night, my friends and I went to dinner. Mark texted: "Where are you guys eating?" I didn't respond.

Day two. Mark showed up at our pool. Still sunburned. Wearing a resort gift-shop T-shirt that said "Tulum."

"One of my bags is still missing."

We went on a snorkeling excursion. Mark didn't come. "Too tired."

Day three. Lunch at the beachside restaurant.

A woman in her early thirties walked past our table. Stopped. Came back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearin' something? Because I've smelled it twice now and I had to ask."

"What do you mean?"

"It's just ... clean. Almost like clean laundry but warmer. My grandmother had it. I haven't smelled it on anyone since she passed."

She laughed at herself.

"Sorry. That's a weird thing to say."

"It's a soap. Japanese."

"What's it called?"

"Kaori."

She typed it into her phone. "I'm gonna find this. Thank you."

She walked away.

Nobody at our table said anything for a moment.

Then Maya: "Becca. That happened yesterday too."

"What?"

"At the front desk. The girl checking us in. She kept leaning in slightly when you were talkin' to her. I noticed. I just didn't say anything."

Mark was at the next table over. He'd watched the woman walk over. He'd heard everything.

He looked at his lunch and didn't look up.

I sat there for a moment. Watched him not looking up.

And I thought about my sister at Thanksgiving. About the long hug at the door. About what she must have whispered to Mark in the kitchen.

She'd told him. Not me.

I think I understood now.

Day four, I posted photos from the snorkeling trip.

Me and my friends. Tan. Smiling. Looking healthy.

Within an hour, the comments rolled in.

My sister: "You look AMAZING."

Emma: "Mom!! This is so cool!"

Then Mark's phone started buzzing. He was at the pool near us.

I could see his face changing as he read.

Dave: "Bro, Becca looks incredible. What are you doing at home?"

Tom: "Your wife's living her best life."

Steve: "Dude. When did Becca get so fresh?"

Mark put his phone down. Looked at me.

"You were right," he said quietly.

"About what?"

"About this trip. About me being wrong."

My friends were pretending not to listen.

"I think I should head home," he said. "Let you finish this with your friends. I'm sorry."

He left that afternoon.

My friends and I spent the last two days at the beach. No interruptions. No hovering.

When I got home, Mark was waiting in the living room.

"We need to talk."

"We do. But not tonight. Tonight you're sleeping on the couch."

He nodded. Grabbed a pillow.

Three days later we talked. Really talked.

He apologized. Admitted he'd been projectin' his anxiety about getting older onto me. That following me to Tulum was wrong. That what he'd been saying for months was wrong.

"I watched you walk into that resort lobby," he said. "And you looked like you'd outgrown me. That scared me."

"It shouldn't have."

"I know that now."

Carol called me last week.

"How was the trip, honey?"

I told her everything. The airport. The woman at the restaurant. Mark sleeping on the couch.

She laughed for a long time.

Then: "I have one bar left from my stash. They opened a new batch but it's already most of the way gone. Once it's out, you wait until next year."

"I'll order another one tonight."

"Good. And tell anyone who asks. Tell every woman you know who's stopped gettin' hugs the way she used to."

I sat there a while after we hung up.

About Mark spending $150 in airline fees and $40 on resort gift-shop sunscreen because he didn't believe me.

About a woman at a restaurant in Tulum smelling something on me that reminded her of her grandmother.

About my sister whispering in the kitchen instead of telling me at the door.

Honey, if somebody you love has been quietly stepping back from you and you cain't figure out why ...

Maybe you don't need to win an argument.

Maybe you just need a better bar.

body.text:
My grandson was at my house every afternoon. He was everything to me. Then one day he was gone.

His name is Jack. His mom dropped him off on her way to work and I'd hear the backpack hit the floor before I even saw him. Shoes kicked off in the corner. Socks across the tiles. Every single day since first grade.

I'd usually have something in the oven. Banana bread, oatmeal cookies, sometimes just biscuits if I'd been busy at the farmers market that morning. I go every Tuesday and Saturday — have for years. I pick my own tomatoes. I talk to the woman who sells the honey. I carry my own bags home. I'm seventy-one and I do everything myself.

I'm not some frail old woman sitting in a chair waiting for company. I have a full life.

But Jack was the best part of it.

He had his spot on the couch. Left side, always. His mug in the cabinet — the blue one with the chipped handle he wouldn't let me throw away. His hook by the door, the low one I screwed in at his height when he was six. He'd do homework at the kitchen table with the cocoa steaming next to his pencil case, and then cartoons or Lincoln Logs until his mom came around six.

Four years of flour on his nose from "helping" me bake. Four years of him falling asleep on the couch on Fridays while I just sat there reading. Perfectly happy.

I don't know exactly when it changed. There wasn't one day where I thought okay, something is wrong. It just crept in so slowly I didn't see it until it was already done.

Jack was ten. And he started coming in a little slower. Standing in the hallway a beat longer. Keeping his jacket on. He stopped going to the couch and sat at the kitchen table instead. Near the window.

He started asking if we could open the window.

In September that didn't seem weird. Still warm outside. But then he asked in October. And November. Then he asked if he could do his homework on the porch. I said honey, it's forty degrees out there.

He just did the homework faster instead. Sat by the front door with his shoes on. Waiting.

He used to cry when his mom came to pick him up too early. Now he was at the door before she even rang the bell.

I noticed. Of course I noticed.

But I told myself what you tell yourself. He's growing up. Boys get restless at that age. He probably wants to be with his friends playing video games. Not sitting in his grandmother's kitchen watching her chop vegetables.

Then his mom mentioned he was going to a friend's house after school now. Study group. I said sure, of course. No problem.

Next day, same thing.

Then "sometimes" became "mostly." Then he only came Fridays. Then not at all.

I still set the table for two for a while. Put out the cocoa. Put it back. Eventually I stopped.

The hook by the door just stayed empty. The mug stayed in the cabinet. The dent in his couch cushion slowly filled back in.

I went through it in my head every night. What did I do? Was it something I said? Was my house just too boring for a ten-year-old — no WiFi, no tablet, just board games and Lincoln Logs?

I asked my daughter, trying to sound like I wasn't dying inside. She said: Mom, he's ten. Kids get independent. It's normal.

But it didn't feel normal. Normal is slow. This felt like a door closing. And it felt like everyone could see what was behind it except me.

Because I started noticing other things too.

My daughter's hugs were getting shorter. My son-in-law started standing a little further away when we talked. The neighbor's kid waved from across the street now instead of coming to the porch.

Little things. But once you start seeing them, you can't stop.

Jack came one more time. My birthday.

He hugged me at the door. Short. Stiff. I could feel him holding his breath. Turning his head away. Pulling back half a second before the hug was really done.

At dinner he sat as far from me as the table allowed. When I leaned over to cut his cake he leaned back — just a little — and something crossed his face. Not mean. Just uncomfortable. The look of a kid trying very hard to be polite about something he can't explain.

That night I took off the cardigan I'd worn all day. Held it up. Smelled it.

Wool. Maybe a little kitchen. Nothing wrong.

But I couldn't stop thinking about his face. The way he turned his head.

It was my friend Donna who finally said it.

We've known each other thirty years. Book club, coffee after church. She's the kind of person who says things everyone else just thinks.

I was telling her about Jack. Just the pulling-away part. And she got quiet for a second. That look people get when they already know where this is going.

"Can I tell you something?" she said. "Promise you won't get upset."

I promised. Already bracing.

"It's not about you. It's not about what you said or did. It's about how you smell."

I just stared at her.

"I don't mean you're not clean. I know you're clean. But there's a smell. I've noticed it for a while. On your cardigan. In your car. I just didn't know how to bring it up."

She didn't have an explanation. She didn't know what it was. She just said what nobody else would say.

I didn't sleep that night. I kept smelling my own wrist, my sleeve, my pillow. Nothing. I couldn't smell anything wrong. But Donna isn't a liar. And she wouldn't say something like that unless she meant it.

So I did what you do at eleven o'clock at night when you can't sleep and you need answers. I typed "why do I smell different as I get older" into Google and went down a rabbit hole I didn't come out of until 2 AM.

And what I found changed everything.

There's a compound called nonenal. Your skin starts producing it around forty. By sixty, seventy, it's just there. On your skin. In your clothes. In the air around you. In Japan they have a word for it — kareishū. Aging smell. Not something embarrassing over there. Just a thing that happens. Like gray hair. Like needing reading glasses.

Your body chemistry changes. The oils on your skin start to oxidize — kind of like how a sliced apple turns brown on the counter. And that process produces this smell — waxy, musty, kind of stale. Not terrible. But persistent. It gets into fabric. It fills up rooms.

And here's the part that broke me.

You can't smell it on yourself. Your nose adjusts to your own scent. Your brain just filters it out. So it's always there — on you, around you, in your home — and you have absolutely no idea.

But everyone else does. Your daughter. Your son-in-law. Your ten-year-old grandson who doesn't have the words to say "Grandma, I love you, but I can't breathe in your house."

So they just pull away. Quietly. Without explaining. Because nobody tells their mother she smells old. Nobody tells their grandmother. You just — stand a little further back. Hug a little shorter. Visit a little less.

And the person it's happening to sits at home trying to figure out what she did wrong.

That was me. That was exactly me. Every single night at my kitchen table, wondering what I did, when the answer was on my skin the entire time.

I kept reading. Regular soap doesn't touch nonenal. Doesn't matter how expensive it is or how good it smells. It's not regular body odor — it bonds to your skin differently. It's not sitting on the surface waiting to be washed off. Regular soap just slides right over it.

That's why nothing changes no matter how much you shower. That's why perfume doesn't help — it just layers on top. You're covering a symptom. The cause is still there, on your skin, every single day.

But then I found the thing that actually made me stop scrolling.

Persimmon. Japanese persimmon extract — kakishibu. It grabs onto nonenal and breaks it apart. Doesn't cover anything. Doesn't mask it. Just dissolves it before it gets on your clothes or your furniture or the air in your living room.

In Japan this is just normal soap. Older people use it the way we use Dove. It's in every drugstore. Nobody thinks twice about it.

We just don't know about it here. Nobody told us.

I sat at my kitchen table that night and suddenly everything made sense. All of it. All at once.

Jack's window. His jacket he kept on. The homework he started rushing through. The porch in November. The Fridays that turned into nothing. The empty hook. The mug in the cabinet. The birthday hug — short, stiff, head turned, breath held.

None of it was about me. None of it was about growing up or video games or WiFi.

It was one compound. On my skin. In my house. In the air between me and my grandson. And everyone I loved had been rearranging themselves around it instead of telling me.

I ordered the soap that week. Real kakishibu extract. Most soaps don't have it — I looked. This was the only one I could find that actually uses the real persimmon compound, not just some fragrance version. Started using it every day — skin, hair, behind the ears. Washed my cardigans. Changed the pillowcases.

After about a week I picked up my pillowcase and held it to my face. Cotton. Just cotton. The cardigan smelled like wool. The house smelled like nothing.

I didn't call Jack. Didn't explain anything. Didn't say "I figured it out" or "please come back." There was nothing to explain. You don't apologize for something your body did without your permission. You just fix it and let the fixing speak for itself.

His mom asked if I could take him the following Friday. Some scheduling thing.

He walked in. Dropped his backpack.

And he didn't stop in the hallway. Didn't keep his jacket on. Didn't go near the window.

He took off his shoes. Walked to the couch. Sat in his spot. Left side.

"Can I have cocoa?"

I made cocoa. Took the blue mug out of the cabinet. He wrapped both hands around it and started his homework. Steam rising next to his pencil case. I started on a batch of oatmeal cookies because it was Friday and that's what we used to do on Fridays.

When his mom came at six he looked up and said "Already?"

Nobody said anything. The thing that was wrong was just gone. Jack was at my table again. Breathing normally. Completely at ease.

When he left, he hugged me. Not the birthday hug. A real one. Arms around me. Face against my cardigan.

Breathing in.

He held on for three seconds. I counted.

If your grandchild has pulled away — if the hugs got shorter, if the visits stopped, if they started breathing through their mouth when they're near you — it might not be what you think.

It's not about growing up. It's not about screens or being busy or kids just being kids.

It might be the one thing no one in your family will ever say to your face.

I lost a year with Jack over this. A whole year of cocoa and homework and Friday nights on the couch. A year I'm never getting back. Because nobody told me. And I couldn't smell it myself.

If any of this sounds familiar — if you've been wondering why someone you love pulled away — I'll leave a link to the one I use below. It's just soap. You just use it and the problem goes away.

I wish someone had told me a year ago. So I'm telling you now.

cards.body:
I lost my granddaughter at 66 because I can't smell. She told her mom my house makes her sick. I can't smell a thing. But that I heard.

I was in the kitchen. She was in the hallway with her mom. She didn't know I was there.

"Mommy I don't want to go to grandma's house. It makes me sick."

My sweet girl. The one who used to fall asleep on my chest every Sunday. That girl just told her mother that being near me makes her sick.

I stood there holding the counter and I couldn't breathe. Makes her sick. What makes her sick? What is she talking about?

I lost my sense of smell a year before Covid hit. It never came back. Not even a little. I can't smell my food, my clothes, my house, my own skin. Nothing. So when my granddaughter says something makes her sick, I can't just sniff it out like a normal person. I'm blind.

That night I didn't sleep.

I crawled through every room on my hands and knees trying to understand what she meant. Pressed my face into the couch cushions. Nothing. Held my curtains against my nose. Nothing. Put my face flat on the carpet. Nothing.

What is it, baby? What are you smelling? I was begging my house to give me an answer my nose couldn't.

I cleaned everything. Every surface, every fabric, every corner. Had the pipes checked. Had someone look for mold. Opened every window for days in the middle of winter. None of it mattered. Because I couldn't tell if any of it helped. I was fixing things in the dark.

And the whole time there was one place I never thought to check.

Something in the back of my mind was already whispering it. I just wasn't ready to hear it.

Then I started remembering things I had been too afraid to connect.

My granddaughter pulling away from me. Not all at once. Slowly. First she stopped sitting in my lap. Then she stopped hugging me. Then she started staying on the other side of the room.

I told myself she was just growing up. Kids do that.

But then I thought about my son. Last time he hugged me at the door, he held his breath. I felt his chest lock up against mine. Just for a second. He thought I wouldn't notice. But when you lose your smell, you start feeling things other people miss. Your whole body pays attention in ways it never did before. I felt him stop breathing.

After the hug he opened both windows in the guest room. It was November.

Then I thought about my neighbor. Every Tuesday we have coffee. And every Tuesday for six months her chair moved a little further from mine. One week she said let's sit outside. It was 45 degrees.

Then my book club. How Carol opens a window when I arrive. How Janet switched seats last month. How nobody says a word but something shifts every time I walk in.

Nobody told me. Not one person. But every single one of them did something.

Standing alone in my hallway at 1 AM, all of it hit me at once. The windows. The chairs. The held breath. The distance. My granddaughter's words.

They could all smell something I couldn't.

It was never the pipes. Never mold. Never the house.

It might be me.

That thought almost broke me.

I stopped inviting people over. Birthdays became phone calls. I quit book club. I couldn't sit in Carol's living room for two hours wondering if everyone was waiting for me to leave.

You want to know the loneliest feeling in the world? Sitting in your own living room afraid to answer the door because you have no idea what hits people when they walk in. And you can't fix it because you can't smell it. And you can't ask because you're terrified of the answer.

I showered twice a day. Bought the most expensive body wash I could find. Scrubbed until my skin turned red. Stayed up past 2 AM searching things I was ashamed to type. "Why do old people smell." "Can you stink and not know it." Found women my age asking the same questions. All of them doing everything right. Not one had figured it out.

I closed my laptop and sat in the dark. This is my life now. A grandmother who makes her own granddaughter sick. And I can't even smell why.

Then Margaret showed up.

No call. No text. She just appeared at my kitchen door on a Thursday with a paper bag. Put it on the table. Sat down. Took both my hands.

And said three words nobody had said to me in years.

You smell, Linda.

I broke down. Not from shame. From relief. Finally someone loved me enough to say what everyone else was too polite to say.

And then she told me something that changed everything.

She said our bodies start making a compound as we age. Called Nonenal. It comes out through the skin. Musty. Stale. Sour. The kind of smell that gets into furniture, blankets, walls.

And here's what made my jaw drop. Every person she ever cared for who had this smell was clean. Bathed. Groomed. It didn't matter. Because Nonenal is not dirt. It's not sweat. It comes from inside the skin. And regular soap, no matter how expensive, no matter how hard you scrub, cannot touch it.

She paused.

She squeezed my hands, got up, and went home.

But I couldn't smell it. I still can't. So I had to wait and watch the people around me.

Week four.

My granddaughter walked through the door. Dropped her backpack. Walked straight to me. Climbed into my lap. Put her little head against my chest.

And fell asleep.

I sat there with her hair under my chin and her breath on my collarbone and cried so hard I had to cover my mouth so I wouldn't wake her.

But she's here now. On my chest. And whatever kept her away is gone.

If nobody in your life is honest enough to be your Margaret, let me be her for you right now.

It's called Kaori. It's the only soap I use. It's the only soap Margaret gives to the people she cares for. And it's the only thing that ever made a difference.

https://try-kaori.com/products/deodorizing-persimmon-soap

And you just stand there. Unable to smell a thing. Hearing all of it.

Don't wait until they're out of stock again. Margaret warned me. She was right.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.
Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.
One bar of it cost me my doctor of eleven years.

I have never told anybody what I paid for that bar.

Now I'm putting it on Facebook.

If you already bought a persimmon soap but got nothing out of it, this is for you. Please read the whole thing.

It's long. You're busy. I know.

It started in September.

I'm 67. Dr. Mercer knew my knees, my blood pressure, the year my mother died.

At the end of my checkup she put her pen down.

"One more thing, Diane. Our skin changes as we get older. It can carry a smell it didn't used to, and nobody ever mentions it."

Then two words. "Persimmon soap."

She said it kindly. She said it once. It wasn't on any of the papers she gave me.

Doctors never said anything. Mine did.

I'd been seeing those ads for weeks. I scrolled past every one. But they made me kind of doubt myself.

For about a year, my daughter Sarah's Sunday visits had been ending a little quicker at the door. No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

I'd asked her once, straight out, because I couldn't tell on myself. "Do I smell like an old lady to you?"

"Mom. You're fine."

My daughter's real frank about things and outspoken. I would've thought she would have told me if I needed it. But you never know.

An ad is one thing. Eleven years of Dr. Mercer is another.

I decided to buy it and not tell my husband the price.

That night I ordered the first one that came up on my phone. $18.99, plus $5.99 to ship it.

It came in a small box with a persimmon printed on it.

The box didn't say much. So I used it like any soap. Every morning, in the shower, down to a sliver I could barely hold.

It was nice but I wasn't sure if that solved the problem.

After, I'd put my nose to the collar of my robe anyway. The sniff test.

Every morning it told me the same thing. Nothing.

The first Sunday, Sarah hugged me at the door with her car keys already in her hand.

The second Sunday, the same.

The third Sunday I said it before she could. "Go on. Beat the dark." She was on her feet before I'd finished.

Fourth Sunday. Keys.

Fifth Sunday, I'd used the last of the bar that morning. Keys.

I wondered if it was just another soap.

My husband Don found the empty box in the bathroom cabinet. "That the fancy stuff?"

"It seems like voodoo," I said. "Not a clue if it is effective."

I didn't tell him what I'd thought every one of those mornings. What Dr. Mercer smelled on me in that exam room. For nothing.

My blood pressure check was a Thursday in October.

Dr. Mercer wrapped the cuff around my arm. "How did you get on with the soap, Diane?"

I waited until I had my coat back on.

Then I said, "Next time, keep your two words to yourself."

At the front desk I asked Patty for the form to have my records sent somewhere else.

"Are you sure, Diane?"

Dr. Mercer stood in the hall with my chart. She didn't say a thing.

I signed it.

That Sunday Sarah got up at a quarter to four.

"You okay, Mom? You're quiet."

"Just tired," I said.

At the door I got the side hug. The back arched and the behind hanging out creating distance between the hugger and the hugged. Her keys were already in her hand.

I knew that hug. I used to give it.

My mother lived alone her last six years, forty minutes from me. Every other Sunday I drove over. Every other Sunday I hugged her at her door exactly like that, with my keys in my hand.

I remember the smell of my mother and my grandmother and just thought it was old people smell.

"Leaving already?" she'd say.

"Traffic, Mom."

I never said a word to her.

That night I lay next to Don with the clock on 11:40.

Five weeks. $24.98. Eleven years.

"Why didn't it work?" I said. Out loud.

Don said, "Hmm?" He rolled over.

Nobody answered.

My hugs had started declining. I noticed but figured it is what it is.

I was an idiot paying so much for soap.

So I stopped. No more sniff test, no more asking Sarah. I didn't go looking for another bar.

Ten days later the phone rang at suppertime.

"Diane, it's Dr. Mercer." A pause. "Not the office. Me."

I nearly hung up.

"I'm not calling to get you back," she said. "I'd like to see what you bought. The box, if you still have it."

"Why?"

"Because I'm the one who sent you to buy it."

I figured she'd be nice to me right up until I bought something.

But she was asking me to bring her the proof she was wrong.

I put the empty box in my handbag. I went to be proved right.

She saw me after her last patient, in her own office.

There were six boxes on her desk. Different names. A persimmon printed on every one.

I wasn't the only one she'd rung.

I set mine down with the others. She looked at them a long time.

"Twenty years I've been saying those two words to women," she said. "I never once told anybody how to choose one."

"So it's a fad."

"How do you know?"

"I really didn't notice a difference."

"When you come home from a week away, what do you smell?"

"The house. Coffee, and Don's old jacket by the door."

"And the next morning?"

"Nothing. It's just the house."

"Where did it go?"

I didn't answer. She waited.

"Nowhere," I said. "I stopped noticing it."

"The brain tunes out a smell that never leaves you. Mine does too."

"Every morning for five weeks I smelled my own collar," I said. "I probably wouldn't be aware of any difference. Either way."

"You weren't a fool, Diane."

"Then who would know?"

"Who did you ask?"

"Sarah. She said I was fine."

"Would she tell you?"

I thought about my mother's front door.

"No," I said. "I never told mine."

"Then how was I supposed to choose one?"

"Now I'm telling women to find a maker who says who it's made for," she said. "One who tells you where to wash with it. Behind your ears, around your neck, your chest, across your back."

"Mine never said."

"Neither did I. You didn't do one thing wrong."

She touched the nearest one. "But that's still only a box talking. It can't tell you whether it works."

"Only Sarah can," I said. "At the door."

"Which one do you use?"

She opened her desk drawer. A bar, still in its paper.

"This isn't a prescription," she said. "It's made only for women over sixty. I'm 64, and it's what I wash with."

The paper said Kaori.

I held it to my nose. "Citrusy."

"Don't ask me if it works. I'd be the last to know."

I knew how I looked. A woman my age, being handed soap across a desk.

Not sure if I was investing in another scam. Always thinking it would be one more thing I'm wasting money on.

"Why that one?" I said. "Any of these would do."

"Maybe. I can't tell them apart, and I've tried. So I take the one where somebody else pays if it does nothing for me."

"I'm not buying another one."

"I'm not selling you anything." She pushed it over to me. "Ring me. Whatever happens."

I drove home with it on the passenger seat. I put it in the shower where the last one had been. I didn't tell Sarah. I didn't tell anybody.

I washed where Dr. Mercer had said, every morning. I didn't do the sniff test once.

The first Sunday on her bar, Sarah hugged me at the door with her keys in her hand. Same as always.

Voodoo, I thought. Again.

That night I nearly put it back in its paper.

The second Sunday it was dark by five. The porch light came on when we stepped out. There were wet leaves all over the step.

Sarah had her coat on. Her keys were still in her bag.

She hugged me with both arms. Her chin on my shoulder, the way she did when she came home from college.

She stood there long enough for the porch light to click off.

I don't know which of us let go first.

Neither of us mentioned it. I didn't ask her. I'm not going to.

Nobody said a word when Sarah started leaving early. Nobody said a word on Sunday either.

My mother never found out. I nearly didn't.

On Monday I rang Dr. Mercer. My turn. She answered on the first ring.

"Well?" she said.

"She didn't get her keys out till she was at the car."

The line went quiet for a second.

"Can you put me back on your list?"

"I never took you off it."

Dr. Mercer can't put any of this on Facebook. I can.

So please. Don't buy persimmon soap to find out with your own nose. Mine told me nothing for five weeks.

Don't ask your daughter either. She'll tell you you're fine.

If you buy one more bar, give it two weeks. Then watch how the people you love say goodbye.

I'm just Dr. Mercer's patient. Nobody pays me a cent for any of this.

The one she gave me is Kaori. One bar is $19.95. Six bars are $60.

If it does nothing for you, they give you your money back.

Sarah's coming Sunday.

Diane

P.S. Don read this over my shoulder. He says he never knew what I paid for that first bar. He also says I can't write all this without saying where to get the other one.

I left it out on purpose. I didn't sit down to sell anybody soap. But he's right, it saves you looking.

body.text:
My husband said I was "getting a little stale" at 63. Then he showed up uninvited to my girls trip in Tulum. He lasted three days.

Mark and I have been married for 26 years.

We met when I was 36. He was 40. Both working in tech in Dallas.

We got married a year later. Had two kids. Emma and Jake. Both grown now. Emma's in Seattle, Jake's in Denver.

For the first nineteen years, things were good.

We traveled. We hiked. We went to concerts.

Then Mark retired early. Two years ago. Sold his company. Made enough that we're comfortable.

That's when things changed.

He started playing golf five days a week. Long lunches with the same four men. His whole life became tee times and the clubhouse.

Most of the men he plays with are on their second wives. Younger. A lot younger.

And Mark started noticing things out loud.

Never about me. Just… out loud.

"You walk past Dave's wife and the whole room smells like a hotel lobby."

He'd say it in the car on the way home. Then he'd talk about the traffic.

I told myself he was just making conversation.

Then Thanksgiving.

Ray hugged me at the door and I felt him turn his head.

Ray has been Mark's closest friend since before I met either of them. He comes every year.

Later he was in the kitchen with Mark a long while. The water running the whole time.

That night, in our bedroom, Mark said: "I asked Ray about it today."

"About what?"

"He said he'd noticed it too. That you smell different than you used to. Older, maybe."

He said it gently. Like he was handing me something helpful.

"It's not a big deal."

It's not a big deal.

Twenty-six years and he never once said a word about it to me.

One afternoon in my own kitchen, and by ten o'clock he had.

A few weeks later, at the neighbors' barbecue, I sat down next to him on the wicker couch.

After a minute he stood up. "Going to get another beer."

He came back. He didn't sit down again.

By January he was stopping in the doorway of our bedroom.

Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold.

"Becca, you've gotten a little… stale. I don't know how else to put it. Maybe look into something. For yourself."

For yourself.

He smiled like it was a joke. Like he was being thoughtful.

I didn't laugh.

In February I got a text from four women I went to the University of Texas with. We'd stayed close for over thirty years.

"Girls trip. Tulum. Five days. March. Who's in?"

I said yes before I put the phone down.

When I told Mark over dinner, he put down his fork.

"Five days? In Mexico?"

"Yes."

"Becca, you sure that's a good idea?"

"Why wouldn't it be?"

He looked at me carefully. "Just… five days in close quarters with four other women. Heat. Sun all day. I'm just thinking about you."

I'm just thinking about you.

"I'm going."

"Of course. Just pack accordingly. Bring whatever you usually use. Maybe more of it."

I left the table before I said something I'd regret.

I didn't pack for a month. Every time I thought about the suitcase I heard him say bring more of it.

Two days before the flight I drove over to Carol's.

Carol's sixty-nine. Twenty-eight years on a geriatric ward before she retired. She lives ten minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her about the doorway. About the wicker couch. About getting a little stale.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon-orange. Characters on the front I couldn't read.

She didn't say a word about it.

"He's right that there's something," she said. "He's a liar about what it is. Those two aren't the same."

"I shower every day."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"Twenty-eight years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes, your eyes go, your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my ward home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. Order more while you can. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone. Once a batch sells out you're waiting months."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That night I finally packed. Mark came into the bedroom. Stopped at the threshold like always.

"That's all you're bringing?"

"That's all I need."

"You sure? You should bring extra stuff. For the heat. You know how you get."

I zipped the bag.

"I'm sure."

The morning of the flight I called an Uber. Mark was making coffee.

"You sure you don't want me to drive you?"

"I'm fine."

"Alright. Have fun. Try not to overdo it."

I left.

The Uber dropped me at the terminal.

I walked in.

And I saw him.

Mark.

Standing at the check-in counter. With two suitcases.

He turned and saw me.

"Surprise," he said.

I just stared.

"What are you doing here?"

"I couldn't stop thinking about it. You going all that way alone. I got worried."

"Mark. I'm going with my friends."

"I know. But still. I just want to make sure you're okay. I booked the same flight. I'll stay at a different resort. Do my own thing. Just be nearby in case."

He said it like he was doing me a favor.

"You booked the same flight without telling me."

"I wanted it to be a surprise."

The agent behind the counter was watching us.

Both his bags came out overweight. $75 each. He paid $150 in fees while I walked to the next counter.

"Just the one bag?"

"Just the one."

At security, Mark got pulled aside. Shoes. Belt. Watch.

I went through and walked to the gate.

We landed in Tulum. I met my friends at the rideshare pickup.

"Is he really here?"

"He's really here."

"What is he thinking?"

"He thinks I need supervision."

I checked into the resort. Unpacked in five minutes. Showered with the bar.

When I came out into the suite my college roommate Maya was sitting on the bed.

She tilted her head slightly.

"You smell incredible. What is that?"

"Soap."

"From where?"

"A friend gave it to me."

She kept her eyes on me a second too long. Then she smiled. "Send me the link when you get home."

I changed into my swimsuit and met my friends at the pool.

An hour later, Mark showed up. At our resort.

Sunburned already. Forgot sunscreen. Same shirt from the plane.

"There you are," he said. "I checked into my place down the road. Just wanted to make sure you got here okay."

My friends stared.

"I'm fine, Mark."

He stood there. Awkward.

That night my friends and I went to dinner. Mark texted: "Where are you guys eating?" I didn't answer it.

Day two. Mark at our pool again. Still sunburned. Wearing a gift-shop T-shirt that said "Tulum."

"One of my bags is still missing."

We went out snorkeling. Mark didn't come. "Too tired."

Day three. Lunch at the beachside restaurant.

A woman in her thirties went past our table. Stopped. Came back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "You smell incredible. Can I ask what you're wearing?"

She laughed at herself.

"Sorry. I've interrupted your lunch. It just stood out to me."

"It's a bar of soap."

"What's it called?"

"Kaori."

She typed it into her phone. "I'm going to find this. Thank you."

She walked away.

Nobody at our table said anything for a moment.

Then Maya: "Becca. That happened yesterday too."

"What?"

"At the front desk. The girl checking us in. She kept leaning in slightly while you were talking to her. I noticed. I just didn't say anything."

Mark was at the next table over. He'd watched the woman come over. He'd heard all of it.

He looked at his lunch and didn't look up.

I sat there a moment. Watched him not looking up.

And I thought about Ray at Thanksgiving. About the hug at the door and his head turning.

About my husband walking into the kitchen to ask his oldest friend whether his wife had started to smell old.

Neither of them ever said it to me. They said it to each other.

I think I understood now.

Day four I posted photos from the snorkeling trip.

Me and my friends. Tan. Smiling. Looking healthy.

Within an hour the comments came in.

My sister: "You look AMAZING."

Emma: "Mom!! This is so cool!"

Then Mark's phone started buzzing. He was at the pool near us.

I could see his face changing as he read.

Dave: "Bro, Becca looks incredible. What are you doing at home?"

Tom: "Your wife's living her best life."

Steve: "Dude. When did Becca get so fresh?"

Mark put the phone down. Looked at me.

"You were right," he said quietly.

"About what?"

"About this trip. About me being wrong."

My friends were pretending not to listen.

"I think I should head home," he said. "Let you finish this with your friends. I'm sorry."

He left that afternoon.

We spent the last two days on the beach. No interruptions. Nobody hovering.

When I got home he was sitting in the living room with the lamp on.

"I don't want us to keep going the way we've been going," he said.

"Neither do I."

"I watched you walk into that lobby in Tulum," he said. "And you looked like you'd outgrown me. That's what scared me. So I made you smaller instead of getting bigger."

"You did."

"I know. I don't want to be that."

We talked until two in the morning. Actually talked, which we hadn't done in about three years.

Carol called last week to ask about the trip.

I told her all of it. The airport. The woman at the restaurant. What Mark did when I got home.

She laughed for a long time.

Then: "They opened a new batch. It's already most of the way gone. Once it's out you're waiting until next year."

I ordered two that night.

Here's the part I keep coming back to.

I didn't win an argument. I didn't say one clever thing to him. I never once told him he was wrong.

I bought a bar of soap. I stood up for myself.

That was the whole of it.

And you've already done the hardest part. You've spent a year noticing something was wrong and being told it was nothing.

All that's left is the shower.

It's called Kaori. The link's below. It costs less than fifty cents a day.

They make it in small batches. When a batch goes you wait months for the next one.

Order the bar. Take the shower. Let them come to you.

If somebody you love has been quietly stepping back from you and you can't figure out why.

Maybe you don't need to win an argument.

Maybe you just need a better bar.

For two years he just drifted. Started sleeping with his back to me, then on the very edge, then some nights in the recliner because of his hip. His hip was fine. I washed the sheets twice a week. I switched detergents three times. I bought a mattress spray that promised lavender fields and delivered a chemical meadow. Nothing changed, because the sheets were never the problem.

It took my daughter, who has no filter at all, to say it in the car: "Mom, it's your side of the bed. It smells like Grandma's house did." I cried in a grocery store parking lot over a pillowcase. Then I did what I always do, which is go looking for the actual cause.

There is a name for it. After a certain age the skin's oils change, and the compound they leave behind does not rinse off with ordinary soap. body.text:
Before my husband died, he made me promise one thing: that I wouldn't stop living.

Four years later, I nearly pushed my own grandson out the door.

Two days into the one summer I get with him all year, and already he was begging to go home.

And his mother was driving down Wednesday to take him home for good.

But I wasn't about to let that be our last summer.

I waited a whole year for this summer.

Daniel is eleven. He lives ten hours away, up in Ohio.

So we don't get weekends like other grandmas. We get one thing. We get summer.

And his mama nearly didn't allow me even that.

Her name is Ashley. She means to keep Daniel on her side of the family.

Three years I asked before she'd give me a whole month. This was the first.

One month. And I'd been counting the days to it since she drove him home last August.

I made up his bed a week early.

I filled the fridge with everything he loves. The cereal in the blue box. The applesauce pouches. The orange soda his mama won't let him have at home.

I was ready.

Ashley drove him down the first Saturday in June.

She stood in my driveway and read me a list. What he can eat. When he sleeps. How much tablet time. Watch him near the pond. Don't forget his sunscreen.

She talked to me like I was a child.

I raised four kids. I buried their daddy. I ran the church kitchen twenty-two years.

I am not some frail old woman. Whatever Ashley thinks.

"Call me if it gets to be too much, Pearl," she said, getting back in the car. "I mean it."

Like she was already waiting for me to fail.

I just smiled and waved.

She had no notion how close she'd come to being right.

Her car was barely out of the driveway before my real summer began.

And oh, that first day.

We were in the garden by nine. Daniel had dirt up to his elbows, picking tomatoes like a little farmer.

We baked cookies after lunch. He cracked the eggs. Half the shell went in the bowl. I didn't say a word.

That screen door banged open and shut all day long.

I don't know a sweeter sound in this world.

That first night, we sat out on the porch swing Earl built. The crickets singing. The lightning bugs rising up out of the grass.

He laid his head on my shoulder.

I looked up at the stars and thought, thank You, Lord. Here it is. Here's my summer.

By the next night, that same little boy would be counting the hours till he could go home.

And I had no idea why.

The next morning, he went quiet on me.

He picked at his food. He asked to sleep with the window open, even with the air on. He sat at the far end of the swing. Away from me.

I didn't understand it.

The second afternoon, I did.

I came in from the garden to pour us some sweet tea. Daniel was in the front room, on the phone with his mama. He had her on speaker. He never heard me come in.

"It's Nanna, Mom. She smells really bad."

A pause.

And then Ashley's voice, tinny through the little speaker. Not a beat of hesitation.

"Oh, baby. I'll come get you. Don't you worry."

I stood in my own kitchen, a glass of sweet tea in each hand. One of them his.

I couldn't move. I couldn't breathe.

My own grandbaby, a room away, begging to get away from me.

And his mama already saying yes.

Ashley called that night, after he was in bed.

You'd have thought the house was on fire.

"Pearl. Oh my gosh. Daniel called me in tears. He says there's a smell over there that's upsetting him, and you know how sensitive he is. He's been beside himself all day."

Then her voice went sharp.

"Honestly? I knew a whole month was too much. I should've trusted my gut. I'm coming to get him."

"...All right," I said.

"I can't get down there before Wednesday. I've got my girls' weekend and I am not missing it. But Wednesday I'm coming, and I'm taking him home."

I held the phone away from my ear.

Now you hear that, honey. The boy cannot bear one more night under my roof. But he can wait, it seems, till her girls' weekend is over.

I did not argue. I know how to keep my voice steady.

"All right, Ashley," I said. "We'll see you Wednesday."

Then I hung up.

And I sat down in Earl's old chair. The house gone quiet around me.

My own grandbaby wanted to run from me. From his own Nanna.

That one cut deeper than the rest.

But here's what scared me most.

I knew Ashley. If that boy went home miserable, she'd have her proof. She would never send him to me again.

And it was about to be the last summer I ever got.

I know children are sharper about smells than the rest of us. But I am a clean woman. Always have been.

So how could it be me?

I did the one thing anybody would do.

I showered.

Twice over that night, scrubbing myself raw. I washed the sheets and the towels and the slipcovers off the couch. I aired out every room in the house.

And still I couldn't smell a single thing wrong. Not on myself. Not anywhere.

That's the worst part. You can't fix what you can't smell.

So I called the one person who'd tell me the truth.

Donna.

My Bible study friend of eleven years. The only soul who'll tell me the truth whether I want it or not.

I told her everything. The list. The phone call. The showering that did nothing.

She was quiet a moment. Then: "Sit tight, honey. I'm coming over."

She was at my door inside the hour, a little canvas bag in her hand.

She set it on my kitchen table and sat down across from me.

And she had a look on her face I didn't care for.

"Pearl. I've got to tell you something. I should have told you a year ago."

My stomach dropped. "Tell me."

"You ever hear of nonenal?"

"Of what?"

"Nonenal. It's an oil. The body starts making it once you're past a certain age. Most women our age have it, plenty of the men too. It's the smell you notice in the nursing homes, honey. And not one of those folks was unclean."

"An oil."

"You know I nursed old folks the best part of forty years." She held my eyes. "I have been smelling it on you for a while now."

I went very still.

"Donna —"

"I'm not saying it to hurt you. I'm saying it because nobody else ever will. It isn't dirt, Pearl. It isn't your washing. It's the skin changing as we get older. It's just chemistry."

I couldn't get a word out.

"You were right that the little ones notice it first. Their noses are sharper than ours. That's all this is with Daniel. He doesn't know what it is. He only knows he wants the window open."

The window. The far end of the swing.

The floor went soft under me.

"Then why couldn't I wash it off?" I said. "Donna, I scrubbed myself raw tonight."

"Because you cannot wash an oil off with soap and water. Think of a greasy pan. You can run the hot tap over it all day and the grease just sits there. Ordinary soap was made for sweat and dirt. You need something that cuts it."

"And what does?"

"Persimmon." She nodded at the bag on the table. "There's a Japanese soap called Kaori. I had half my patients on it over the years. The cheap ones are mostly fruit water, not near enough of the extract. Kaori's the only one that gets it right."

"I heard they were pausing it for the season, so I bought a whole stack and put them away. Otherwise you wait till next year. I've been saving one for you."

I picked it up. Wrapped in soft paper. It smelled sweet, and warm, like the inside of a ripe peach.

"Use it tonight," she said. "Don't say a word to the boy about why. He'll come around."

She squeezed my hand.

"And Pearl. Don't you dare be ashamed of this."

She kissed my forehead and drove home.

That night, I used it in the shower.

And I prayed in there. Lord, if this can help, please help. Don't let this be the last summer.

I dried off, and that soft peach smell came up off my own skin.

I caught myself standing straighter at the mirror. I hadn't done that in a while.

Not the frail old woman Ashley took me for. Just me again.

Ashley wasn't coming till Wednesday. That gave me three days with my grandson.

Maybe the last three I'd ever get.

I wasn't going to waste a minute.

The first morning, nothing. He still sat at the far end of the table.

But the second day, something changed.

He wandered out to the garden where I was down on my knees in the dirt. Started pulling the ripe tomatoes into a bowl. Without me asking.

At supper, he dragged his chair around next to mine. Not across the table. Next to me.

Later that evening, a storm rolled through.

After it passed, the whole yard went cool and quiet and dripping. The lightning bugs came back out.

Daniel scooted across the swing. He leaned into my side. He put his head on my shoulder.

He pushed his nose against my arm. The way he used to when he was little.

He was quiet a long while. Then:

"Nanna?"

"What, baby?"

"You smell good."

I had to look up at the sky a moment. So he wouldn't see my eyes.

But his mother was still coming to take him.

Wednesday afternoon, Ashley's car pulled in.

She came up the walk fast. Sunglasses on, keys in her hand. Wearing the face of a woman who'd driven ten hours to be proven right.

"Okay, baby. Mommy's here. Grab your bag, let's go."

Daniel didn't move off my shoulder.

"I don't want to go, Mom. I want to stay with Nanna. The whole summer. Like we said."

Ashley stopped on the walk. The sunglasses came off.

For once in her life, that woman had nothing to say.

I could've said plenty. I didn't.

I know what it costs a mother to drive ten hours and get sent home.

"Ashley, honey. You've had a long drive," I said. "Come in. Have some sweet tea and a bite to eat. Sleep in the guest room. You can head back in the morning."

She stayed the night.

The next day, she drove back to Ohio. Alone.

Daniel stayed every single day of that summer.

And oh, what a summer.

The screen door banged from sunup to dark. We were out in the garden before the dew had lifted, his bowl filling up with tomatoes still warm from the vine. I drove into town twice more for orange soda, and we drank it on the porch steps in the heat of the day.

We fished the pond till the water turned gold, and I never once let him out of my sight.

In the hot part of the afternoon I tried to teach him the piano. He never did get past the first line of "Heart and Soul."

But Lord, we laughed.

And every night he fell asleep against my shoulder on Earl's old swing, the lightning bugs rising up out of the grass, the crickets singing. I'd sit there a long while after, holding still, so as not to wake him.

On Sundays he sat beside me in church and didn't complain once.

Donna told me later that Ashley had messaged her. A quiet little message. Asking about "that soap Pearl uses." She ordered a bar for herself. Never said a word to me about it.

Ashley never apologized, either. That's not her way.

But the next June, for the first time in eleven years, I didn't have to ask.

She called me in April. To set the dates herself.

The little boy who demanded to go home after two days?

He cried in the driveway when summer was over.

I'm the one who had to walk him to the car. I'm the one who had to make him go.

"I'm coming back next summer, right, Nanna?"

I told him, every summer, baby. I'll have the bed made up.

I sat on that porch a long while after she drove off.

Thinking about a little boy on the phone, his voice gone low, saying his Nanna smelled bad.

About the bed I made up a week early. The orange soda nobody else would touch.

About how close I came to losing my summers with him for good.

Earl made me promise, near the end, that I wouldn't stop living.

I mean to keep it. For every summer I've got left.

So here's what I'll tell you, honey.

If one of your grandbabies has started pulling back. If you can't for the life of you think what you've done wrong. If you've started hugging them quick and letting go first, before they can do it to you.

It maybe isn't anything you did.

Maybe you just need a better bar.

It's only a bar of soap. It costs less than a bottle of perfume, and they stand behind it with a guarantee. There's no harm in trying.

They press it once a year, so if it's on the shelf, I wouldn't wait too long.

Just try it. The link's below. It's the one that worked for me.

Then make up the bed, and call that child home for the summer.
