body.text:
My ex-husband told me I was the most beautiful woman at our grandson's graduation.

His new wife was standing three feet away.

And honestly. She started it.

It started about six weeks ago.

My grandson Leo was graduating. Big fancy school out East. Black tie dinner. Donors. The whole thing.

Tiffany is David's new wife. About fifteen years younger than me. She used to be a model and she makes sure you know it. She added me to a group on Facebook Messenger. Called it "Graduation Weekend."

She typed out this long message. Where to go. What to wear. How hot it was going to be. Then she wrote a list. She called it "freshness tips for the family."

And at the bottom she added something that almost sounded nice.

"I know the humidity can be hard on all of us as we get older. I'm packing extra myself just in case. It's nothing to be embarrassed about."

Then she wrote a second message. To me. In the group. Where David and everyone could see it.

"Karen darling, please pay attention to number four. We really can't have you showing up to the Welcome Dinner looking wilted. It puts pressure on Leo."

And then:

"If you don't have a good way to stay fresh on a long trip, let me know. I can send you something. I just want the photos to come out nice."

I stared at my phone.

Number four on her list said "rinse hair with vinegar to fight travel odor."

I am sixty-six years old. I have taken a shower every single morning of my life. I have never smelled bad. Not once.

I thought she was just being mean. The way she always is.

But then something happened that changed what I thought I knew about myself.

That night my phone buzzed. It was Leo.

"Grandma. I'm sorry. I think you should see this."

He sent me a picture of his screen. It was from a different group. One I'm not in. Just Tiffany and David and some of their friends.

Tiffany had written: "Fingers crossed Karen doesn't show up smelling like her basement again üôÑ Last time she hugged Leo at Christmas I watched him hold his breath the whole time."

Three laughing faces underneath.

One of them was David's.

My Leo. My sweet grandson. Holding his breath when his grandma hugged him at Christmas.

I read it four times. Then I put my phone on the counter and just stood there.

Twenty-three years I was married to that man. Two children. One grandson. And he sits there laughing while his new wife tells their friends I smell.

I walked into my bedroom. Pressed my face into my pillow. Took a big breath in.

Nothing. Just my pillow. Same as always.

I went to the closet. Pulled out the cardigan I wear around the house. Held it to my nose.

Nothing.

I called my sister.

"You won't believe what she wrote about me."

My sister didn't laugh.

She got quiet. Real quiet. The kind of quiet that means someone is about to say something hard.

"Karen. I need to tell you something. You're not going to like it. But I love you. And somebody has to."

My heart started beating fast.

"What."

"Do you know what happens to a woman's skin after sixty."

I didn't say anything.

"There's a smell that starts. Your own nose can't pick it up. But other people can. Your grandkids can. Regular soap doesn't fix it. Perfume just covers it up for an hour."

My stomach dropped.

"That's not right. I shower every morning."

"So did I. So did Margaret. It's not about being dirty, Karen. It's something in the skin. And nobody tells us."

I sat on the edge of my bed.

"Leo didn't hold his breath because you were dirty. You were showered. You were dressed nice. You just had something on your skin that nobody ever told you about."

"Why didn't anyone tell me."

"Because nobody does. That's the problem."

She was quiet for a second. Then her voice changed.

"Now listen. I know what Tiffany is. She's going to show up with a suitcase full of perfumes and fancy creams. She thinks smelling clean is a show. She wants everybody to see how hard she tries."

"You know what drives women like that crazy?"

"What."

"Somebody who shows up with nothing and smells better. Somebody who doesn't need a bag full of bottles."

"What do I do."

"You show up with one bar of soap. Nothing else. And you watch her fall apart."

She sent me a link on WhatsApp.

"It's called Kaori. It's a soap from Japan. A little island called Okinawa. There's something in the fruit that gets rid of the smell I'm talking about. The one nobody tells us about. I tried it before my trip to Italy. For the first time in years, I actually smelled clean. Not covered up. Clean."

She told me they only pick the fruit once a year. And this year's batch was almost gone.

I ordered it that night. My daughter Emma helped me on her laptop. I told her it was a gift.

The box came four days before the trip. Small green package on my doorstep. I almost missed it between the electric bill and a church flyer.

I sat at the kitchen table and unwrapped it. Pink paper. Heavier than I expected. I held it in both hands.

The smell came up before I brought it close. Not perfume. Something like clean wood and warm linen. Like the closet at my grandmother's house when I was seven.

I thought about Tiffany's little list. Her freshness tips. Her laughing faces.

Four days. That's all I had.

I showered with it that night. And the next morning. And the morning after.

The morning before the trip, I was getting dressed. My nightgown was hanging on the bathroom door. I held it up without thinking. It just smelled like laundry. Clean laundry. Nothing else.

I stood there for a long time. Because it had not smelled like just laundry in a while. I just hadn't known.

Airport day.

I was at the counter with my coffee and my bag.

David and Tiffany showed up like they were moving house.

Some poor man pushing their cart. Three big suitcases. A whole separate bag just for her perfumes. A makeup bag the size of a suitcase. Tiffany already snapping at David about the weight.

She saw me. Looked at my little bag.

"That's it?" she said. Loud enough for the whole line to hear.

"That is everything I need."

She looked at David. "See honey. I told you. She thinks this is a camping trip."

She turned to me. "Karen. There's a Welcome Dinner. There's a Gala. You can't get through four days in this heat with one little bag."

"I'll be fine, Tiffany."

"Well don't come asking me for my perfume when you smell like the airplane. I'm not going to have time to help you."

I walked through security. I was at the gate in ten minutes.

They almost missed the plane.

We landed in Boston. Ninety degrees. Sticky.

I texted Leo and walked right past baggage claim.

And there was Tiffany. Screaming at the airline lady. Actually screaming.

"What do you MEAN it went to Atlanta."

Two of her suitcases didn't make it. The ones with all her perfumes and creams.

David saw me walk past. He looked like he wanted to disappear.

"You're not waiting for bags?"

"Everything's with me," I said. "See you at the hotel."

That night was the Welcome Dinner.

Tiffany spent the whole afternoon on the phone with the airline. Her bags weren't coming until after the Gala.

She came down to the lobby in the same leggings and sweater she traveled in. Hair a mess. No makeup. No perfume. She looked small.

The elevator opened.

I walked out.

I had taken a long shower with my soap. Done my hair. Put on a simple silk dress. Not a wrinkle on it.

And there was something on my skin. Warm. Light. Like clean air after rain.

David stopped talking in the middle of his sentence. He just looked at me.

"Wow," he said. "Karen. You look beautiful." He kept looking. "You smell wonderful."

Tiffany's mouth fell open.

"What IS that. What are you wearing."

A woman walked over before I could answer. Silver hair. Tall. About my age. The Dean's wife. I had seen her picture in the welcome letter.

She leaned in close and said, "I'm sorry. I have to ask. What are you wearing."

"It's a soap," I said. "From Japan. It's called Kaori."

Her face lit up.

"My daughter writes about beauty for one of the big magazines. She's been trying to find this soap for months. She told me it's almost impossible to get right now."

She turned to the couple next to her. "This is what I've been telling you about. The one from Okinawa. Something in the fruit that actually gets rid of the smell that shows up after sixty. Regular soap can't touch it."

She looked back at me. "You smell like you're forty years old. In this heat."

I saw Tiffany across the lobby.

Leggings. Frizzy hair. No perfume. Watching people gather around me.

The Dean's wife noticed her and smiled.

"Rough trip, dear? Airline lose your bags?"

Tiffany nodded. Barely.

"That's awful." The Dean's wife shook her head. Then she looked at me. "That's why I always say. If you need a suitcase full of bottles to smell clean, you probably don't really smell clean."

I have never seen Tiffany's face turn that color.

She said something about making a call and disappeared.

We went in for dinner.

Leo was at the table. Handsome in his blazer. He saw Tiffany in the back. Then he saw me.

He walked over. He hugged me. Not a quick hug. A real one. He held on. His face pressed right into my shoulder. Like he used to do when he was little.

"Grandma. You smell like home."

He didn't say it quiet enough.

"Thank you for just being you. Tiffany is having a meltdown about her suitcases. She's driving Grandpa nuts. You're the only one here who looks like everything is fine."

He pulled back and looked at me.

"Grandma. You're the classiest person in this room."

Tiffany was watching from across the room.

She heard every word.

I just smiled at Leo and squeezed his hand.

Next morning David found me at breakfast.

Tiffany was at the buffet in yesterday's clothes. Still on the phone.

David sat down.

"How did you do it," he said quiet. "Tiffany brought enough perfume for ten women. She's got nothing. You brought one bar of soap and you smell like a garden."

"I just found something that works, David."

He looked at his coffee. Then back at me.

"You always did smell like home."

He stopped.

"I miss that."

He said it so quiet. Like he didn't mean to.

Tiffany was coming back.

I took a sip of my coffee and smiled.

My sister sent me a message on WhatsApp that afternoon. She'd seen the pictures on Facebook.

"You look beautiful. But the look on Tiffany's face in the background is the best part."

Then she sent a warning.

"Kaori just sent an email. They're stopping orders Friday. The farmers finished early this year. Price goes up when the next batch comes in spring."

She said all her friends were trying to order before it was too late.

"Once this batch is gone, you're waiting four months."

I thought about Tiffany.

Three big suitcases. Running around the hotel trying to find something to spray on.

I showed up with one little bar of soap.

And I smelled better than her all weekend.

She told the whole family I needed freshness tips.

She laughed about me with my ex-husband in a chat I was never meant to see.

She showed up to our grandson's graduation smelling like a stale airplane while the airline searched for her bags.

I showed up smelling like something she couldn't buy.

My sister was right.

You don't need more. You just need the right thing.

David told me I was the most beautiful woman there.

Tiffany was three feet away.

Some things you don't get back. But some things you get to prove.

That you were never the mess they said you were.

That you never needed his money or her advice or her little list.

That the grandmother who got "replaced" showed them all. Without even raising her voice.

If you have a Tiffany in your life. Or a grandchild who once held his breath when you hugged him.

You need this soap.

Not for the fruit.

For the look on her face when you walk past and she can't stop breathing in.

For the moment your grandson puts his face in your shoulder and says "Grandma, you smell like home."

For the morning your ex-husband looks at you and says, real quiet, "I miss that."

You'll know when it's time.

body.text:
After my divorce my best friends lied about excluding me from Italy. But they missed my ex-husband more. So I booked the flight and took care of that.

Cassie and I have been best friends for 20 years.

She and Greg. Mike and Pam. Dave and Rachel. Three couples, plus Mark and me.

Every September for 16 years, the 8 of us traveled together.

I researched the towns. I found the excursions. I booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics.

For 16 years this was the best week of my year.

Then Mark and I divorced. 14 months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, sweetheart, we thought you needed a little time for yourself. After everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And it's close quarters over there. One apartment, six of us, the heat in August. Ever since the divorce you just haven't been yourself, Susan."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing Amalfi in September. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing."

I said, "Sure, Cassie. I'll put something together."

Then I hung up. I sat in the kitchen for an hour.

Why did I say yes.

That's the part I kept going back to. She left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. And I said sure. Like it was nothing.

Maybe I was being unfair to her. It really could have been last minute. Cassie has not been cruel to me one day in 20 years.

Or maybe I said yes because it was the only thing they still wanted me for.

I sat there a while longer. Then I got the laptop.

I started planning it. Spent weeks on it.

Found a private lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through the terraces that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE. You're amazing. This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house. "Just a little get-together," she said. "Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out. Candles lit. All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in. The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about September."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Mark and Brittany took your spot this year."

Mark.

And Brittany.

The woman he left me for. She was 34. She'd been in his life for two years, one of them while he was still married to me.

"Mark reached out," Cassie continued. "He and Brittany just got engaged. And honestly, we've all known Mark for 20 years. It felt wrong to exclude him forever."

Exclude him.

The man who cheated on me for a year. Who left me for a woman half my age. Who kept the house in the settlement because I couldn't afford to fight him for it.

He's the one they were worried about excluding.

"Susan, we love you. You know that. But nothing has changed since we talked on the phone."

Close quarters. The heat. I just hadn't been myself.

She looked around the table. Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way. You have to understand."

You have to understand.

I looked at Cassie. At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get. Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass. Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry. I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

She wasn't wrong. That was the part I couldn't put down.

The next morning I drove over to Nora's. My sister. 28 years a nurse, most of it on a geriatric floor. She lives 20 minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her everything. The photos from Florence. The "you're so good at organizing" call. The dinner. Cassie's voice. "Ever since the divorce."

And the part I could barely say out loud: that Mark and Brittany were taking my spot. On the trip I planned.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She didn't say a word about it.

"They're right that there's something," she said. "They're wrong about what it is. Those two aren't the same thing."

"Nora, what is this about?"

"28 years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then that's not me. I'm a clean person, Nora. I always have been. I buy the good body wash."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"And people notice it," she said. "Not that they know what they're noticing. They couldn't tell you. They just start standing a little further back, and they make up a reason for it afterward."

"Nora."

"You didn't do anything, Susan. Nobody did this to you. Your skin changed at 60 the same way your eyes changed at 45, and nobody sent you a letter about either one."

"So it was never me."

"It was never you."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my floor home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

I picked it up and held it to my face. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It's called Kaori. I'm down to two bars myself."

I was at the door when she said the other thing.

"Book the flight, Susan. Go on your own."

"Cassie isn't going to un-invite Brittany."

"I'm not talking about Cassie. You found that grove because you wanted to see a grove. You got that table because you wanted to sit at it."

She held the door open.

"So go sit at it."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That afternoon I ordered two more. Then I booked the trip.

Same week. Same coast.

Their hotel. One floor up.

Paid for with the money from my half of the retirement account. The only thing I got in the divorce that was actually mine.

And I told no one.

September on the Amalfi Coast is hotter than people think.

I was on the hotel terrace with a glass of prosecco when I saw them come up from the road below. Cassie fanning herself with a folded map. Brittany walking ten feet behind Mark, not talking.

Twenty minutes later Cassie appeared on the terrace. Flushed. Hair coming undone.

She froze.

"Susan? What are you doing here?"

"Same week. Same coast."

She stared a second too long. Then she went to her room without saying anything else.

I didn't move. I had nowhere to be. And a very good glass of prosecco.

Day three. The lemon grove.

Twelve spots. I'd booked one for myself. The group had the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I got there first. Signora Rossi walked me up through the terraces and showed me how they wrap the lemons in cloth for the winter.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi looked up and waved at me across the terrace.

"Susan. You are the one who wrote to me. In Italian."

The whole group turned around.

Mark saw me. He stopped.

"Susan? You're on this tour?"

"I found this tour, Mark."

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked at Brittany.

Brittany adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

There was a woman on the tour with her daughter. About my age. She ended up next to me at the wall while Signora Rossi was talking.

She leaned in slightly. Then leaned back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearing something? I've been trying to place it since the van."

"It's a soap."

"It smells so good. Like citrus. Fresh." She laughed at herself. "Sorry. I've been behind you for twenty minutes trying to work out what it was."

"It's called Kaori."

She typed it into her phone right there against the wall.

Cassie was three feet away with her hand cupped over her eyes against the sun.

She didn't say anything.

I thought about that on the walk back down.

We've been talking, all of us. That is what Cassie said at the table.

All of them. Talking. And not one of them ever talked to me.

I think I understood now.

That evening the group was at the bar on the hotel terrace. I was two tables away with a book.

Dave came over. The quietest of the husbands. He sat on the edge of the chair next to mine.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip," he said. "And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar. Then he got up and went back to it.

I didn't read another page.

Night four. The dinner Cassie had booked for the group.

I came down at eight.

Cassie was already seated, fanning herself with the menu. Brittany's shoulders were burned across the top. She kept shifting in her chair.

Mark looked up when I walked in.

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-50s. Elegant. Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But I have to ask what you're wearing."

"It's a soap."

"A soap." She put her hand on her chest. "I write for a travel magazine. I've been trying to place that since you sat down. It isn't perfume. It's citrus, and it's fresh. It's lovely."

"Kaori. My sister gave it to me."

"Can I get it here?"

"They only make it when the persimmons come in," I said. "Once a year."

She wrote it in the journal anyway.

Brittany leaned over and said something to Mark. He didn't answer her.

Cassie watched all of it.

The woman with the journal. The pen.

She picked up her wine glass. Took a long sip. Set it down. Looked straight ahead.

Brittany had stopped shifting in her chair.

Mark was watching me. Not Brittany. Me.

Day seven I ate alone at the cliffside table in Positano. The one I'd booked three months earlier, for them.

They had tried for it that morning. Fully booked, the restaurant told them.

Last night. Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the terrace afterward. Water black. Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Greg hasn't left the room with the air conditioning since Tuesday," she said.

"That's a shame."

"Brittany's shoulders are blistering. She had to wear a shawl to dinner."

"I noticed."

She looked at me.

"People keep asking about you."

"They do."

"The woman with the journal. The girl at the front desk asked me what my friend uses."

Silence.

"Where did you get it?"

I looked at her.

"Kaori," I said. "But they only make it when the persimmons come in. That batch is gone."

She looked down.

"Of course it is."

"They restock when the fruit comes in. If you wait, you wait a long time."

She nodded.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my room without looking back.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

They left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. Apparently I'm capable enough to find a restaurant with a three-month waitlist. Just not capable enough to sit at one.

"We thought you needed a little time for yourself."

"Ever since the divorce, you just haven't been yourself."

Not one of them ever told me what they actually meant.

My sister did. In her kitchen, in about ten minutes.

Nora called last week. Kaori has a new batch up. It's already most of the way gone.

They're doing September again next year. Sicily, someone said.

Nora has already asked whether Sicily has lemon groves.

I told her yes.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost yourself.

You don't need to be replaced.

You need to be underestimated one more time.

So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the Kaori. Run the bath. Go anyway.

It costs less than fifty cents a day. Less than the coffee I drink while I plan other people's trips.

They only make it when the persimmons come in. Once a batch goes, you wait months.

Cassie asked where I got it. I told her it was sold out.

She's waiting until next year.

I was already home.

Your move.

body.text:
I bought the persimmon soap the internet keeps telling women my age to buy.
I used it every day for 3 weeks, morning and night, the whole bar.
My husband is still sleeping in the spare room.

I am 61. Ron and I have been married 34 years. He retired last September after 38 years at the county.

He was still in our room at Christmas. I want to be accurate about that, because I have gone over the order of it more times than I can tell you.

This is what happened in between, and what it cost me to find out.

By January he had stopped coming into our bedroom.

He would stand in the doorway with his coffee and tell me about the gutters from there. Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold like a man delivering something.

In March he moved his pillow into the spare room. He said it was his back, and that the mattress in there was firmer, and that he was sorry, and he was sorry the way you are sorry when you have already decided.

I bought him a mattress topper in April. The expensive one, the one the man in the store said was for people with backs.

In June I went in there for the window fan and I found it behind the door. Still in the plastic. The tape had not been broken.

I stood there holding a mattress topper for a long time.

He had not been sleeping badly. He had been sleeping somewhere else, and he had found a reason for it that I could not argue with, because you cannot argue with a man's back.

Kate is our daughter. She is 33 and she is 40 minutes away, and she is the kind of daughter who calls on the drive home.

She had been putting the window down in my car since about February. Two inches. Then she would say something about the heat, in February, in Ohio.

In May she drove us both to my sister's and she had the air on the whole way with the windows cracked, and when I asked her she said she gets carsick if it is stuffy. She has never been carsick in her life.

In April, at my own table, she suggested we eat out on the porch. It was 48 degrees. We ate out on the porch, all of us, in coats, and everybody said what a lovely idea.

I want to be fair to them. Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not once. Not one word.

They just kept finding reasons, and the reasons were all good ones, and there were a lot of them.

The night I found the topper I sat up until 2 in the morning with my phone, typing things into it I would not have said out loud in an empty house.

I will not write out what I typed. Any woman my age who has done it knows what I typed.

I found women saying the same 3 words to each other on a page I will not name. Persimmon soap. That was all of it. Nobody said why it was persimmon and I did not care why.

I ordered a persimmon soap that night. 9 dollars, an orange bar, persimmons all over the box, a bit of Japanese on the front. It came on the Thursday.

I used it every day for 3 weeks.

I want to tell you exactly how careful I was, because I need you to understand what it did to me when nothing happened. Every morning. Every night. The whole bar.

Ron stayed in the spare room.

Kate put the window down in July.

And I stopped, because there is only one thing left to think when the answer does not work. It is not the answer that is wrong. It is you. And you are not fixable.

I put the wrapper in the bin and I did not tell one living person I had bought it.

In August I went into the pharmacy on Harrison for Ron's back. That is the part I still cannot get over. I was in there buying a heat patch for the back he does not have a problem with.

Maggie has been behind that counter 17 years. She did my mother's blister packs for the last 2 years of her life and she never once made me feel like I was asking too much.

She rang up the heat patches and she said, "How is he doing?"

And I said, "He's fine," and then I stood there and did not move away from the counter.

There was nobody behind me. She waited.

"Maggie, can I ask you something that isn't about him."

She put the patches in the bag and left the bag on the counter.

"Is there something about me. A smell. I have thought about it every day since March and I cannot ask anybody in my own house."

She did not look surprised, which was the first kind thing that happened to me all year.

"There's something," she said. "You're not imagining it. But it isn't what you think it is."

"I shower every day. I have showered every day of my life."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"I've stood here 17 years. Things change for women our age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She leaned on the counter.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"That can't be right."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I put my hand on the counter.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

"Persimmon. The tannins take it apart. It doesn't cover it."

And I heard myself say it out loud in a pharmacy at 20 past 4 in the afternoon.

"I bought that. I bought a persimmon soap in June. I used it for 3 weeks and nothing happened, so I stopped."

She did not say anything for a second.

Then she said, "Have you still got the box?"

I said it was in the bin in June.

"Then buy another one and bring me the box before you use it. Any of them. Whichever one you like the look of."

I did. I brought it in the following Tuesday in my purse.

She turned it over on the counter and put her finger on the list on the back and read it to me out loud, the way she reads a label to somebody's mother.

Water. Palm oil. Glycerin. Fragrance. A color, with a number on it.

She got to the bottom of the list and stopped.

"Now find me the persimmon."

It was on the front of the box 4 times. It was in the name of the product. There was a photograph of one on it.

It was not in the list at all.

"That's what you bought in June," she said. "You didn't try persimmon soap. You tried an orange soap that had been told to look like one."

I stood in that pharmacy and my eyes went, which I had not done in front of anybody all year, including in the spare room doorway in March.

"So it was never me."

"It was never you. And it wasn't even your judgment. It was one line on a label that nobody has ever told you to read."

She reached under the counter for her handbag, which is a thing I had never seen her do, and she took out a small parcel wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon orange. Characters on the front I could not read.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"I can't take yours."

"I buy 3 at a time. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone, so I've learned."

"Does it work?"

"I've used it 6 years. One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped standing a bit back from people. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. I can't sell it to you. That is more or less the point of it."

I used it that night. It is a bar of soap. I did not expect anything, because I had already been here in June.

The first week I could not tell.

The second week Kate drove me to my sister's again and we had the windows up the whole way and she talked about her job the entire time and I do not think she noticed she was doing it.

At the end of August, Ron came into our bedroom to get a book off his own shelf, which he had been doing from the doorway since January.

He came in. He sat on the end of the bed while he found his place in it. He stayed about 20 minutes.

He did not say anything and neither did I. I have learned something about what does not get said in that house.

In September a woman waiting for her prescription behind me at Maggie's counter said, "I'm sorry, what is that? It's citrus. It's lovely."

I said it was a bar of soap.

Maggie did not look up from her computer. She said, "Isn't it."

Ron came back into our room on the 4th of October. He carried his own pillow in and put it down and said, "I've been sleeping badly in there."

I said, "Have you."

That is as close as either of us is going to get, and after 34 years I find I do not need the rest of it.

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

I was right in June. I had the right idea in the middle of the night on my own phone, and I paid 9 dollars for it, and it did nothing, and I decided that meant there was something wrong with me that could not be fixed.

It was the bar. It was only ever the bar.

Maggie texted me last week. Kaori is back on the website. She has ordered 3, because that is what she does.

Kate is driving us both to my sister's for her birthday on the 2nd.

She has already asked if I am bringing the good pie. I told her yes.

If your husband has found a reason he can live with and moved down the hall.

If somebody has started opening a window in your car and telling you it is the heat.

If you have already tried the thing that was supposed to work, and stopped, and quietly decided the problem is you.

You do not need to be fixed.

You need to find out what you actually bought.

Get the soap. Take the shower. Turn the box over first.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

It was never me.

It was never going to be me.

Your move.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.

Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.

My name is Dr. Margaret Ellis. I'm a geriatrician and I've been doing this for 22 years

I want to be clear about something before I say anything else. I don't recommend products. My patients will tell you that. When I finally do tell someone to buy something, it's because I've watched it work, over and over, for years.

Which is why what happened last year bothered me so much. But let me start from the beginning.

I did part of my training at a geriatric hospital in Japan.

Part of the reason why I went to Japan was to find out why they live so long.

What I found was, a big part of that is that they are extremely comfortable and confident with aging, you would love to see how most of them go so confidently into their 90's

And this isn't just a feeling. There's real research behind this.

How you feel about aging changes how you age.

In the most famous study, people with a positive view of getting older outlived the people who feared it by around seven and a half years.

Which is exactly why the next thing I learned in Japan stuck with me. Because there is one thing that can quietly take all that confidence away

That's where I first heard a word we don't have in English.

Kareishu.

Aging odor.

In Japan, nobody pretends it isn't real, it's common sense there, the way gray hair is common sense.

Everyone knows that around sixty, your skin starts making a compound called 2-nonenal. Everyone knows what it smells like. And everyone knows what to do about it.

Because they've been dealing with it for centuries.

The answer there has always been the same.

A soap made from fermented persimmon. They call it kakishibu.

Unripe persimmons, pressed, then left to ferment for months, until they're full of tannins.

And tannins are one of the only things that actually grab onto nonenal

At the hospital, nurses handed those bars to patients the way we hand out blood pressure pamphlets.

Then I finished my training, came home, and learned something strange. Here, none of this existed.

No word for it. No pamphlet. In 20 years of practice, not one patient has ever brought it up with me first.

But I would watch what it did every single week.

One of my patients taught second grade for 41 years. Then one September the school gave her class to a teacher half her age and called it restructuring.

It took her months to get the real reason out of her principal. Parents had complained about a smell.

Patients noticing their grandson's hugs getting shorter.

Family becoming more and more distant.

So I did the only thing I could.

Quietly, in my office, I started telling people about persimmon soap. I've been doing it since the year I opened my practice.

Back then my patients had to order it from tiny importers and wait weeks for it. But it worked, over and over, right in front of me.

For twenty years it was the one product I broke my own rule for.

Then, about a year ago, everything changed. Persimmon soap was suddenly everywhere.

Suddenly, patients were asking me about it.

People walked into my office holding their phones, showing me ads.

After twenty years of explaining kakishibu from scratch, I didn't have to convince anyone anymore.

You have to understand what that means in my office. Telling a patient about aging odor is the most delicate conversation I have.

I am telling someone they carry a smell they cannot smell.

So when patients started bringing it up themselves, it honestly felt like a relief.

Last year alone, sixty-one of my patients bought a bar on my recommendation. I know the exact number, because I keep track of everything I recommend.

Then the calls started.

"Be honest with me, doctor. Was this supposed to do anything at all?"

By the end of the year, nineteen of those sixty-one patients had left my clinic. A few told my receptionist why. Most just stopped booking.

One woman had been with me for eleven years. On her way out she said she didn't need "this old people smell nonsense." Eleven years, gone.

And I had no answer.

Same soap, as far as I knew. Same instructions I'd given for two decades. It had never failed like this.

So I did something I've never done in my career. I started calling the ones who would still take my call, and I asked them to bring me what they had bought.

The first bar arrived on a Monday morning. A patient named Ruth set it on my desk, still in its box.

And the moment I put my eyes on that bar I knew something was wrong.

That bar was bright orange, looked like a block of cheddar

The Kakishibu I knew from Japan was nothing like that.

So I did the test the nurses in Japan taught me.

I carried her bar to my office window and held it up against the light. The light hit it and stopped. Nothing came through.

Real kakishibu is translucent. Hold it to a window and the light passes straight through it, and it glows amber, like honey held up to a lamp.

The next day I brought my own bar from home and held them side by side at the same window and sent her a photo.

Mine glowed. Hers might as well have been a brick.

Two more patients brought theirs in that week. Different brands, different boxes.

Same brick.

Not one of them had ever touched the thing I was recommending.

Here's what they'd actually bought. Juice soap. Ripe persimmons pressed for juice, stirred into an ordinary soap base, dyed orange.

And juice has none of the tannins.

The tannins come from fermenting the unripe fruit for months. Skip the fermentation and you have a bar that smells nice, looks the part, and does absolutely nothing about nonenal.

That glow isn't a color anyone can add. It's the material itself. Which is why no dyed bar can fake it.

My patients had been washing with orange dye for months. And here is the part that made me genuinely angry. It's completely legal.

Juice, dye, a persimmon on the label, and the box gets to say persimmon soap.

Nineteen people trusted me, scrubbed every day with colored soap base, smelled exactly the same, and decided I was a fool. And honestly, they were half right.

Because I'd been saying "persimmon soap" for twenty years, when I should have been telling them exactly what to look for.

So I started doing the research I should have done a year earlier.

Out of everything sold online, there were only two brands that looked like they produced real kakishibu.

One of them is the famous one, The girl that owns it has been on shark tank.

It looked like something I could actually trust, but I'd already lost nineteen patients to a label. I wasn't going to risk a twentieth.

So I dug deeper.

On that Shark Tank episode, the founder said each bar costs about a 1.85$ to make.

AND they sell it on a subscription, every month, all year round. And it has never, as far as I can tell, been out of stock.

Not once.

Now remember what kakishibu is. Persimmons ripen once a year. The unripe fruit gets pressed and then ferments for months. There is only ever as much real kakishibu as the last harvest gave.

A dollar eighty-five, unlimited supply, forever, from a once-a-year fruit. I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm telling you I cannot make that math work.

That was enough for me to keep looking.

So I ordered a bar from the other brand, shipped to my clinic. This time I was going to test it myself before it went anywhere near a patient.

The bar arrived two days later, from a small brand called Kakiyu.

I took it straight to the same window where Ruth's orange bar had failed, and held it up.

The light went straight through it. That deep amber glow, exactly like the bars the nurses handed out in Japan.

My receptionist asked me why I was smiling at a bar of soap.

It looked like a scene coming out of a Indiana Jones movie

Then I took it home and used it for two weeks, because a glow isn't a result.

It was the first bar I'd held in a year where everything matched: the color, the light, the one-harvest story, even the fact that it kept selling out while I was researching it.

And it held up.

So I went back to their site and ordered nineteen more.

All nineteen bars went out the same week, to their homes, each with a handwritten note.

I kept the note short. The soap was real. The bar you bought was not. Hold this one up to a window and you'll see the difference for yourself. Then call me.

The first call came nine days later.

It was Ruth. She didn't say hello. She said, "My daughter hugged me goodbye yesterday, and she didn't rush it."

Then she went quiet, and we stayed on the phone like that for a moment, and I didn't mind one bit.

Within two weeks, my front desk had heard from fourteen of the nineteen.

One man told me his wife had started sitting on his side of the couch again.

Another patient said her grandkids stayed the whole sunday afternoon, and nobody found a reason to leave early.

Here's the thing about this problem.

Nobody ever announces the change, in either direction. Nothing gets said when people drift away, and nothing gets said when they drift back. They just lean in again.

But you can see it. My patients walk into my waiting room differently now. Straighter. They linger at the front desk to chat.

That confidence I saw everywhere in Japan, the one the research says is worth seven and a half years, I watch it come back one appointment at a time.

I now tell every patient the same thing.

If you're going to try persimmon soap, you have exactly one job. Make sure it's real kakishibu. Hold the bar up to a window.

If the light passes through and it glows amber, it's real. If the light stops, you're holding dye.

Kakiyu is the only bar I've found that passes every test I know how to run. I don't get a cent for saying that, and they have no idea I'm writing this

There's a sixty day guarantee, so the test costs you nothing. Use it for two months. If nobody around you moves closer, send it back. I only wish the nineteen orange bars had come with those terms.

So this is me, asking you the same thing I asked at the start. Please don't buy persimmon soap. Buy the real thing once, or don't buy anything at all.

Twenty-two years, and this is the first time I've ever written something like this about a product. But I watched nineteen people spend months getting quietly written off by the people they love, over a bar of dyed soap.

If this reaches even one person before they buy another orange bar, it was worth writing.

PS. A few people asked me to put the link here. I didn't include one when I first wrote this, I was writing a warning, not an advertisement. But you're right that it saves you searching, so here it is: https://kakiyucare.com/products/kakiyu-persimmon-soap

PPS. Since posting this, I've had people tell me they went looking for Kakiyu on Amazon. Please don't. Kakiyu doesn't sell there, and what comes up when you search the name is exactly the orange soap this whole letter is about. The real bar exists in one place, their official website. Use the link above and nowhere else.

Does it name the process? Fermented and aged. That is what turns green persimmon juice into a tannin strong enough to hold on to anything. It is the difference between a grape and a glass of wine. Same fruit. Not the same thing at all.

Is the base sulphate free? The skin gets thinner as you get older, so a harsh base just trades one problem for another.

I read the labels on 5 of them. One passed all 3.

body.text:
For 11 months, my ex told our friends I was "struggling" after the divorce.
Last weekend, I shut him up.

At a party.

In front of every one of them.

I never said a word.

Greg and I met thirty-one years ago.

We married that spring. Thirty years, twenty-six of them good.

Every Fourth of July he'd watch me carry the whole party, grinning like he still couldn't believe his luck.

The man I married went into the recliner. He mostly didn't come back out.

I still made his coffee every morning. Two sugars, left by his chair.

Somewhere in there he stopped saying thank you.

Then he stopped saying my name.

One night there was a young singer on the TV, younger than Katie.

He turned the volume up for her the way he hadn't turned anything up for me in years.

"Now that's the whole package right there," he said. To the screen. Not to me.

I stepped in front of it.

I asked him when he'd last looked at me that way.

He leaned to see around me.

Then he got the remote back. Turned her up.

Thirty years, and there he was, mouth a little open, leaning after some girl on the screen.

So at fifty-seven, I signed the papers on a Tuesday.

My hand shook. Twenty-six good years are hard to sign away.

I sat in that parking lot afterward. Didn't start the car for ten minutes. Then I drove out with the window down, lighter than I'd been in four years.

Wine with supper on a Tuesday. Nobody to answer to.

I called it freedom.

It lasted three weeks.

Then the calls started.

Women I hadn't heard from in a year, suddenly checking in on me.

"Greg says you're struggling, hon. I just wanted to see how you were holding up."

"I'm alright," I'd say.

"Bless your heart."

Poor Greg. Have you heard? She couldn't last a month on her own.

He kept it up for eleven months. He made sure every word got back to me.

That was the point.

I didn't fight it. You can't call thirty people to swear you're fine.

You only end up sounding like a woman who isn't.

What got me wasn't the lie. It was that nobody blinked.

Thirty years of friends. Not one of them thought, that doesn't sound like her.

Somewhere in my fifties I'd gone invisible. I was just the last to know.

I didn't want another husband. I'd spent thirty years ironing one man's shirts. I was done being somebody's wife.

I just wanted to be seen again. A little company, maybe. Somebody to sit beside who didn't need a thing from me.

So when Katie set me up on one of those apps, I let her. She hit save before I could lose my nerve.

"Mom, you're a catch," she said. "Trust me."

The only man who messaged me twice was seventy-nine, hunting for someone to drive him to his dialysis.

"A nurse with a purse," Sue said when I told her. "That's the whole market for us, hon."

Some women just don't get a second look, I decided. I'd had mine.

I'd started to think I could go quiet in that little house and nobody would even notice.

"Enough, hon," Sue said, when I finally broke down and called her. "You've given that man enough of your good years."

"Here's what you're going to do tonight. Run yourself a hot bath. And use the good stuff."

She came by twenty minutes later anyway. Pressed a little wrapped bar into my hand.

"This is the good stuff," she said. "It's persimmon. Kaori."

"Why do I need this?"

"Just trust me. We swore by it on the ward."

She held my eyes. "You know how your skin changes as you get older, hon. This soap is for that. I found out about it a few years back, and I haven't gone without it since."

"Persimmon is about the only thing that cleans out the scent your skin starts making as you get older. This one is the best out there."

"And this bar smells like heaven." She held it up between us. "Go on. Smell it."

I did. She wasn't wrong.

She closed my fingers around it. "That's the last bar I've got, if you want the truth. They sell out faster than they can make them."

"But you take this one. Do it for you, not for him. Now go run that bath. I'll wait right here."

I felt ridiculous, a grown woman handed a bar of soap like it might fix anything.

But I ran the bath while she waited. Not for Greg. Not for anyone.

The whole room filled up with it. Warm, clean, a little sweet.

The first kind thing I'd done for myself in longer than I could remember. So I kept doing it.

After a while, I caught myself standing taller in the mirror.

Shoulders back. Looking myself in the eye for the first time in years.

I felt like me. The one from before all of it.

A week later, Sue wouldn't take no for an answer. A bar across town, a bluegrass band.

I went for the music. I'll say that for the record. I was finished with men.

Then a man folded himself down onto the floor by the fiddle player. Eyes shut, grinning like it was the best thing that had happened to him all year.

Ray. Gardener's hands, dirt under one nail, a laugh that came easy.

He ended up on the stool next to mine. That was the last I heard of the band.

An hour in, I realized I hadn't once braced for the catch.

He walked me to my car. Didn't try a thing. Just asked, hands in his pockets, if he could call.

Three days later, before I could talk myself out of it, I texted first.

By then he was around most evenings. He still had a way of making me blush, at fifty-seven.

"I always love how you smell, Linda. Reminds me of my citrus tree."

I turned to the window so he wouldn't see my face.

Last weekend, my old friends Don and Marion threw a party for their fortieth. I was excited to finally introduce them to Ray.

Greg was there too. Alone.

I walked in with Ray, in a blue dress I'd bought myself that morning.

Ray had the whole party won over by the second drink. Don dragged him off to look at the tomatoes.

The whole night was just fun. I hadn't had one like it in years.

I was over by the bar when a woman I'd never met leaned across. Marion's sister, in from Denver.

"I'm sorry, I have to ask," she said. "What is that you're wearing? It smells so good."

I wrote Kaori down for her on a cocktail napkin.

Later in the evening, I glanced around and noticed Greg off in a corner, just watching the room. All I felt was relief. He wasn't mine to worry about anymore.

Ray and I are driving up to a little cabin this weekend. Just the two of us.

Sue called this morning. "Well?" was all she said. She could already hear the answer.

She told me the new batch of Kaori just landed. It's already going fast. I ordered myself one before we hung up. Marion did too.

body.text:
We made a soap that pulls odor out of your skin instead of covering it with fragrance.

It sounds almost too simple — until you learn why nothing else has worked.

Let me explain.

We didn't set out to make another "clean" soap. We set out to solve a problem most people don't even have a name for.

Around your mid-forties, your skin starts producing more of a compound called nonenal. It's what causes that faint musty smell on collars, pillowcases, jackets. It isn't sweat. It isn't hygiene. It's chemistry.

And here's the part nobody tells you: nonenal isn't water-soluble. Soap and water slide right past it. Deodorant lays perfume on top and hopes.

So for years, people over 40 dealt with the same frustrating loop:

Showering twice a day and still noticing it on a pillowcase. Washing a jacket that came back smelling the same. Buying stronger deodorant, then stronger perfume. Quietly wondering whether other people notice — and knowing nobody would ever say anything.

They'd try premium body washes. Same result. Because the problem was never how hard they scrubbed. It was that ordinary soap can't dissolve an oil-based compound.

The answer wasn't a stronger cleanser. It was a different ingredient entirely.

Persimmon tannin doesn't cover nonenal — it binds to it. Japan has used persimmon this way for centuries. It was never a secret. It's just not a business model, because you only need one bar.

Here's the catch: tannin is the expensive part. Most persimmon soaps use barely enough to justify the word on the label, then fill the gap with synthetic fragrance — the exact thing you were trying to get away from.

So we source ours from a family farm in Italy. Century-old trees. Picked by hand, once a year. Small batches, cured slow instead of stamped out by the thousand.

What customers tell us actually changed:

✅ Pillowcases stopped smelling musty between washes
✅ No perfume layered over the problem
✅ One bar — face, hands, body
✅ No sulfates, parabens, or synthetic fragrance

One bar. One job.

Try Cachi Naturals risk-free. If you don't notice a difference, send it back for a full refund.

You were never unclean. You were just using the wrong thing.

Get Cachi Naturals → https://cachinaturals.com/products/persimmon-nonenal-deodorizing-soap

cards.body:
¿Piel seca, roja y con tanta comezón que hasta te cuesta dormir? 😣

Si ya probaste cremas, lociones y humectantes que solo ayudan por unas horas, probablemente ya sabes lo frustrante que es sentir que el problema siempre vuelve.

Porque no se trata solo de “hidratar” la piel.

Cuando tu barrera cutánea está irritada y debilitada, tu piel puede volverse más vulnerable a bacterias, resequedad y nuevos brotes.

Por eso creamos Wonder Naturals con dos ingredientes simples pero poderosos:

🍯 Miel de Manuka para ayudar a combatir las bacterias y calmar la piel irritada.

💧 Tallow para hidratar profundamente, nutrir la piel y ayudar a restaurar su barrera natural.

Juntos ayudan a darle a la piel seca, sensible y con comezón el apoyo que necesita para sentirse más tranquila, hidratada y protegida.

Y sin llenar tu piel de ingredientes innecesarios.

✅ Sin esteroides
✅ Sin alcohol
✅ Sin fragancias añadidas
✅ Hecha para piel sensible

Si estás cansado de usar productos que solo parecen cubrir el problema, prueba una fórmula hecha específicamente para piel seca, irritada y propensa a brotes.

Además, tu compra está protegida por una garantía de devolución de 90 días.

👇 Haz clic en el enlace para ver si todavía está disponible.

I've painted faces in Seoul for over twenty years. Thousands of them. And when a woman over 40 sits in my chair, the first thing I do is take the bag off her shoulder and empty it onto the table.

Four products. Almost always the same four. And all four are working against her.

Nobody in this industry will say this out loud, so I will: after 40, your hormones change the way your skin makes melanin. Your face stops being one color. Forehead one tone, jaw another, a different tone in July than in January. That is not damage. That is biology.

Now look at what they sell you for it. One fixed color. Mixed in a factory months ago. Matched to a paper chart.

The viral color-changer that stays white on most women — or goes green-grey. The "age rewind" concealer that creases into the exact lines it was supposed to erase, by two o'clock. The BB cream that blends out to nothing on mature skin and is gone by three. And the $40 counter foundation, where an artist matched you once, under store lighting, on one day of your life. The other 364 days are a guess.

They are not selling you a match. They are selling you a guess with your name on it.

In Korea, we fix the color first. Before brushes, before powder, before anything. And we do not pick the shade — we let the skin choose it.

Luxe pH-Adaptive Foundation leaves the bottle white. It has no color in it. What it has is thousands of pigment microbeads that your own skin ruptures on contact — so it reads the pH of your forehead, your jaw, your under-eyes separately and becomes a different shade in each place. Lighter at the cheek. Deeper at the jaw. No line at the neck. No orange at hour three.

You already know this technology by its other name: custom blending. The thing a Hollywood actress pays an artist to mix by hand every morning. In America they sell it as a luxury. In Korea it has been the standard for years. We put it in a bottle you shake and dot on.

My clients tell me the same thing every time. They stopped hearing "are you feeling all right?" They stopped carrying a compact. Women who hadn't let anyone photograph them in years are in every picture now.

So: keep replacing four products that were never built for the face you have now? Or try one bottle that reads your skin instead of guessing at it?

Right now it's buy one, get 2 free. Free shipping. Thirty days to send it back — no forms, no conditions.

You've already paid for the guess. Try the one that reads.

And before you buy any tallow balm, ask them one thing: where does your tallow actually come from?
Because most tallow companies, around 80% of them, don't make their own tallow. They buy it pre-made from a supplier.
Which usually means one of two things. Either it's highly processed commercial tallow from who knows where, called grass-fed because a supplier said so. Or it's been treated with things to control the color, smell, and hardness.
So here's the test: ask a tallow company to show you their real ingredients and process. If they can't, don't buy it.
Ours is made by hand, fresh every week, right here in the USA, from grass-fed tallow. And it's mostly tallow, with just raw Manuka honey, olive oil, and beeswax mixed in.
