body.text:
I get my grandson one week a year. I have 1 left.
He is 9. This summer he got out of my pool and said,
"Not while you are in it."

Everybody said it was his age.

Owen gets the first week of July at my house, on his own, since he was 5.
We call it Grandma Camp.

His mother drops him off Sunday, then she goes.
That is the whole rule. Parents don't stay.

There are 3 of them. Owen, then Ruby, then Nate.
They each get their own week.

Nicole lives 20 minutes away. It is not that I never see him.
Last July he was in my pool by 9 every morning.
Every time he climbed out he came to me for his towel.

I start on the week in June. Special never just happens.

Camp is mine. Bill was at work for every one of them.
He retired in March, so this year he was out there too.

I had the pool out on the Friday before. The little blue one, with the hose run to it from the spigot.
The sprinkler out too, the green one that goes back and forth.
His backpack on the bed in the spare room, with a flashlight, a whistle, and the sour candy his mother says no to.

The sign on the porch said Dinosaur Camp. Every year gets a name, and this year that is what he is.

I had the week written out on a card. Monday the sprinkler. Tuesday the library. Wednesday the fort. Thursday the lake.
I know how that sounds. But I have watched people wing a week with a kid, so by Wednesday it is television.

Nicole pulled in at 10 on the Sunday. She had him out of the car before she had the engine off.
She kissed the top of his head and he put both arms around her neck, the way he does.
Then she left, because that is the rule.

He found the candy in 40 seconds.

By 11 he was in the water. It was 90 out.

I got the little steps, set them at the side of the pool, and sat down on the bottom one with my feet in.
Owen was on the far side with a plastic dinosaur, doing the thing where the dinosaur talks.

I slid the rest of the way in. That pool comes up past my knees if I am sitting down in it.

He stopped doing the voice.

He stood up and said he wanted a popsicle.

I said we had just got in. I said get one after.

He said, "I want to get out."

He went over the side, up onto the porch, and sat down on the step with his back against the post.

I said come back in, it is 90 degrees, I am not going to splash you.

He said, "Not while you are in it."

He did not shout it. He said it the way you say you do not want peas, and then he ate his popsicle.

10 minutes later Bill came out in his shorts, no shirt, 68 years old, and got in.

Owen was in that water before Bill had both feet in it.

I was still sitting on the bottom step.

He is 9. He has said worse than that about broccoli.
That is what I told myself, and I went in and made his dinner.

That is what I keep coming back to.
Every single thing that boy did that week had a reason sitting right there next to it.

Monday I ran the sprinkler for him. He went through it 20 times, screaming every time, the way he has since he was 3.

I stood at the edge of the grass with his towel over my arm.
He ran past me to the porch and pulled the other one off the rail himself.

There were 2 towels on that rail. He took the one that was not in my hand.

I said I had his right here.

He said, "I want Grandpa to do it."

Bill was 20 feet away with a coffee, and he had not done one thing.

Tuesday at the library he took his stack to the table by the window.
That is the table I have sat at with him since he was 4.

Then he took the stack back off it and sat down on the floor in the aisle.

I stood there with my car keys in my hand, working out whether a person is allowed to be hurt by that.

In the car on the way home he sat behind Bill.

That night I read to him. Bedtime is the best part of the whole week for me. It always has been.
I have sat on the edge of that bed and read to that boy 2 chapters a night for 3 summers.
That is where I first heard about the mosasaur.

I picked the book up off the nightstand and sat down.

He said, "I want Grandpa to do it."

I said Grandpa does not do the voices.

He said, "I don't want you to do it."

I sat there on the edge of that bed with the book open on my knee.

So Bill read it.
I stood in the hallway with my hand flat on the wall and listened to my husband of 41 years get the voices wrong.
That boy laughed at them anyway.

Then I went and did the dishes, which were already done.

He wanted me and no one else, once.
When he was 2 he would put both arms straight up in the air at me across a room full of people.
You do not get that back. Everybody knows you do not get that back. That is not what this is about.

Wednesday we built the fort over the clothesline, the way my mother did it.

He asked Bill to hold the corner. I was standing right there with a clothespin in my hand.
Bill held the corner. I gave Bill the clothespin.

I brought them out lemonade, but I did not go in, because it is a fort, and grandmothers do not go in the fort.
That is what I told myself while I was standing outside of it.

Wednesday afternoon is the one I keep.

Owen came out of the water and stood on the grass, dripping, with his arms out from his sides the way they do.

I had his towel. I had taken it off the rail 2 minutes before.
I was holding it open with both hands, about 4 feet from him.

That is what I have done every July since that child was 5 years old.

He looked at me holding it.

Then he walked past me to his grandfather.

Bill did not even have a towel. Bill had a garden hose.
Bill said, "Hang on, bud," put the hose down in the grass, and pulled the other towel off the rail.

And Owen stood there and let him.

He let a 68 year old man in wet shorts wrap him up in a towel while his grandmother stood 4 feet away holding one open.
And while Bill was doing it, Owen took a step backward. Away from me. To get the room.

He was not upset. He was talking the entire time about a reptile.
Bill did not notice one thing. Bill said, "You are going to be a prune."

I stood there holding that towel open until it got ridiculous. Then I folded it over my arm.

There is no version of that I can explain with his age.
Bill is 2 years older than I am.
He was 4 feet away with a garden hose in his hand, and that child walked into his arms.

I went in and put the towel in the dryer. It did not need it. It was dry.

Then I stood in the laundry room with my hand flat on top of that dryer and hated my husband for about 4 minutes.

41 years, and I had never done that once.

Bill was at work for 5 summers of that boy's life. He has never planned a week. He has never bought a whistle.
He held a corner.

And that child would climb over me to get to him.

I did not cry in front of him.

I cried that night with the shower running so nobody would hear it.
I am 66 years old and I sat down on the floor of my own shower.
I have not done that since the day my mother died.

Then I lay in bed with my phone and typed in 9 year old pulling away from grandmother.
Which is not a thing I am proud of.

It is a phase. It is developmentally normal. They need room for friends their own age.

Every one of those pages would have been right, if Bill had not been standing in the same yard.

Because he is not doing it to Bill.
He is not doing it to his mother either. He got out of the car on Sunday and put both arms around her neck.

I lay there at 1 in the morning working out what Bill has that I do not, and I could not find one thing.

If it is his age, then it is his age with everybody. That is what age is.

Thursday morning I was in the shower at 5, before anybody in the house was up.
I put a clean shirt on so he would not get the one I slept in.

There is a cardigan that lives on the hook by the back door.
I took it down and held the collar of it up to my face in the hallway, with the house asleep.

It smelled like a cardigan. I put it back on the hook.

It took me until Thursday to say the true thing in my own head.
I was not afraid he had gone off me. I was afraid he was being polite to me.

A 9 year old. Being polite to his grandmother. In her own back yard. For a week. Because his mother raised him right.

Thursday was the lake, which was the big thing I had planned.
I did the whole cooler the night before. Bologna sandwiches cut in triangles, crusts off.

He asked for them that way when he was 6 and has never once asked since.
I have made them that way for 3 years anyway.

He had a good day. I am not going to pretend he did not. He had a really good day.

I waded in to my knees and stood there. He came past me 6 or 7 times going after those frogs. Right past my legs.
He did not once stop where I was standing.

He did bring me a frog.
He came up out of that water with it in both hands and held it up in front of me at arm's length.
Then he took it back before I could get a finger on it.

He wanted me to see the frog. He did not want to be standing there while I saw it.

That is the thing nobody warns you about. It does not look like anything.
Nothing happens that you could tell another person about without sounding like you have lost your mind.

That night I put out the treat plate.
A biscuit, a marshmallow, strawberries and grapes, and the Nutella in the middle.
That plate is the whole reason he thinks I am worth coming to. I know it, but I do not care.

I brought it out on the porch, but he did not look up. I put my hand on the top of his head, the way you do.

He said, "You are annoying me."

Then he ate 2 marshmallows and asked if we could do the sprinkler again tomorrow.

He did not mean it the way it landed. I know that. He is 9. But something happens to you after enough of them.

I did not read to him that night. I told him Grandpa does it better, which he took as a fact, because it is one.

By Friday I had stopped.

I did not get in the water when he was in it. I sat in the chair at the edge with the cooler and the towels.
That is a job. It looks like a job. Nobody asks a woman with a cooler why she is sitting where she is sitting.

Every time he climbed out I got up and went to get something.
Ice. A different popsicle. The bug spray off the windowsill.
So that it looked like I was the one leaving.

When I hugged him I did it fast and I let go first. I have never in my life let go of that child first.

I am 66 years old, and I was running a distance in my own back yard like a seating chart.

Nicole called Friday around lunch to see how it was going. I told her it was going great. I told her about the frogs.

She said, "He is having the best week."

I said he was. That was true. He was.

I sat there on the phone with her doing arithmetic. He is 9. The camp runs until they are 10.
After that they have friends and travel ball and they would rather be anywhere in the world than at my house.

1 more. I had the number before she finished the sentence.

1 more week with that boy, and I had spent this one moving my chair.

Friday afternoon I told Bill I had to run out for hamburger buns for the cookout.
I sat in my car in the lot at the grocery store for 25 minutes without going in.

I did not know what I had done.

I went back over that whole week looking for the thing I had done, and there is no thing.

My grandson would rather I was not out there at all. He is 9 years old and he would rather I stayed in the house.

So I called Marlene from that parking lot, which I would not have done on any other day of my life.

Marlene is 71. She was a nurse for 30 years in an assisted living building on the north side.
She has been my friend since our girls were in the same 3rd grade class, which is 38 years now.
She is the only person I know who does not soften a thing.

I told her all of it right there in the lot. The pool. The book. The floor of the library. The towel.
I told her I had been getting up out of my own chair to fetch things, so that his leaving would look like my going.

I heard myself say that out loud, so I had to stop for a second.

She let me finish. Then she said, "I am coming over."

She came at 5 with the folding table for the cookout and a paper bag, and she did not say one word about the bag.

I poured the coffee.

"He is not doing it to Bill," I said. "He is not doing it to his mother. I do not see him doing it to anyone else."

She said, "Then it is not his age, is it."

"That is what everybody keeps telling me."

"I know what everybody keeps telling you."

I said, "I shower every morning. I put clean clothes on before I go out there. I do not wear perfume."

"I know you do."

"Then what," I said. "Just tell me what."

"30 years I worked in that building with women our age and older," she said.
"Things change on a person. Your hair goes. Your knees go.
Nobody's fault. You color it. You get a brace."

"Your skin starts making something it never made before. It has a smell on it. Not a nice one."

"I have never heard of that in my life."

"Nobody has. Some women early, some late. Nobody warns you. It just turns up, like the gray."

"And not one of those women was dirty," she said. "Not one of them.
Some of them had daughters in there washing them twice a day."

I sat with that a second. "Then I will shower twice a day."

"That," she said, "is the part everybody gets wrong. Regular soap does not take it off."

"Now you are being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic," she said. "You chop garlic. Then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed on them anyway.
Because garlic leaves something behind that soap does not touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal," she said. "It works the same way. Soap runs off it."

I sat there with my hands around a cup of coffee I had not drunk.

"Then why has nobody ever told me?"

"Who would. Bill would not notice a fire in this kitchen.
And the ones who would notice are grown women, so they will not say it.
I would not be saying it now if you had not called me straight out of a parking lot."

Then she said the sentence I have thought about every day since.

"Owen is 9. He has not learned yet to say nothing.
That is the whole difference between that boy and the rest of us out in that yard."

I put my hand over my mouth.

"He is not being cruel to you, Jo. He does not know he is telling you anything at all.
He only knows he wants to be over there."

I went back through the whole week right there at that table with her.

The pool. I got in the water. That put me 3 feet from him.
The book. I was sitting on the edge of the bed with my arm behind his head.
The car. I put him next to me.
The fort. I was standing at the corner with the clothespin.
The towel. I was holding it open with both hands, which means he had to walk into it.

Every one of them was a time I was close to him.
Not one of them was a time I asked him for something, or told him no. Just close.

He had not been pulling away from me.
He had been pulling away from a distance, and I was the one standing in it.

And the times he came running at me. The frogs. The sprinkler. Every one of them was from 6 feet away.

"It is not dirt," Marlene said. "It is not your washing.
You are one of the cleanest women I have ever known.
It is chemistry, and it did not ask you first."

"Then what gets it off."

She pushed the paper bag across the table. "I was hoping you would ask me before I had to offer it."

I opened the top of the bag.
There was a bar in there, wrapped in soft paper, orange, with writing on the front I could not read.

"It is soap," she said. "Persimmon. It does not cover it up. It takes it apart."

I turned the corner of the paper back. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It is called Kaori," she said.
"I bought a stack of them in the spring, when I heard they were stopping for the season.
They only press it once a year. When a batch is gone, you wait on the next harvest."

"And this works."

"I sent half that building home with one. I have used it 9 years.
You changed your face cream at 50 and never thought twice about it. You are still washing with what you used at 30."

She got up and put her cup in the sink.
"Use it tonight. And do not you say one word to that boy about any of this.
Not one word. He is 9."

At the door she turned around.
"And do not sit in here being ashamed of something your own skin did without asking your permission."

Then she went out on the porch to say hello to Owen, who ran at her, because he does.

I used it that night, after they were both asleep.

It is a bar of soap. I stood in my own shower at 10 at night and did not expect one single thing from it.
I got out and dried off. It was still there on my arms. Warm. Not sweet.

Saturday I did the whole routine anyway. The fetching. The quick hug.
I did not know how to stop.

Sunday morning I made myself sit still.

He was in the pool by 8, because it was the last day and he knew it.
I brought the little steps over and sat down on the bottom one with my feet in the water.
Which is what I did the Sunday before. Which is the thing that started all of this.

I did not look at him. I looked at the fence.

He stayed in.

He was on the far side with the mosasaur, and then he was not on the far side.

He came over and stood in front of me in the water.
He told me that a mosasaur is not a dinosaur, actually, and that everybody gets that wrong.
He stayed there talking at me about it long enough that my feet went cold in 14 inches of water in July.

That is the whole thing that happened. A boy stood in front of me and talked about a reptile.

He never said one word about any of it. He does not know there was anything to say.
He only knew he wanted to be over there. That morning he wanted to be here.

He got out at 10 to get in the car. I was standing at the rail with the towel.
He came up the steps to me, dripping the whole way, and let me put it around him.
Then he leaned his forehead on my stomach for a second, the way he did when he was 4.

I had about 4 things I wanted to say to that boy and I did not say one of them.

At the car, with the door open, he asked when his week was next year.

He asked Nicole. Nicole said, "Ask Grandma."

He looked at me and said, "When is it."

I said the first week of July. Same as always.

He said, "Okay," and got in the car.

The 3rd week of August, Nicole texted me the dates for next summer. I had not asked her.
5 years I have asked her every August, and this year I did not have to.

I quit standing back from people. I did not know I had been doing it until I stopped.

I keep the Kaori in the shower now. In the dish on the left.
Marlene texted me last week. The new batch lands the 1st of September.

Owen turns 10 in March. He has 1 of these left after this one.
I am going to be in the water for it.

If one of your grandchildren has started pulling back from you, and you cannot think of one reason why.
If everybody in your family keeps telling you it is just his age.
If you have started hugging them quick and letting go first, before they can do it to you.

It maybe is not anything you did. Maybe you just need a better bar.

It is a bar of soap. It costs less than a bottle of perfume.
They give you 60 days on it. You can use the whole thing and still send it back.
There is no harm in trying it.

They press the persimmon once a year. The new batch lands the 1st of September.
When a batch is gone, you wait on the next harvest.

It is called Kaori. The link is below. It is the one that worked for me.

Then get the pool out, and put the sign back up, and ask for the week.

It was never his age.

Your move.

body.text:
Please stop buying the orange ones. I know that sounds odd. Every box in the category is orange. Every listing has persimmons photographed on it. The orange is the whole reason you recognise it as persimmon soap in the first place.

It looks logical. Persimmons are orange, so persimmon soap is orange. Basic sense.

Except it's backwards. And the reason it's backwards is the entire difference between a bar that works and £22 in the bin.

Women aren't failing with persimmon soap because persimmon soap doesn't work. They're failing because of which fruit is in the bar.

Buying a dearer orange one doesn't fix that. It just costs more.

Here's what's actually going on. Because nobody selling these will ever explain it to you.

There are two completely different materials being sold under one word.

Kakishibu is fermented persimmon tannin. Unripe astringent persimmons are picked green and hard - at the stage where biting one shuts your mouth up - then pressed, and left in a vat to ferment for months. What comes out is dark, thick and nearly black. Japan has used it for four hundred years, on paper, on fabric, on wood and on skin.

Persimmon juice is the pressed ripe fruit. It's cheap, it's orange, and it photographs beautifully in a bar of soap.

Both are legally allowed to print the word persimmon on the front of the box, in the same size type.

Now here's why the difference decides everything.

The compound behind aging odour is called 2-nonenal. Japanese researchers identified it in 2001. It is not sweat, it is not bacteria, and it has nothing to do with hygiene.

It's an oil. Which is why ordinary soap cannot lift it - soap is a detergent built for sweat and water-soluble dirt, and oil and water don't mix. You already know that from a roasting tin.

What lifts it is the tannin. Tannins are polyphenols; they carry several binding sites that latch onto the molecule and carry it off with the rinse water.

And the tannin is concentrated in the unripe fruit. It is what makes the green one astringent. As the fruit ripens and sweetens, that astringency goes - which is the same thing as saying the tannin goes.

So the glossy orange persimmon on the front of the box is not a decorative choice.

It's the wrong fruit, photographed.

That escalating feeling - that you've tried this and it doesn't work on you, that you're somehow the exception - isn't in your head. It's real. But it isn't what you think it is.

Now here's where it gets worse.

You cannot smell this on yourself. Your own nose adapts within days and you go completely blind to it - not "hard to detect", impossible.

Which means you cannot evaluate a bar of soap. You use one for three weeks, you notice nothing, and you have no way on earth of telling the difference between "this bar is dyed glycerin" and "this bar is working perfectly and I simply cannot tell."

Buy the wrong fruit. Feel nothing. Get no feedback. Conclude the idea is nonsense. Give up on the one thing that was going to help.

That is the loop this whole category runs on, and it is why so many women have three of these in a drawer.

This is why nothing has worked.

"Persimmon fruit extract" on a panel is the ripe fruit. A trace of it, usually below the fragrance.

"Persimmon" on the front of the box and nowhere in the ingredients means there is no persimmon in the bar at all.

CI 15985 is an orange food colouring. It is the reason the bar is orange and it is doing no work whatsoever.

A Japanese-looking font is not a Japanese product. One of the bars I was shown had Japanese characters on the front and Guangdong on the bottom, in six-point type.

And four and a half stars from two thousand people means two thousand people found it pleasant in week one. It does not mean it worked, because none of them could have known.

And the price tells you nothing either.

That is worth saying on its own, because it is the trap almost every woman falls into. The first bar does nothing, so you buy a dearer one — which is the correct instinct in every other category and is worthless in this one.

Price has no relationship to which fruit is in the bar. I have seen dyed glycerin sold at thirty pounds and I have seen a genuine fermented bar sold for less than that. The cheapest real one costs a little more than the dearest fake, and that is the whole of the relationship.

Nor does the country on the front. Two bars I was shown had Japanese characters printed across them. One said Guangdong on the base, in six-point type, where nobody would look.

Nor do the reviews, and this is the one that costs women the most. Four and a half stars from two thousand people means two thousand people found a bar pleasant in its first week. Not one of them could have known whether it worked, because none of them could smell it on themselves. Those reviews are honest. They are simply measuring the wrong thing.

The label has been the only real evidence the entire time. And almost nobody turns the box over.

Except there is one thing that cannot be faked, and it takes ten seconds.

Hold the bar up to a window. Fermented kakishibu is translucent amber and the light goes straight through it, like a piece of resin. A dyed bar is opaque all the way through.

Then look at the panel for two words: Diospyros Kaki.

That's it. That's the whole test.

I grew up with the real thing in my grandmother's bathroom in Mino, in Gifu, which is where it has been made for centuries, and I have written down exactly what I check. Including:

• Where on the ingredient panel it has to sit before the amount means anything - which matters far more than whether the word is there at all.

• The window test, and the one lighting condition where it will fool you.

• What "fermented" is allowed to mean on a British box, and what it usually means.

• Why the bar being unscented is the thing I'd check second, and what a fragrance in this particular product is almost always covering.

Read it before you buy another one - from us or from anybody 👇

cards.body:
I lost my granddaughter at 66 because I can't smell. She told her mom my house makes her sick. I can't smell a thing. But that I heard.

I was in the kitchen. She was in the hallway with her mom. She didn't know I was there.

"Mommy I don't want to go to grandma's house. It makes me sick."

My sweet girl. The one who used to fall asleep on my chest every Sunday. That girl just told her mother that being near me makes her sick.

I stood there holding the counter and I couldn't breathe. Makes her sick. What makes her sick? What is she talking about?

I lost my sense of smell a year before Covid hit. It never came back. Not even a little. I can't smell my food, my clothes, my house, my own skin. Nothing. So when my granddaughter says something makes her sick, I can't just sniff it out like a normal person. I'm blind.

That night I didn't sleep.

I crawled through every room on my hands and knees trying to understand what she meant. Pressed my face into the couch cushions. Nothing. Held my curtains against my nose. Nothing. Put my face flat on the carpet. Nothing.

What is it, baby? What are you smelling? I was begging my house to give me an answer my nose couldn't.

I cleaned everything. Every surface, every fabric, every corner. Had the pipes checked. Had someone look for mold. Opened every window for days in the middle of winter. None of it mattered. Because I couldn't tell if any of it helped. I was fixing things in the dark.

And the whole time there was one place I never thought to check.

Something in the back of my mind was already whispering it. I just wasn't ready to hear it.

Then I started remembering things I had been too afraid to connect.

My granddaughter pulling away from me. Not all at once. Slowly. First she stopped sitting in my lap. Then she stopped hugging me. Then she started staying on the other side of the room.

I told myself she was just growing up. Kids do that.

But then I thought about my son. Last time he hugged me at the door, he held his breath. I felt his chest lock up against mine. Just for a second. He thought I wouldn't notice. But when you lose your smell, you start feeling things other people miss. Your whole body pays attention in ways it never did before. I felt him stop breathing.

After the hug he opened both windows in the guest room. It was November.

Then I thought about my neighbor. Every Tuesday we have coffee. And every Tuesday for six months her chair moved a little further from mine. One week she said let's sit outside. It was 45 degrees.

Then my book club. How Carol opens a window when I arrive. How Janet switched seats last month. How nobody says a word but something shifts every time I walk in.

Nobody told me. Not one person. But every single one of them did something.

Standing alone in my hallway at 1 AM, all of it hit me at once. The windows. The chairs. The held breath. The distance. My granddaughter's words.

They could all smell something I couldn't.

It was never the pipes. Never mold. Never the house.

It might be me.

That thought almost broke me.

I stopped inviting people over. Birthdays became phone calls. I quit book club. I couldn't sit in Carol's living room for two hours wondering if everyone was waiting for me to leave.

You want to know the loneliest feeling in the world? Sitting in your own living room afraid to answer the door because you have no idea what hits people when they walk in. And you can't fix it because you can't smell it. And you can't ask because you're terrified of the answer.

I showered twice a day. Bought the most expensive body wash I could find. Scrubbed until my skin turned red. Stayed up past 2 AM searching things I was ashamed to type. "Why do old people smell." "Can you stink and not know it." Found women my age asking the same questions. All of them doing everything right. Not one had figured it out.

I closed my laptop and sat in the dark. This is my life now. A grandmother who makes her own granddaughter sick. And I can't even smell why.

Then Margaret showed up.

No call. No text. She just appeared at my kitchen door on a Thursday with a paper bag. Put it on the table. Sat down. Took both my hands.

And said three words nobody had said to me in years.

You smell, Linda.

I broke down. Not from shame. From relief. Finally someone loved me enough to say what everyone else was too polite to say.

And then she told me something that changed everything.

Margaret worked in elder care for 30 years. Thousands of older people. And she told me something no doctor, no family member, no friend ever did.

She said our bodies start making a compound as we age. Called Nonenal. It comes out through the skin. Musty. Stale. Sour. The kind of smell that gets into furniture, blankets, walls.

And here's what made my jaw drop. Every person she ever cared for who had this smell was clean. Bathed. Groomed. It didn't matter. Because Nonenal is not dirt. It's not sweat. It comes from inside the skin. And regular soap, no matter how expensive, no matter how hard you scrub, cannot touch it.

Every shower. Every body wash. Every time I scrubbed my arms raw. None of it could have worked. Not because I wasn't trying hard enough. Because soap was never built to fight what was actually on my skin.

Margaret said her staff tried everything for 30 years. Air fresheners. Essential oils. Special detergent. Organic soap. Nothing worked. Because nothing was going after the actual cause.

Until one day a nurse brought in a soap made with Japanese persimmon. Persimmon has something that grabs onto Nonenal and breaks it apart. Not covers it up. Not hides it. Breaks it down. Gone.

Within days the staff saw the difference. Not air freshener fighting something underneath. Just clean.

Then she opened the paper bag. Inside was a bar of Kaori soap. She put it in my hands like it was medicine.

"I already ordered it for you. Two more bars are coming next week. This is the one we use. Has been for years. The concentration is right, it actually works, and it's made with real Japanese persimmon. Not some watered down version. The real thing."

She paused.

"Just so you know, they sell out. A lot. So when you get low, don't wait."

She squeezed my hands, got up, and went home.

I used it that night. Didn't expect anything. First thing I noticed was my skin. Softer. Like something that had been sitting on it for years was gone. A layer I didn't know was there.

But I couldn't smell it. I still can't. So I had to wait and watch the people around me.

Week one. My daughter sat right next to me on the couch. Arm against arm. She hadn't done that in a very long time.

Week two. Margaret came by and didn't say a word about any smell.

Week three. My son hugged me at the door. His chest opened up. He breathed in. Full breath. Face near my neck. Like it was nothing. Like I was just his mom again.

Week four.

My granddaughter walked through the door. Dropped her backpack. Walked straight to me. Climbed into my lap. Put her little head against my chest.

And fell asleep.

I sat there with her hair under my chin and her breath on my collarbone and cried so hard I had to cover my mouth so I wouldn't wake her.

I thought about the nights on my knees begging my house to tell me what was wrong. The scrubbing. The shame. The years alone. It was never the house. It was on my skin the whole time. And nobody told me. And I couldn't smell it. And nothing I tried was ever going to work.

I can't get those years back. The Tuesdays alone. The birthdays by phone. The nights replaying what my sweet girl said about me.

But she's here now. On my chest. And whatever kept her away is gone.

If nobody in your life is honest enough to be your Margaret, let me be her for you right now.

It's called Kaori. It's the only soap I use. It's the only soap Margaret gives to the people she cares for. And it's the only thing that ever made a difference.

https://try-kaori.com/products/deodorizing-persimmon-soap

It costs less than the fancy body wash I was already wasting money on. The one that was never going to work.

Because every day you spend guessing is another Tuesday alone. Another birthday by phone. Another moment where the person you love most buries her face in her mother's sleeve because she can't stand to be near you.

And you just stand there. Unable to smell a thing. Hearing all of it.

Don't wait until they're out of stock again. Margaret warned me. She was right.

body.text:
My Seven-Year-Old Granddaughter Asked Me Why I Am Not in Any of the New Photographs. I Did Not Have an Honest Answer for Her. I Am Sixty-Two and I Had Been Quietly Hiding for Two Years.

I am writing this because four people I see regularly have asked me in the last two months what I have been doing differently.

My hairdresser of eleven years.

A woman in my book club.

My daughter.

I have been giving them the short answer. I am writing the long answer down now so I can hand it to the next person who notices.

I am Margaret. I am sixty-two. I retired three years ago after twenty-nine years teaching grade three. I am married to Ray. He is sixty-four, retired the year before I did. We have one daughter, married, and one granddaughter, who is seven. We have lived in the same house for twenty-six years.

For most of my adult life, I had been a woman who was in the photographs.

I do not mean anything dramatic by that. I mean that things happened, and someone took a picture, and I was in it. I did not think about it.

Then about two years ago, I started volunteering to hold the camera.

I did not notice it at first.

Christmas, I took the photos. Her birthday, I took the photos. Easter, I took the photos.

By last spring I had not been in a family photograph in over a year, and I had been pretending I had not noticed.

It was not the only thing that had been quietly changing.

Dorothy and I had been having coffee on Thursday mornings for nine years. I started begging off about a year ago. I told her my mornings had gotten busy. My mornings had not gotten busy. I had been at home.

My daughter and I had been video calling on Sunday evenings. About eight months ago I started leaving my camera off. I told her my connection was poor. My connection was fine.

And I had started buying blouses with higher necklines, which I told myself was a change in taste.

Every morning for two years I had been doing the same thing at the bathroom mirror. Washing my face. Feeling it go tight within a minute. Putting on more cream. Waiting. Putting on foundation and watching it settle straight into the dry patches around my mouth and into lines I did not remember having.

Then rubbing at it with my finger. Then putting more on top.

I had been doing that every single morning for two years and I had never once said it out loud to anybody.

My granddaughter, who is seven, had been quietly noticing that Grandma was not in the pictures.
I did not know she had been noticing.

I want to tell you the afternoon I found out.
It was a Sunday in October. She was at our house for the afternoon. She had found the photo albums in the hall closet, the paper ones from before everything went on phones.

She was on the living room floor turning pages.

She said: "Grandma. Come look."

I said: "Of course, sweetheart."

I sat down on the floor next to her. She was looking at a page from about ten years ago. Me and her mother at a picnic table.

She said: "That's you."

I said: "That's me, love."

She turned a few more pages. Then she stopped and looked up at me.

She said, quietly: "Grandma. Why aren't you in the new ones?"

I said: "What do you mean, sweetheart?"

She said: "In the new ones you're always the one taking it. You're not in any of them. Don't you want to be in them?"

I did not say anything for a second.

I looked at my seven-year-old granddaughter sitting on the floor next to me.

She was looking at me with the careful face of a child who has been noticing something for a while and has finally decided she is brave enough to ask.

I said: "Sweetheart. I do not know why."

She thought about that for a moment.

Then she reached up and put her hand on my cheek, the way children do.

She said: "Grandma. Are you okay?"

I said: "I think so, love. I am going to find out."

She nodded. She patted my cheek. She went back to the album.

I sat on that living room floor and tried to remember when I had become a woman whose granddaughter was asking her quietly if she was okay.

I could not remember.

I had been holding the camera for two years. A seven-year-old had named it in two sentences on a Sunday afternoon in October.

I did not tell Ray about it that day.

I went to bed that night and I lay in the dark and I tried to be honest with myself for the first time in two years about what I had been pretending not to notice.

The photographs were one thing.

There were other things.

Dorothy on Thursdays. The camera off on Sunday calls. The necklines. The mirror every morning.

I had been telling myself for two years that this was sixty and sixty-one and sixty-two.

I had been telling myself the skin changes.

What I had not been telling myself was that my mother had not hidden from a camera at seventy.

I told Ray the next morning at breakfast.

He did not look surprised. He listened. He did not interrupt me.

When I was done, he reached across the table and put his hand on my hand.

He said: "Margaret. I have been waiting for you to be ready to say it."

I made an appointment with my doctor that morning.

She ran everything. Bloodwork. Thyroid, because that can do this. She looked at my skin properly.

Everything came back fine.

She sat down with me at the follow-up.

She said: "Margaret. Your bloodwork is unremarkable. Your thyroid is fine. There is nothing here I would treat."

She paused.

She said: "What you are describing is real. It just does not show up on the standard panel."

She explained that after menopause, oestrogen drops, and the skin stops producing the oils it had been producing for forty years. It gets drier. It holds water less well. It is not a disease. It is not something she would prescribe for. It is real, and it is what I was feeling.

She gave me the standard advice. Gentle cleanser. Moisturise. Sunscreen. Come back if anything changes.

I thanked her. I drove home. I sat in the driveway for a while before I went inside.

I am going to skip the part where I read for the next three weeks.

Most evenings at the kitchen table after Ray went to bed, with my laptop and the notepad I had taken to keeping beside it.

I taught school for twenty-nine years. I read carefully. I do not believe things easily.

Here is the short version of what I concluded.

My skin had stopped making its own oils. And every single product I owned was mostly water.

I went and looked. I turned over every jar in my bathroom. Water was the first ingredient on almost all of them.

Water evaporates. It was never going to replace an oil.

What replaces an oil is an oil.

The one that kept coming up was beef tallow. Not because it is exotic but because the fats in it are close to the fats human skin makes for itself. Oleic acid. Palmitic. Stearic. It is what women used before any of this was an industry.

I also read about how most of it is processed. Cheap tallow is bleached and deodorised to take the smell out, and that stripping takes the nutrients with it. If it is snow white, something has been done to it.

I found a small Canadian company called The Tallowed Truth. They triple-purify theirs instead of bleaching it. Five ingredients: grass-fed tallow, raw honey, beeswax, cold-pressed olive oil, frankincense.

Before I ordered anything, I called my doctor's office.

I told the nurse I had been reading about a tallow balm and wanted to make sure the doctor was comfortable with me trying it.

The nurse called back the next afternoon.

She said: "She says it is a sensible thing to try. It is a moisturiser, not a medication. Add it to what you are doing. Come back at your next visit."

I ordered a tin that evening.

I started using it the following Monday. A small amount at night, on damp skin. I did not change anything else.

I want to tell you what I noticed over the next four weeks. I am not going to make a claim about what caused what. I am going to tell you what happened in the order it happened.

The first thing was small.

About four days in, I washed my face in the morning and my skin did not go tight.

I noticed it about a minute later, standing at the mirror with nothing in my hands.

I did not know whether that was the first morning it had happened or whether it had happened the day before and I had missed it.

I did not say anything to Ray. I did not want to draw attention to it in case drawing attention to it broke something.

I just noticed.

About two weeks in, my foundation stopped catching. It went on the way it used to. I sat in the car afterwards and looked at my face in the visor mirror for longer than I would like to admit.

A week after that, I rang Dorothy on a Wednesday and asked if she still had Thursdays free.

She said: "Margaret. I have had Thursdays free for a year."

We have been going every week since.

Around the end of the first month, my daughter called on a Sunday and I left the camera on.

She stopped mid-sentence.

She said: "Mum. You look really well."

I said: "Thank you, love."

She did not say anything else about it. But she noticed.

In December we were at her house and she took a photograph of me on the front step holding my granddaughter.

I did not ask her to delete it.

It is on our fridge.

I want to be careful here.

I am not a doctor. I am not in skincare. I am a retired schoolteacher.

I am one sixty-two-year-old woman who had been quietly holding the camera for two years and pretending she was not, and who finally heard the truth said out loud by a seven-year-old sitting on the living room floor.

I do not know for certain that the balm is responsible for what changed.

I know what I was doing before. I know what I added. I know what has happened since. I know the timing.

I also know I am sixty-two, and there will come a day when no jar holds back the slow turning of the years.

I am not pretending otherwise.

What I am telling you is what I tried and what I noticed.

That is all.

Sometimes the things we miss in ourselves are the small ones.

The camera we keep volunteering to hold.

The coffee we have been begging off from.

The video call we take with the camera off.

The blouse we bought because of the neckline.

If you are a woman somewhere in your fifties or sixties or seventies, and you have been quietly stepping out of your own photographs for a year or two, and you have been telling yourself it is just age, here is what I would say.

Talk to your doctor. Tell them what you have been pretending not to notice. Get things ruled out.

If everything comes back fine and the answer is moisturise and wear sunscreen, then consider that the problem may not be that you need a stronger cream.

It may be that your skin stopped making something, and you have been putting water on it ever since.

Do not subtract anything. Do not change anything else.

Give it a few weeks before you decide anything.

Skin is different from person to person. For me, the first thing I noticed was washing my face and not going tight, at about day four.

That is the whole story.

P.S. I told my granddaughter at Christmas that I wanted her to keep telling me when she notices things. She was very serious about it. She said: "Grandma. Like what?" I said: "Like the photographs, love. If you ever see me not in them again, you can tell me." She said: "Grandma. Okay." That is how this works. A seven-year-old asks her grandmother why she is not in the pictures. The grandmother reads for three weeks. She starts. A month later she leaves the camera on. In December there is a photograph on the fridge.

P.P.S. Here is what I would tell you to do if you are thinking about trying it. Check with your doctor first. Then a small amount at night, on damp skin. Do not change anything else. Give it a few weeks. Some people notice something in the first week. Others take longer. Be patient with your skin.

P.P.P.S. There is a thirty-day money-back guarantee. If you are not satisfied for any reason, every penny back. That is what made me willing to try it in the first place.

P.P.P.P.S. Dorothy started using it in January. She has not said one word to me about it. But she has been in the last two photographs.

body.text:
I've been a geriatric nurse for twenty-one years. I can tell exactly who's still taking care of themselves and who's secretly starting to slip. And it always shows up in the same place first. 

Everyone expects it to happen suddenly.

A fall. A stroke. One bad day that splits someone's life into a before and an after.

That's not how it usually goes.

It comes on so slow that nobody can say when it started. A little at a time. And by the time it's plain enough to put a name to, it's already been happening for years.

I've watched it creep up on more of my clients than I could count.

It always starts with something they mention in passing. They can't quite reach things the way they used to. Can't twist the lid off a jar, can't fasten a necklace behind their own neck anymore. They laugh it off. 

'Their shoulders just aren't what they were.'

Then they complain about their back itching at night. It keeps them awake. And they've already settled on a reason before I can ask. 

Dry skin. The new detergent. Something they can wave a hand at.

None of it seemed like much on its own. It never does.

But there was one more thing. And this one never came from the residents themselves.

It came from their family. Their sons and daughters.

One of them would catch me in the hallway on my way out, once her mother was settled back in her chair. She'd lower her voice so it wouldn't carry through the door. And she'd ask me, careful as she could, whether I'd noticed anything.

A smell. Faint. Underneath the perfume and the fresh-pressed blouse. Something she'd caught when she hugged her mother goodbye and had been turning over in her mind ever since.

She didn't know how to bring it up with her own mother. She couldn't stand the thought of embarrassing her. So she brought it to me instead. A stranger in scrubs.

That's the part that always stayed with me. They'd tell me. They would never tell her.

The shoulders. The itching. A faint smell the family only ever whispered about in doorways.

For twenty-one years I watched those three things line up client after client. And every single time, I told myself the same tidy little sentence.

It's just age. It’s normal.

I believed that sentence for two decades. Didn’t waste a second thought about it.

Then the thing with Margaret happened. 

And looking back, that's the moment everything changed. Not when I found the research at 1 AM. Not when I finally found the real reason behind all these symptoms.

It was the moment her daughter called me and told me about her mother.

Margaret had thirty years on me, and from the very first visit we got on like we'd known each other our whole lives. She was sharp. Funny in that dry way that sneaks up on you. The kind of woman who had her lipstick on and the good cups set out before I ever reached the door, because she would sooner go without than let anyone catch her looking less than herself.

She'd lived on her own for years and had no intention of changing that. Did everything herself. Was proud of it, and she'd earned every bit of that pride.

She was the visit I looked forward to all week.

Then one morning I got a call from her daughter. Her name was Sarah.

She told me Margaret was in the hospital.

Cellulitis. A skin infection that had gotten into her blood.

Forty-eight hours. That's all it took to go from feeling a little run down to a hospital bed.

The doctor told her it started from a small skin break, on her back. The kind that opens up on skin that hasn't been properly cleaned in a long time. Somewhere she couldn't see or reach.

They came very close to losing her.

I got off the phone and I sat down at my kitchen table. And I stayed there a long while before I did anything else.

Because something had just come back to me.

A few things, actually.

The last few visits, Margaret had struggled to get herself out of her own cardigan. She'd laughed it off, said her shoulders just weren't what they used to be. I'd smiled and let it go.

She'd mentioned, more than once, that her back had been keeping her up at night with the itching. She'd said it the way she said everything she didn't want fussed over. Dry skin, she figured. I'd nodded and moved on.

And when I'd leaned in close to take her blood pressure, I'd caught something I'd been pushing out of my mind ever since. Her perfume smelled the same. Her powder smelled the same. But underneath all of it, there was a faint odor I'd never once associated with Margaret before.

The stiff shoulders. The itching. The faint smell I'd caught myself and never said a word about.

The exact same three things I'd been brushing off as ordinary old age in a dozen other clients of mine .

I couldn't stop the next thought if I tried.

How many men and women on my list right now had all three? And how long before I got the same call about one of them that I'd just gotten about Margaret?

That night I couldn’t sleep. 

Instead, I sat at the kitchen table and started searching online.

It was past 11 PM. I had my laptop open and a half-cold cup of tea next to me, and I typed in everything I could think of.

"Old people smell." 

“Mobility issues seniors.” 

"Skin infection older people cellulitis." 

I went down a long, frustrating rabbit hole.

Most of what I found was about moisturizers. Recommendations for ceramide creams. Articles about "barrier repair" and retinol and a hundred different products I could ship to my house tomorrow.

But somewhere around one in the morning, I clicked on something different.

It was a medical article by a dermatologist who specialized in older adult skin care. And one paragraph stopped me cold.

The dermatologist explained something I'd never consciously thought about before.

She wrote that genuinely clean skin requires three things working together. Not one. Not two. Three.

Water. Soap. And friction — actual scrubbing of the skin. 

Your hand on a washcloth. Your fingers working lather into your chest. Something physically moving across the skin to lift away what's sitting on top of it.

She wrote that all three have to be present. Water without soap doesn't dissolve oil. Soap without water doesn't rinse. And water plus soap without mechanical action doesn't actually remove anything. It just makes the skin wet.

I sat at my kitchen table and thought about my own shower that morning.

For my arms, I had all three. Water. Body wash. My own hands lathering it in.

For my chest, my belly, my legs. Same. All three.

For my back — and I had to stop and actually picture it — I had water. That was it. Maybe a bit of soap that ran down my back during the rinse. But my hands never touched my back. The water flowed over it for maybe forty-five seconds and that was the entire wash.

Just water. For the part of my body I couldn't reach.

And I'm 46. My shoulders work. I could scrub my back with a washcloth if I really tried.

Margaret is 76. And I knew her shoulders had been bothering her for years.

I kept reading.

The article said the back is the single most important area of the body to clean properly with all three steps. Not because of how it looks. Because of what's on it.

The skin on the back produces more natural oil than most other areas of the body. Normally, that's not a problem. But when that oil isn't properly removed, it mixes with dead skin and gradually forms a sticky, invisible layer on the surface of the skin. And because dead skin tends to build up faster with age, that layer can become thicker over time.

I had to read that twice.

A sticky layer. On the back. Building up over time.

The article went on. That layer doesn't just sit there. It feeds bacteria.

Bacteria naturally live on everyone's skin and are usually harmless in small amounts. But when they have a continuous food source and an undisturbed environment, they multiply. And as they feed on the oil and dead skin, they produce waste compounds.

Body odor.

She wrote it plainly. Body odor isn't sweat. Sweat is mostly odorless. Body odor comes from bacteria feeding on the oil and dead skin buildup that hasn't been properly removed.

And the back, with its high oil production and the fact that it's so difficult to reach, creates the perfect place for buildup to collect over the years. That makes it one of the easiest places on the body for bacteria to grow. As a result, it's the area most likely to develop a persistent odor that no amount of showering removes.

I had to put the laptop down for a second.

Because I was thinking about when I took her blood pressure. The faint odor I tried to push out of my mind.

I picked the laptop back up and kept reading.

The article anticipated the question I was already forming. I was thinking, but if she smells, wouldn't she know? Wouldn't she notice?

No. The dermatologist explained this directly. The human nose adapts to constant smells within minutes. It's why you can't smell your own house or your own perfume after wearing it for an hour. Neither can the people who live with you, because they're habituated too.

The only people who can smell it are people who don't live with you. The daughter who flies in once every few months. The grandchildren who haven't seen her since Christmas. The neighbor she chats with at the mailbox.

Her own husband would have stopped being able to smell it years ago.

She would have no idea.

The article explained that most older adults assume the water and bit of soap reaching their back during a shower is enough to keep it clean.

But dead skin isn't loose dirt and sweat waiting to be rinsed away.

It's a literal layer that's attached to the skin.

She can shower twice a day, every day for a decade. And the layer on her back will keep growing, the bacteria will keep multiplying, and the odor will keep getting stronger. The shower routine she trusted was never reaching the problem in the first place. 

The article was reaching its end and I was reading faster now.

The dermatologist wrote that the persistent itching many older adults feel on their back at night. The kind that nothing seems to relieve. That they blame on dry skin or laundry detergent or aging. Is most often bacterial irritation underneath the buildup. It's not the surface skin that itches. It's what's living and feeding underneath.

I was nodding at my kitchen table at 1:30 in the morning like she was sitting across from me.

The last section of the article was the one I didn't want to read. But I read it anyway.

In older adults, the dermatologist wrote, the consequences of letting this layer accumulate are not just cosmetic. As skin thins with age, it becomes easier to tear. A small scratch or tear can happen without the person even noticing. And if bacteria are already growing on the buildup, that tiny opening can give them a way into the body.

That's when more serious problems can begin.

Cellulitis. Sepsis. The kind of skin infection that, in a 70-year-old woman with a weakened immune system, can become an ER visit in under 48 hours.

The exact thing that happened to Margaret.

I closed the laptop.

I sat there in the dark kitchen and I understood, for the first time, exactly what had happened to her. And exactly what was happening to my other clients, right now, in their own house, in their own shower, without them knowing.

They had no idea their routine wasn't reaching the part of their bodies that mattered most. They had no idea the layer was growing on their backs every single day they stood under that water thinking they were clean.

Even after I finally closed the laptop, I couldn't stop thinking about Margaret. 

Every visit. Every time she'd waved a hand and told me she was fine, that her shoulders were just getting old, that it was nothing worth fussing over. And I'd taken her at her word.

Margaret came home from the hospital a few days later. I gave her time to settle back in. Then I called her.

We talked for a while about how she was feeling. And then, gently, I asked her the one thing I'd never once thought to ask in all the years I'd known her. Whether she'd been able to reach her own back to wash it properly.

There was a long pause on the other end of the line.

Then she told me, very quietly, that she hadn't been able to properly reach her back in years.

She said it the way someone confesses something shameful.

She told me her shoulders just didn't rotate the way they used to. She'd tried a long-handled brush and it hurt to use. She'd tried stretching a washcloth across her back and it didn't really do anything. She'd just been hoping the warm water and the time she spent in the shower were doing enough.

She told me she'd been embarrassed about it for years. That her back had been itching at night for a long time. That she'd started showering twice a day a few months back, because she'd been worried she didn't smell right anymore.

She'd never mentioned it to a soul. She'd just been hoping nobody would notice.

I sat there and felt my eyes get hot.

This was the sharpest, proudest woman I knew. Who'd lived on her own for years and never once asked anybody for a thing. And she'd been quietly, privately losing the ability to take care of her own body, and was far too proud to ever say a word.

I told her I was going to find her something. She said I didn't need to. I told her I was going to anyway.

That afternoon I started looking for a solution.

Then I remembered my friend Jenny.

Jenny and I were roommates during junior year of college and stayed loosely in touch ever since. She'd gone into occupational therapy after graduation and spent almost twenty years in geriatric rehab.

She picked up on the second ring.

I didn't bother with small talk. I told her I needed her professional opinion.

I told her about Margaret. What had nearly happened to her. And I told her I couldn't stop thinking about how many of my other clients had the exact same problem.

There was a pause on the other end of the line.

Then Jenny made a small sound, like she'd heard it all before.

"You'd be surprised how often I get this call."

She told me she'd worked with plenty of older adults who could no longer comfortably reach their own backs. The itching. The buildup. The smell family members sometimes noticed before the person did.

None of it was new to her.

She said what these women needed was a way to actually clean their backs the way they'd cleaned the rest of their bodies their whole lives. 

Something they could use on their own, every day, without straining their shoulders or asking for help. Something that would physically lift the buildup off the skin instead of just sliding water over it. 

"Like one of those long-handled brushes?" I asked.

Jenny paused before answering.

“No, we usually don’t recommend those. The bristles trap bacteria between uses and then scrub it right back into the skin. They're also too rough for older skin. I've seen women come into our unit with small skin tears on their upper back from using them too aggressively. Those breaks are exactly where infections start."

I went very still.

I was thinking about Margaret. About the doctor explaining the cellulitis had probably started from a small skin break she hadn't noticed. On her back.

I asked Jenny if that's what could have happened to her.

There was a long pause on the other end of the line. 

"I can't say for sure. But yes. We see it."

I felt my stomach drop. 

What if Margaret had bought the brush because she knew something wasn't right? And what if the thing she thought would help had actually made things worse?

I asked Jenny what they recommended instead.

She responded almost immediately.

“We use a long, woven exfoliating towel.”

She explained it in a few sentences. 

About forty inches long. You hold one end in each hand, drape it across the back, and pull it slowly back and forth.

The leverage does most of the work, so the shoulders barely have to move.

The woven fabric holds onto soap and creates the gentle scrubbing action needed to lift away oil and dead skin buildup. The same buildup water alone can't remove. 

And because it's soft and flexible, it's gentle on aging skin while still cleaning properly.

Jenny said her own mother had been using one for years and wouldn't shower without it.

“It's not a fancy product. It's just the right tool. The design has been used by the Japanese for generations. Specifically to allow people to wash their own backs into very old age.” 

Then she said something that stayed with me.

"Look. Your patients probably aren't going to want to talk about this. They'll be embarrassed. Don't make them talk about it. Just give it to them. Tell them it's a Japanese thing you read about. They'll figure out how to use it in about thirty seconds and never bring it up. That's how it goes. They don't thank you. They just stop having the problem."

Jenny had to run. A patient was waiting. She said she'd text me the link to the towel they used at the clinic.

My phone buzzed two minutes later.

I ordered one that evening and had it sent straight to Margaret's house.

I saw her again at my next visit, about two weeks after the towel arrived.

I knew something was different the moment she opened the door.

I couldn't have told you what it was at first. She had her lipstick on, same as always. The good cups were already out. But she was lighter somehow. Like a woman who'd set something down she'd been carrying so long she'd forgotten the weight of it.

Then, halfway through her coffee, she brought it up herself. Almost shyly.

She said the towel I'd sent had arrived. She'd nearly set it aside, wasn't sure what to make of it. But she'd tried it in the shower that first night, and she wanted to tell me about it. 

She said she'd held one end in each hand, lathered it with her good Persimmon soap, and drawn it slowly across her back. And she'd barely had to move her shoulders at all. The towel did the reaching for her.

The first shower, she said, the water ran brown at her feet. Years of it, lifting off her skin all at once. She could see it caught in the weave of the towel when she rinsed it out. She said she stood there and watched it swirl down the drain and could hardly believe it had all been sitting on her.

By the third or fourth night, the itching that had kept her up for longer than she could remember had simply stopped.

She told me it was the first time in four years she'd felt truly clean.

She didn't say a word about the smell. She didn't have to. She had no idea it had ever been there, and she never would.

But I knew.

Because when I leaned in to take her blood pressure, the same way I had a hundred times before, there was nothing underneath the perfume this time. No faint note I had to pretend not to notice. Just clean skin. 

I sat back and wrapped the cuff around her arm and I had to work to keep my face steady.

She was still talking, telling me she'd already worked out which drawer to keep it in. Completely unaware that the thing that had put her in a hospital bed and nearly taken her, had quietly disappeared from her life.

Then she said something I've thought about many times since.

She looked down at her coffee and said, almost to herself, "I didn't realize how much I'd given up until I got it back."

After Margaret, I couldn't keep telling myself it was just age.

So one by one, quietly, I began giving those towels to my other clients. I never made a thing of it. I'd just leave one behind and tell them it was a Japanese thing worth trying. 

The way Jenny had told me to.

They almost never brought it up the first time. But by my next visit, it would come out. A little at a time. The same way the problem had, only in reverse.

One woman told me she hadn't felt that clean since before her grandchildren were born. That she'd stopped dreading the shower and started looking forward to it.

Another, seventy-nine years old, told me he could finally reach his whole back without that sharp pull in his shoulders. He said he felt like he could take care of himself again. He said it like it meant everything, because it did.

And I noticed something myself, too. With the new clients I started giving the towel to, the families stopped pulling me aside. 

No more quiet questions in the hallway on my way out. No more daughters lowering their voices to ask if I'd noticed anything. The thing they'd never had the heart to say to their mothers or fathers just quietly stopped being there.

None of them ever named the real reason any of it had changed. They didn't know there was anything to name. They just knew they felt like themselves again.

That's the part I wish I'd understood twenty years ago. This was never about smelling a certain way, or being clean for the sake of it. It was about staying the woman or man they'd always been. The one who takes care of themselves. The one nobody has to worry about.

That's what the towel really gave back.

If you'd like to try it yourself, I've put a link to it below. 

It's the same one my friend Jenny recommended to me, the one I've handed to more clients than I can count.

https://toshiico.com/pages/Toshi-Exfoliating-Towel

body.text:
"If your surgeon says a neck lift is the only fix for your double chin, read this first. I'm writing it from a hospital bed.

My name is Cheryl. I'm 58, I live outside Dayton, Ohio, and two weeks ago I had a neck lift for my double chin. The first night home, I almost died.

For fifteen years I hated what I saw under my chin. And I'm not someone who sits around and complains. Face yoga every morning in the car. The gua sha. The chin straps from Amazon. Twenty pounds lost. My chin didn't move. I cut myself out of my own grandkids' birthday photos, and when my husband Gary said I looked beautiful, I looked away.

So I paid. Almost five thousand dollars on double chin injections, three rounds. A year later, it was back. (Fewer than half the women who review those injections say they were worth it. Nobody showed me that number either.)

My surgeon looked at me and said, honestly, the only real fix is a neck lift. I believed him. He was the expert. I signed.

The first night home, I woke up at two in the morning and my neck felt hot and tight, like a belt pulled around it. I couldn't swallow. Then I couldn't breathe. I have never seen Gary scared in 34 years. He called 911. The last thing I remember is the ceiling of the ambulance. They opened my neck back up in the middle of the night to stop the bleeding.

Two days later, the head of the emergency surgery team sat on the edge of my bed. He asked, ""Why did you get this done?"" I said, ""My double chin."" He nodded like he'd heard it a hundred times. Bleeding like mine, he said, happens in up to one in twenty neck lifts. Nobody had ever told me that.

Then he said the thing that made me cry from anger. ""For most women your age, a double chin isn't even fat. Between thirty and fifty, your skin loses about half of its collagen. The skin under your jaw loses its hold, and it folds."" That's why it sags no matter how much weight you lose. And anything you rub on it is dry in about sixty seconds, so it never gets in.

He said skin like mine needs retinol, collagen and hyaluronic acid held flat against it for ten full minutes a day, in something shaped for the chin. My daughter Kayla heard everything. Three days later she walked in with a little blue and white pouch. I told her I was done with gadgets. She said, ""Mom. Just read it.""

It's called the Chinology Mask. A soft medical-grade silicone mask shaped for the chin, soaked in retinol, collagen and hyaluronic acid. It loops over your ears and cups your chin. The technology is called LiftPlus: instead of a serum that's dry in sixty seconds, it holds those three actives against the skin under your chin for ten full minutes. It comes from France, where women have used it for years. Over 500,000 women use it.

Fifteen years. Nobody ever looked at my skin. They measured my fat and sold me procedures, and I almost died for it. So yes, I was skeptical. I had a drawer full of things that ""worked."" Here's what made this different, and it's the only reason I let her put it on me: every single thing I'd tried was aimed at fat or at muscle. This was the first thing aimed at the skin itself, and the first one that stays on long enough to do anything.

The first time Kayla put it on me, it was cool, and snug enough that I could feel it lifting my jaw. I thought, okay. That's different.

I've worn it ten minutes a day, right here in this bed. I'm lying here anyway. You don't do anything. You put it on, you set a timer on your phone, you take it off. The nurses started timing it for me.

When I came in, my neck was so swollen I couldn't find my jaw. On day 10, the nurse took a photo of me from the side for my chart. There was a shadow under my jaw again. My jawline. She actually asked me if they had done another procedure. The emergency surgeon looked at me the next morning and said, ""Whatever you're doing, keep doing it.""

I'm still here because they're watching my airway. But yesterday my grandkids climbed up on this bed, Mason is 7 and Lily is 5, and Lily took a selfie with me. I didn't hide my chin. I held them, and I cried, because I almost didn't see them again.

Here's what I know now. Whatever you try for your chin has to do five things:

1. Work on the skin's hold, not only the fat.
2. Give the skin retinol, collagen and hyaluronic acid.
3. Keep them there long enough to matter. Sixty seconds is not enough.
4. Take ten minutes, not a hospital bed.
5. Put the risk on the company, not on you.

The Chinology Mask is the only thing I've found that does all five. The pack comes with 5 masks, and there's a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Some of you will ask the questions I asked Kayla, so here are the answers. No, it doesn't hurt. It feels cool, then snug. No, it's not a strap that squeezes and lets go; the ingredients stay on your skin. No, you don't need a surgeon's approval to put a mask on your chin. And no, it's not instant. Ten minutes a day. The difference showed up in photos, not in my imagination, and it showed up in someone else's eyes before mine.

And to the woman who thinks, ""It's too late for me, I'm too old for anything but the knife."" I'm 58, in a hospital bed, with a neck that just went through surgery twice. If it's not too late for me, it's not too late for you.

I kept thinking about the women who crop themselves out of every photo. The one who already booked her consultation because someone told her surgery is the only way. If one of you reads this and doesn't end up in a bed like this one, it was worth writing.

The link is below. It's the same page my daughter found. Wear it for three weeks, then look at your profile. Please, look at it before you book anything.

Cheryl, Dayton, Ohio

P.S. I'm not telling anyone surgery is always wrong. I'm telling you nobody told me the risk, and nobody told me the real reason my chin never changed. Now you know both."
