body.text:
Just threw them away. All three. I'm going to be honest with you – I should have turned them over two years ago.

I'm not someone who gets taken in easily. I'm 63 years old and I've been round the block enough times to know when something's too good to be true.

And persimmon soap? That screamed too good to be true. "Four hundred years of Japanese use. Lifts the compound behind aging odour. One ingredient."

Come on. I've heard promises like that a thousand times. From supplement companies, from adverts, from women in groups who swear by whatever the latest thing is.

And every single time I tried one? Nothing. Absolutely nothing.

I've spent probably six hundred pounds over the years on this – the musty note back by three in the afternoon on a day I've already showered twice, the pillowcase I check every morning and have never mentioned to a living soul, the coat I keep on indoors, the way I plan where I'll sit before I sit down. Antibacterial wash that stripped my skin and did nothing. A charcoal bar that dried my forearms out for a fortnight. Two "all day" sprays. A perfume I don't even like.

And three persimmon soaps. Nine pounds, fifteen, twenty-two.

Every one of them did precisely nothing, which is exactly why I decided the whole category was a con — and that is the part I want to talk about, because I was wrong in a very specific way.

So when I saw yet another one, my first instinct was to keep scrolling. Not interested. Been here three times. Next.

But then I actually read the piece about it.

And it said something no listing had ever said to me: that there are two completely different things being sold under the same word.

Kakishibu is the fermented extract of the UNRIPE persimmon. Picked green and hard, when it's so astringent it shuts your mouth. Pressed, then left in a vat for months until what comes out is dark and thick and nearly black. The tannin is in that. It grips the oil and takes it off the skin.

Persimmon juice is the ripe orange fruit. Cheap, orange, photographs beautifully in a soap, and has barely a trace of the tannin left in it.

Both can legally say persimmon on the front of the box, in the same size type. There is no standard behind those two words at all.

And I'll admit, it sounded... plausible? Like it actually explained WHY nothing had worked, which is more than any of the others even attempted.

Here's what got me though.

I got up, went into the bathroom, and turned all three of mine over on the side of the bath.

Not one of them listed persimmon anywhere in the ingredients.

One listed CI 15985. That is an orange food colouring. That was the only reason that bar was orange at all. And persimmon appeared on the front of that box four separate times.

I stood there in my dressing gown at half past nine at night doing sums.

Three bars. Two years. Forty-six pounds on soap, and about six hundred on everything else I bought because the soap "didn't work".

I hadn't tried persimmon soap three times and found it useless.

I had never once tried persimmon soap.

They went in the bin that night. All three. Including the twenty-two pound one I'd never even opened, which is the one that still annoys me, because by the time it arrived I had already given up.

What I keep coming back to is that I did everything right.

I read the front of the box. I checked the reviews — four and a half stars, two thousand of them. I paid more when the cheap one failed, which is what any sensible person does.

Every single one of those was the wrong thing to check.

And there's a reason this particular category gets away with it, which took me a while to work out.

You cannot smell this on yourself. Your own nose adapts within days and you go completely blind to it. It is not difficult to detect on yourself — it is impossible.

Which means you can't test a bar of soap. Not really. You use one for three weeks, you notice nothing, and you have no way of telling the difference between "this is dyed glycerin" and "this is working and I simply cannot tell."

So you buy another one. And when that does nothing, another.

The people printing persimmons on the front of those boxes know perfectly well that their customer has no way of checking. That's not a conspiracy. That's just what the category is built on.

Which is why the ingredient panel matters here more than in almost anything else you will ever buy. It is the only part of the box that cannot be written by the marketing department.

There's a second thing I got wrong, and I'd like to save you from it.

When the first bar did nothing, I upgraded. Nine pounds to fifteen to twenty-two.

That is the correct instinct in every other category on earth and it is completely useless in this one, because price has nothing whatsoever to do with which fruit is in the bar. My twenty-two pound one and my nine pound one were, as far as their ingredient panels are concerned, the same product with different photography.

The cheapest genuine one I have found costs more than the dearest fake I bought — but only just, and there are dyed bars sold at thirty pounds. The price tells you nothing. Only the panel does.

The third thing, which took me longest: I assumed a Japanese-looking box meant a Japanese product. Two of my three had Japanese characters printed on the front. One of them was made in Guangdong and said so, in six-point type, on the bottom.

None of that is illegal. That's the part that took me a while to accept. Nobody is doing anything they can be stopped from doing. There is simply no standard behind those two words, so all three of those bars and the real one are, legally, the same category of thing.

I'm not a woman who gets excited about a bar of soap. I'm the opposite of that woman. I'm the sceptical one rolling her eyes at wellness fads.

But I got it wrong for two years, and I got it wrong by being sensible.

If you're someone like me – sceptical, tired of being let down, already sitting on two or three orange bars that did nothing – please do one thing before you write the whole idea off the way I did.

Go and get them. All of them. Turn them over.

Look for two words: Diospyros Kaki. Then hold the bar up to a window — the real thing is translucent amber and the light goes straight through it. The dyed ones are opaque.

It takes ten seconds a bar and it is the only part of this that is genuinely hard to fake.

👉 And read this before you buy another one. The woman who makes the bar I use now grew up with it in Japan, in the town where it's made, and she's written down exactly what she checks and why what's sold here under that name usually isn't the same thing at all.

I wish I'd read it three bars and two years ago.

body.text:
I bought persimmon soap 4 times. I have only ever opened 1 bar. I have never told one living person why I bought them. You are not getting it out of me here either.

Not because I am being dramatic about it. I am 61 years old and I have never been dramatic in my life.

It is because if I tell you now, you will nod, and you will skim, and you will miss the part that cost me 2 years.

The part where I bought the right idea 4 separate times in the wrong form.

Bear with me.

It started the fall I turned 59, and it started with other people.

Ellen has us for Sunday lunch, or I have them. Her girl Sophie was 5 then.

Sophie used to come at me at the door like something fired out of a gun. That fall she started arriving and going straight past me to Frank.

At the table she asked to sit next to her mother. She asked nicely. She is a nicely brought up child.

Ellen started opening the kitchen window while we cooked. In November. She said it was the onions, and we were doing a chicken.

And nobody was unkind to me. I need to say that at the start, because if you are waiting for somebody in this to be cruel, nobody is.

They were all completely lovely to me the entire time, which is its own kind of thing to live through.

So I started making arrangements.

I got up before Frank so I could have the bathroom first, and I have been married to that man 39 years and he has never once beaten me to it since.

I started keeping my coat on indoors. I told everybody I was always cold, which is a strange thing to say about a woman who slept with the window open for 30 years.

I told my closest friend I had been sleeping badly, so she would stop asking me why I had stopped coming to things.

I stopped coming to things.

In March, Sophie was in my kitchen while I was getting the plates down, and she said, "Grandma, why do you keep your coat on in the house?"

Frank laughed. Ellen said Sophie, don't be rude.

I said I was cold, and I heard how it sounded, and I stood at that counter with a stack of plates in my hands and understood that a 6 year old had been the only person in my family willing to ask me a direct question.

That was the week I started buying.

That was the March I turned 60. The first one was 9 dollars. An orange bar, persimmons all over the box, a bit of Japanese writing on the front, 4 and a half stars from 2,000 women.

I used it every day for 3 weeks. Nothing.

In the summer I bought a dearer one, because that is what you do. 12 dollars. It said authentic on the front. Nothing.

At Christmas the third one was 15. It said lab tested, without naming a lab anywhere on the box or the listing. I used that one 4 days.

The fourth came this March, a year to the month after the first one. 22 dollars, and I never opened it at all. It is still in the drawer in its wrapper, and it is the one that upsets me the most, because by the time it came I had already decided the whole idea was nonsense and that I was going to have to live like this.

In April I went to the doctor.

I had rehearsed 2 sentences for a fortnight so I could get them out without stopping, and I got them out.

I said I thought there was a smell about me and that I could not tell, and that my family had started standing further away.

She was kind about it. She really was.

She said, "A lot of women become more sensitive to smells around and after the menopause. It's very normal at your age."

She had heard it the other way round. She thought the problem was my nose.

Normal.

That word went into me like a stone into a pond.

Because normal means there is nothing to be done. Go home. Get used to the smaller, quieter version of yourself that everybody apparently expects now.

I sat in that parking lot for 15 minutes before I drove home.

Here is the thing nobody tells you, and it is the reason there are 4 of them in that drawer.

You cannot check. There is no test. You cannot lean into your own shoulder at 11 at night before your granddaughter's birthday and settle it one way or the other.

So when a bar does not work, you cannot tell the difference between this did nothing and this worked and I still cannot tell.

Which means you buy another one. And another one.

I was not being stupid. I was doing the only thing available to a woman who cannot audit her own body.

In May I cancelled Sunday. Ellen said no problem, we'll do it next week.

In June I cancelled again. She said don't worry about it, Mom, honestly.

The third time, in July, she did not argue with me at all.

She said, "Okay. Next time then." Warm as anything. And she hung up first.

I stood in my kitchen with the phone in my hand and thought, she has stopped trying to get me there.

Being let off is worse than being pushed. Nobody tells you that either.

I have lunch with Marge on the last Thursday of the month at the diner on Route 9. We have done it since our girls were at school together.

Marge is 74. She was the school nurse at Lincoln for 30 years and she has a way of waiting that gets things out of people.

She asked me why I had not been at Carol's thing in June, and I gave her the sleeping answer, and she put her fork down and did not pick it back up.

"Try that again," she said.

So I told her. All of it, in the wrong order, in a diner booth, including the drawer.

She listened to the whole thing. Then she said the thing I did not expect.

"The idea was right."

"What?"

"Persimmon. That part is not nonsense. It's the only thing I've ever seen shift it."

"Marge, I bought 4."

"I know. Hold on. You've got the front of this back to front."

She moved her coffee to one side, which is what she does when she is going to be a nurse at you.

"There's something," she said. "You're not imagining it, and it isn't your fault, and it isn't dirt."

"I shower every day. I have showered every day of my life."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"30 years I looked after other people's children and their grandmothers came in too. Things change for women our age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Then what have I been doing since March."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

The waitress filled us up and went away again.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

"Tannins. Which are in persimmon. That's why you went and bought 4 of them, and you were right to."

"They did nothing."

"Go home and get the boxes. All 4. Turn them over and find me the persimmon in the ingredients."

I said the fruit is on the front of every one of them.

"I know what's on the front," she said.

I did it that night at my own kitchen table with Frank watching a ball game in the next room.

Water. Palm oil. Glycerin. Fragrance. A color with a number after it.

The first box, nothing. The second box, nothing. The third box, nothing.

The fourth one I had to take the wrapper off after 5 months to read it, and it had a fruit extract in it, second from the bottom, after the color.

4 bars. Four times I had said to myself, well, I have tried persimmon soap.

I had never once tried persimmon soap.

Marge put a small parcel on the table at the diner the following month, wrapped in tissue paper, persimmon orange, with characters on the front I could not read.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart. And it is in there, which you know how to check now. Check it before you use it. I would rather you checked mine than took my word for it."

"Does it work?"

"I've used it 8 years. One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing when somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. Order more while you can. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone. Once a batch sells out you're waiting months."

I used it that night. It is a bar of soap. I did not expect anything, and I want to be honest, because by then I had 4 reasons not to.

The first week I could not tell, and there is no way for me to tell, and that is exactly the thing this whole story is about.

So here is how I found out instead.

In August I went to Sunday lunch at Ellen's for the first time since April, and I hung my coat on the hook inside her door.

Sophie came into the hall to see who it was.

She stopped and looked at the coat on the hook, and then at me, and she said, "You're not cold today."

I said no. Not today.

She took my hand and pulled me into the kitchen to show me a thing she had made out of a paper plate, and she stood against my leg the whole time she was explaining it, the way she used to.

In September Ellen came for coffee at mine and we did the chicken and she did not open the window, and I watched her not open it.

At Thanksgiving my sister put her chin on my shoulder while I was doing the potatoes and said, "You smell like somebody who has been peeling oranges. What is it?"

I said it was a bar of soap.

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

I spent 2 years and about 60 dollars being careful, and hiding, and lying to my closest friend about sleeping, and turning down my own daughter.

The idea was right the whole time. I had it in March, in my own bathroom, in a drawer.

Nobody had ever told me to turn the box over.

Marge texted me last week. Kaori is back on the website. She has ordered hers already because she has been through a batch running out before.

Sophie starts second grade after Labor Day and I am doing the first Sunday.

She has asked if we are making the paper plate thing again. I told her yes.

If you have told somebody you were cold when you were not cold.

If you have stopped going to things and given a reason that was not the reason.

If you have already bought the answer, more than once, and decided it does not work on you.

You do not need to try harder.

You need to find out what was actually in the bar.

Get the soap. Turn the box over. Then take your coat off.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

There are still 3 of them in that drawer.

I keep them where I can see them.

Your move.

body.text:
I’ve owned a small landscaping business for fourteen years. Every Wednesday for almost three years, I took care of the same woman’s yard. 3:40 on the dot. Every week without fail.

She’d come out to the truck herself when I was finishing up. Pay with a check, already filled out. Say the same words to me as she handed it over.

Then one Tuesday night there was a voicemail. “No need to come for a while, dear.” No reason. Clients pause service. It happens.

Two months passed. Then a younger woman called my business and asked if I was the one who had been taking care of her mother’s yard every Wednesday.

I’d heard a rumor about what had happened.

She wanted the yard cleaned up one last time before she listed the house. I did it myself. When I was done, she brought out two cups of tea and we sat down on the porch steps.

Looking back, that was the moment everything changed. Not when I heard about June. Not when I found the research at one in the morning. Not when my own mother called me from her bathroom a few weeks later. It was the moment Laura sat down next to me on those steps and started telling me about her mother.

Her first name was June. I’d seen it on her checks a hundred times, but I never once said it. To me she had always been “Mrs. Whitaker, Wednesdays.” Soft silver hair. A different colored cardigan every visit. She’d walk the flowerbeds with me at the end, touching the roses like she was checking on old friends.

Every single Wednesday. “This is for me. Wednesdays are my little gift to myself.”

I’m 47. She had thirty-something years on me. But we always got on like old friends.

When she cancelled I didn’t make much of it. A few weeks later I drove past her house on the way to a job. The mailbox at the end of the drive was overflowing. The flowerbeds she had always kept herself looked like nobody had touched them in weeks. The kind of slow neglect that piles up without anyone noticing.

Two months later her daughter was sitting next to me.

Laura was about my age. She had flown in from Seattle to start clearing out her mother’s house, and she had called me because she found a stack of my invoices in a kitchen drawer.

“My mom loved this yard,” she said. “I wanted it to look the way she kept it before anyone else sees it.”

She poured us both a second cup.

I could see she had something pressing on her. She just hadn’t had anyone to say it to.

“My mom was so independent,” she said. “She lived on her own for ten years after my father died. She drove. She cooked her own meals. She hosted every single Easter. She called me every Sunday afternoon at four and told me about her week.”

She wrapped both hands around the warm cup.

“She never told me anything was wrong. Not once. Not about any of it.”

I asked her what had happened.

“Everyone thinks it was sudden. It wasn’t. She went piece by piece.”

“It started about two years back. She mentioned, just in passing, that her back was itching at night. I told her to try a new lotion. She said ‘oh, I will,’ the way she always agreed with anything I suggested. I didn’t think about it again.”

“Then her shoulders started bothering her. She brought it up once, casually, that she couldn’t reach things the way she used to.”

“Then last spring I flew out to visit her. And I noticed something else.”

Laura paused for a long time before she said it.

“She didn’t smell the same when I hugged her. There was a faint odor I’d never associated with my mother. Not strong, just something off. I told myself it was old laundry. Or the soap she’d switched to. I never brought it up.”

She kept going.

“Itchy skin. Stiff shoulders. That faint old smell. All things I noticed over the course of two years. None of them felt like a big deal on their own.”

Laura looked down at her hands.

“I never said a word. She would have been humiliated if I had brought any of it up. I just kept telling myself I’d handle it next time.”

But there wasn’t a next time.

“She got an infection. The doctors called it cellulitis. They told me it probably started weeks earlier from a small break in the skin she hadn’t noticed, somewhere on her upper back where she couldn’t see and couldn’t reach. By the time she felt sick enough to call me, it had already gotten into her bloodstream.”

Forty-eight hours.

“The doctor told me afterward that her immune system at that age just couldn’t keep up with the kind of bacteria that builds up on skin that hasn’t been properly cleaned for a long time.”

She lifted the cup but didn’t drink.

“I keep going back to every Sunday phone call. Every visit. Every time she said ‘oh, I’m fine, honey, don’t worry yourself about me.’ And I just believed her.”

I cancelled the rest of my jobs that afternoon. I drove home and I sat in my own driveway for almost twenty minutes before I went inside.

Because something had just come back to me.

A few things, in fact.

The last time I had visited my own mother, about three weeks earlier, she had asked me to open a jar she couldn’t get open. She had brushed it off, laughed about her shoulders not being what they used to be. I hadn’t thought twice.

She had mentioned, twice during the same visit, that her back was itching at night. She had said it the way she always says anything she doesn’t want me to fuss over.

And when I had hugged her goodbye on her porch, I had noticed something I had been pushing out of my mind ever since. Her hair smelled the same. Her perfume smelled the same. But underneath all of it there was a faint odor I had never associated with my mother before.

Itchy back at night. Stiff shoulders. A faint smell I had never noticed on her before.

The exact same things Laura had just described to me.

I walked inside. My husband Tom was already asleep. I sat at the kitchen table and started searching online.

It was past eleven. I had my laptop open and a cup of tea going cold beside me, and I typed in everything I could think of.

“Old people smell.”

“Mobility issues seniors.”

“Skin infection older women cellulitis.”

“Skin buildup on aging skin.”

I went down a long, frustrating rabbit hole.

Most of what came up was about moisturizers. Recommendations for ceramide creams. Articles on barrier repair and retinol and a hundred different products I could overnight to my mother.

But somewhere around one in the morning, I clicked on something different.

It was a medical article by a dermatologist who specialized in older adult skin care. And one paragraph stopped me cold.

The dermatologist explained something I’d never consciously thought about before.

She wrote that genuinely clean skin requires three things working together. Not one. Not two. Three.

Water. Soap. And friction — actual scrubbing of the skin.

Your hand on a washcloth. Your fingers working lather into your chest. Something physically moving across the skin to lift away what’s sitting on top of it.

She wrote that all three have to be present. Water without soap doesn’t dissolve oil. Soap without water doesn’t rinse. And water plus soap without mechanical action doesn’t actually remove anything. It just makes the skin wet.

I sat at my kitchen table and thought about my own shower that morning.

For my arms, I had all three. Water. Body wash. My own hands lathering it in.

For my chest, my belly, my legs. Same. All three.

For my back — and I had to stop and actually picture it — I had water. That was it. Maybe a bit of soap that ran down my back during the rinse. But my hands never touched my back. The water flowed over it for maybe forty-five seconds and that was the entire wash.

Just water. For the part of my body I couldn’t reach.

And I’m 47. My shoulders work. I could scrub my back with a washcloth if I really tried.

My mother is 73. And I knew her shoulders had been bothering her for years.

I kept reading.

The article said the back is the single most important area of the body to clean properly with all three steps. Not because of how it looks. Because of what’s on it.

The skin on the back produces more natural oil than most other areas of the body. Normally, that’s not a problem. But when that oil isn’t properly removed, it mixes with dead skin and gradually forms a sticky, invisible layer on the surface of the skin. And because dead skin tends to build up faster with age, that layer can become thicker over time.

I had to read that twice.

A sticky layer. On the back. Building up over time.

The article went on. That layer doesn’t just sit there. It feeds bacteria.

Bacteria naturally live on everyone’s skin and are usually harmless in small amounts. But when they have a continuous food source and an undisturbed environment, they multiply. And as they feed on the oil and dead skin, they produce waste compounds.

Body odor.

She wrote it plainly. Body odor isn’t sweat. Sweat is mostly odorless. Body odor comes from bacteria feeding on the oil and dead skin buildup that hasn’t been properly removed.

And the back, with its high oil production and the fact that it’s so difficult to reach, creates the perfect place for buildup to collect over the years. That makes it one of the easiest places on the body for bacteria to grow. As a result, it’s the area most likely to develop a persistent odor that no amount of showering removes.

I had to put the laptop down for a second.

Because I was thinking about the hug on the porch. The faint odor I’d told myself was the cardigan.

I picked the laptop back up and kept reading.

The article anticipated the question I was already forming. I was thinking, but if she smells, wouldn’t she know? Wouldn’t she notice?

No. The dermatologist explained this directly. The human nose adapts to constant smells within minutes. It’s why you can’t smell your own house or your own perfume after wearing it for an hour. Neither can the people who live with you, because they’re habituated too.

The only people who can smell it are people who don’t live with you. The daughter who flies in once every few months. The grandchildren who haven’t seen her since Christmas. The neighbor she chats with at the mailbox.

Her own husband would have stopped being able to smell it years ago.

She would have no idea.

The article explained that most older adults assume the water and bit of soap reaching their back during a shower is enough to keep it clean.

But dead skin isn’t loose dirt and sweat waiting to be rinsed away.

It’s a literal layer that’s attached to the skin.

She can shower twice a day, every day for a decade. And the layer on her back will keep growing, the bacteria will keep multiplying, and the odor will keep getting stronger. The shower routine she trusted was never reaching the problem in the first place.

The article was reaching its end and I was reading faster now.

The dermatologist wrote that the persistent itching many older adults feel on their back at night. The kind that nothing seems to relieve. That they blame on dry skin or laundry detergent or aging. Is most often bacterial irritation underneath the buildup. It’s not the surface skin that itches. It’s what’s living and feeding underneath.

I was nodding at my kitchen table at 1:30 in the morning like she was sitting across from me.

The last section of the article was the one I didn’t want to read. But I read it anyway.

In older adults, the dermatologist wrote, the consequences of letting this layer accumulate are not just cosmetic. As skin thins with age, it becomes easier to tear. A small scratch or tear can happen without the person even noticing. And if bacteria are already growing on the buildup, that tiny opening can give them a way into the body.

That’s when more serious problems can begin.

Cellulitis. Sepsis. The kind of skin infection that, in a 70-year-old woman with a weakened immune system, can become an ER visit in under 48 hours.

The exact thing that happened to June.

I closed the laptop.

I sat there in the dark kitchen and I understood, for the first time, exactly what had happened to her. And exactly what was happening to my own mother, right now, in her own house, in her own shower, without her knowing.

She had no idea her routine wasn’t reaching the part of her body that mattered most. She had no idea the layer was growing on her back every single day she stood under that water thinking she was clean.

I didn’t sleep that night.

I lay in bed thinking about every Sunday phone call I’d had with my mother. Every visit. Every time she’d said “oh, I’m fine, honey, don’t worry about me.” And I’d just taken her at her word.

Just like Laura had.

I called my mother the next morning.

I was careful about how I brought it up. I didn’t want to embarrass her. I didn’t want her to feel like I’d been studying her body during my last visit.

I just casually mentioned that my own back had been giving me trouble lately. I couldn’t seem to get it really clean in the shower and asked if she had any tips.

There was a long pause on the other end of the line.

Then she told me, very quietly, that she hadn’t been able to properly reach her own back to wash it in probably four years.

She said it the way someone confesses something shameful.

She told me her shoulders just didn’t rotate the way they used to.

She’d tried a long-handled brush and it hurt to use. She’d tried stretching her washcloth and it didn’t really do anything. She’d just been hoping that the warm water and the time she spent in the shower were doing enough.

She told me she’d been embarrassed about it for years. That her back had been itching her at night for a long time.

That she’d started using persimmon soap a few months ago because she’d been worried she didn’t smell right anymore.

She told me she’d never mentioned any of it to anyone. She’d been hoping nobody would notice.

I sat at my kitchen island and felt my eyes get hot.

This is the woman who stayed up with me when I had pneumonia in the third grade. Who flew across the country to be with me the week each of my kids was born. Who has been quietly, privately losing the ability to take care of her own body for four years, and was too proud to ever tell me about it.

I told her I was going to find her something. She said I didn’t need to. I told her I was going to anyway.

That afternoon I started looking for a solution.

Then I remembered my friend Beth.

Beth and I were roommates during junior year of college and stayed loosely in touch ever since. She’d gone into occupational therapy after graduation and had been working in geriatric rehab for almost twenty years.

She picked up on the second ring.

I didn’t bother with small talk. I told her I needed her professional opinion.

I told her about June. What had happened to her.

I told her I was worried about my mother. She hadn’t been able to properly wash her own back in years because her shoulders wouldn’t cooperate.

And after everything I’d read the night before, I couldn’t stop thinking about it.

I needed to know what to do.

There was a pause on the other end of the line.

Then Beth laughed softly.

“You’re not the first daughter who’s called me about something like this.”

She told me she’d worked with plenty of older adults who could no longer comfortably reach their backs.

The itching. The buildup. The smell family members sometimes noticed before the person did.

None of it surprised her.

She said what my mother needed was a way to actually clean her back the way she’d been cleaning the rest of her body her whole life.

Something she could use on her own, every day, without straining her shoulders or asking for help. Something that would physically lift the buildup off the skin instead of just sliding water over it.

“Like one of those long-handled brushes?” I asked.

Beth paused before answering.

“No, we usually don’t recommend those. The bristles trap bacteria between uses and then scrub it right back into the skin. They’re also too rough for older skin. I’ve seen women come into our unit with small skin tears on their upper back from using them too aggressively. Those breaks are exactly where infections start.”

I went very still.

I was thinking about June. About the doctor explaining the cellulitis had probably started from a small skin break she hadn’t noticed. On her upper back.

I asked Beth if that’s what could have happened to June.

There was a long pause on the other end of the line.

“I can’t say for sure. But yes. We see it.”

I felt my stomach drop.

What if June had bought the brush because she knew something wasn’t right? And what if the thing she thought would help had actually made things worse?

I asked Beth what they recommended instead.

She responded almost immediately.

“We use a long, woven exfoliating towel.”

She explained it in a few sentences.

About forty inches long. You hold one end in each hand, drape it across the back, and pull it slowly back and forth.

The leverage does most of the work, so the shoulders barely have to move.

The woven fabric holds onto soap and creates the gentle scrubbing action needed to lift away oil and dead skin buildup. The same buildup water alone can’t remove.

And because it’s soft and flexible, it’s gentle on aging skin while still cleaning properly.

Beth said her own mother had been using one for years and wouldn’t shower without it.

“It’s not a fancy product. It’s just the right tool. The design has been used by the Japanese for generations. Specifically to allow people to wash their own backs into very old age.”

Then she said something that stayed with me.

“Look. Your mom probably isn’t going to want to talk about this. She’s going to be embarrassed. Don’t make her talk about it. Just send it. Tell her it’s a Japanese thing you read about. She’ll figure out how to use it in about thirty seconds and she’ll never bring it up. That’s how it goes. They don’t thank you. They just stop having the problem.”

Beth had to run. A patient was waiting. She said she’d text me the link to the towel they used at the clinic.

My phone buzzed two minutes later.

I ordered one that evening and had it shipped directly to my mother’s house.

I called her four days after it arrived.

There was a different kind of pause this time.

She told me, almost shyly, that it was the first time in four years she’d felt completely clean. She said the water had run brown for the first shower. Years of buildup finally lifting off her skin. The itching at night had stopped.

She didn’t say anything about the smell. She didn’t have to. I could hear it in her voice. The relief of someone who hadn’t even realized how much she’d been carrying around with her until she’d put it down.

But what stayed with me most was something she said at the end of that call.

She said, “I didn’t realize how much I’d given up until I got it back.”

I called Laura a week later. She’d flown back to Seattle by then but we’d exchanged numbers before she left.

I told her what I’d found. She went quiet on the other end of the line for a long time.

When she finally spoke she said:

“If someone had given this to my mom two years ago, she’d be sitting in that chair right now arguing with me about what to watch.”

Then she said something I think about every single day.

“You don’t count Wednesdays until they’re gone.”

I’m a landscaper. I’m loading the truck at six in the morning and coiling hoses until the light goes.

But I know what Laura told me about June. And I know what I watched happen with my own mother in less than a couple of weeks.

If you have noticed your parents getting older, if you have noticed them quietly struggling, their hygiene slowly slipping, please pay attention to the small things they aren’t telling you.

Those things are not separate problems. They are often one problem wearing different faces.

I’ve linked the towel I sent to my mother below.

She may never tell you it changed anything.

But trust me, it will.

You don’t get those Wednesdays back.

https://toshiico.com/pages/Toshi-Exfoliating-Towel

P.S. — I sent my mother a second towel about six weeks after the first one. She called me the same day it arrived, not to thank me, but to tell me she had already ordered one for her neighbor Lorraine, who she had apparently been quietly worrying about for months. That is how I knew it had really worked. My mother does not recommend things she doesn’t believe in.

We had dinner at her kitchen table about a week after that. At one point she reached across the table to take my plate and I caught a glimpse of her upper arm. The skin looked different. Softer. The flakiness was gone. The dull, congested texture I had been pretending not to notice for two years had just... cleared.

She didn’t say a word about it. She never would. That isn’t who she is.

But I saw it.

P.P.S. — You’ll know it is working before you can see it. My mother felt it around day four. The itching changes first. Then the skin. Then the smell — not all at once, but like someone slowly opening a window in a room that had been shut too long. If you have been watching your mother quietly manage this for years, you have gotten used to it. You have adjusted to it. You have told yourself it is just aging. When it starts to change, even a little, you will notice. Because you will remember what she used to feel like when you hugged her. And you will realize that version of her is still in there. The buildup didn’t change who she is. It just buried her underneath it. The towel brings her back.

P.P.P.S. — Don’t overthink this. You noticed something. That’s why you have read this far. The itching. The dry skin. The smell you blamed on the cardigan. The shoulders that couldn’t reach anymore. You noticed and you kept reading because somewhere in the back of your mind you already knew something wasn’t right. Trust that. Act on it. You don’t get those Wednesdays back.

body.text:
My husband divorced me for a pregnant 37-year-old.
Then I heard my daughter say "she has her dog."
I wish somebody had told me how to get out of a kitchen like that.

Rick and I were married 32 years.

I kept the books for a dentist on Water Street. He sold farm equipment, so he was gone Tuesday to Thursday.

Thursday nights were the good ones. We ate late. We had the same 6 people over for New Year's, 20 years running.

People assume you miss the big things.

What I miss is having somebody to tell a small thing to. The dentist's wife had her hip done. A raccoon got in the Nolans' trash. Nothing you would pick up a phone for.

He went the February before last. The house sold in the spring, so I bought the little brick one on Fairmount with my half.

I got Sadie that summer because the house was too quiet to sit in.

The first time the whole family was in one room after all of it was Nora's birthday in May.

I got there at 3 to do the potatoes.

Meg had 14 people. Tom's parents. 2 women from her street.

I stayed at the counter with the peeler. There is a lot to do for 14.

We sat down at 6. I was between Nora and the end of the table.

It went along nicely a while. Then one of the women from Meg's street turned to me. Sharon. Her boy is in Nora's class.

She was being kind. She meant nothing by it.

"So are you seeing anyone yet?"

I had my fork halfway up.

15 months I had had to think of an answer to that question. A year and a half on my own in a small house with nothing but time, and I never once worked out what I was going to say.

Meg got there before I did.

"Mom. Do you want more potatoes."

She said it too loud, so it went across 2 people. Every single person at that table heard exactly what she was doing.

Then Nora looked up at me with her fork.

"Who are you seeing?"

She is 6. She had caught a word, so she wanted the rest of it.

Nobody answered her. Somebody laughed at something down the other end.

"Nobody, sweetheart," I said.

That was the first time I ever said that word out loud about myself.

I said yes to potatoes I did not want. I put them on my plate. I ate them.

Later I leaned in to ask Sharon about her boy. She leaned back the same amount I leaned in.

It was nothing. People do that.

When the cake came out Nora got down off her chair, went round the whole table, and climbed up on Tom's mother to watch it.

I have had that child asleep on me since the day she was born.

Then I got up and started clearing. There were plates.

Clearing is a thing you can do with your hands while your face does whatever it is doing.

I was at the sink with the water going when Sharon started up again in the dining room. She was apologising to Meg.

"I did not mean to put her on the spot."

"No, God, don't." Meg's voice went down the way it goes down when a person thinks you cannot hear them. "She is doing okay. She really is."

I turned the water off so I could hear it.

"She has her dog."

Then I turned the water straight back on so nobody would know I had ever turned it off.

15 months. That was the first time I ever heard my own daughter explain me to somebody.

There is no walking out of a kitchen like that. Not without going back in there and letting her know I had heard it.

So I stayed at that sink. I dried her plates. I put them away in cupboards that were not mine.

There is a sentence you say to yourself at a moment like that, and mine was that she is tired, she has had 14 people, she did not mean it the way it sounded.

I have used that sentence a lot since February. It has never once been true.

I did not come out until my face was doing the right thing.

Not one word of it was cruel. That is the part I could not put down.

I drove home and sat in my own driveway a while with the engine off.

She has her dog.

I am 61 years old. I know what I look like.

Rick did not leave for a mystery. He left for a woman of 37 who was 5 months pregnant when he told me. She had the baby that July.

So there it was. Rick had traded me for a woman of 37, and my own daughter had explained me to a room with a dog.

After that I stopped looking for a more complicated answer.

People know what to do with a woman of 61 whose husband has gone. Apparently so did I.

Once you have decided a thing like that, you stop deciding anything else. You just start checking.

There was a flyer at the library for a Thursday morning class at the Y, so I signed up. My first one was the 15th of May.

9 of us in the same water. 45 minutes, 8 o'clock.

They go for coffee after, at the place across the lot. I had been watching them through that glass from my car since May.

I bought a coral blouse at the outlet that June because the woman working there said the color was good on me.

The 24th of July was the 11th one.

That morning, in the water, I decided I was going to say something to them. I had it worked out by the last lap.

I might go and get a coffee myself.

That was the whole sentence. I said it the length of that pool and back.

We got out at ten to 9.

"Are you coming, Pat?"

"Two minutes."

I did the buttons on that blouse twice because I got them wrong the first time.

They went out the door in twos.

Then I did not go to my car.

I walked across that lot behind them, the way you walk behind people you are not with.

They took the big table in the window, the same one every week.

I got in the line. There were 2 people ahead of me, so I let them both go in front of me.

Then I stood at that counter with my purse in both hands for 4 minutes. 6 feet from that table.

You hear a lot in 4 minutes. Somebody's grandson had got into the college he wanted. Somebody else was having a knee done in September and was not looking forward to it.

I knew the knee. I had been in the water next to that knee since May.

I never said my sentence. There was never anywhere to put it.

I never ordered a coffee either.

Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not one of them, not one time.

That was almost the worse part. If Pat had been rude to me I could have disliked Pat.

She held the door. She smiled. Then she went back to that table.

So I did the arithmetic I had been doing since February.

Nobody had anything against me. They just did not particularly want me there.

Bev called me on a Tuesday evening at the end of July. I had one chop under the broiler.

Bev is one of the 6 who used to come to us for New Year's. In 20 years not one of us ever needed inviting. We simply knew who was coming.

This time she asked me which day I thought I might drive up.

There was nothing wrong with the question. That was the trouble. By then I could make a meaning out of anything.

I heard myself tell her I already had something that weekend.

I did not have anything that weekend. I had 3 days and a dog.

But if I stayed home, then nobody at that lake had to look relieved when I left.

After that I quit. Not all at once. You do not catch yourself quitting.

I never went back to that class after the 24th. Meg asked me about a Sunday twice, so I told her I was busy twice. After the second one she stopped asking.

My sister Joyce called every Sunday, the way she always has. I told her I was fine, honestly.

Joyce did 40 years at the county hospital. 22 of them on a geriatric floor.

She let me say it.

By the end of August I had taken myself out of every single thing a woman can take herself out of.

The one thing I could not get out of was my dog. Sadie goes out at 7 whether you are fine or not.

So the only people I saw all that summer were the ones on those 4 blocks. And that is where it stopped adding up.

Diane comes out of the yellow house at the same time with her beagle. We have walked the same 4 blocks together since last spring.

The Tuesday after Labor Day. Fairmount down to 9th. Carl was out with his hose at the end of his drive, so he turned it off.

He turned the water off to talk to Diane about the storm. He said good morning to me over her shoulder.

9th along to Bell. The girl who runs the coffee place came out onto the sidewalk in her apron with a cup in her hand. For Diane.

I told her it was going to be a warm one. I said it to be in it.

She said it certainly was, without turning round, the way you do when somebody behind you says a nice thing.

By then I had got very good at noticing who people move toward.

Diane is 62. Her husband left too, 4 years back, for a woman from his office. She lives 2 doors from me in a house bought out of the same kind of settlement.

She is not younger than me. She is not prettier. She is not happier either, and I know that because I watched her cry on the corner of Fairmount and 9th in March and walked her home.

And they still step toward her.

I had been carrying the question for 3 weeks by then. It is not a thing one woman asks another woman. You are asking her to say out loud that she has got something you have not got.

So at the light on 9th, on the way back, I asked her anyway.

"Diane. What is it that you do."

"What do you mean."

"People stop for you. They do not stop for me. We are the same woman."

She did not laugh at me. I was ready for her to laugh at me.

"I do not do anything."

"You must."

"Ruth. I put my pants on and I walk the dog."

"People come toward you."

She looked at me then, and she was working on it same as I was.

"Maybe you are watching them too hard."

"What does that mean."

"I do not know. Maybe nothing."

Then the beagle got into the Nolans' hedge, so we walked the rest of it about their roof.

I went home and put the kettle on and did not make anything with it.

Maybe you are watching them too hard.

I sat at my own table and went back through the whole spring. Sharon leaning back the same amount I leaned in. 11 Thursdays. 4 minutes at that counter with my purse in both hands.

Bev on the phone, and me saying I had something on. That one was mine. I did that one to myself.

But I did not make Sharon lean back.

I had been calling all of it being 61.

And 2 doors down there is a woman who is 62 and does not have to call it anything.

Joyce came that Saturday with a chicken, because she has decided I do not eat.

It was the first cool day we had had. The sun gets into my kitchen after 2, so it was all over the counter while we worked.

I was at the stove. She came in behind me for the salt.

She reached past me and stopped.

Not stopped exactly. She changed the angle of herself.

I had spent a whole summer watching people do that. I know that movement better than I know my own signature.

"You moved."

"I was getting the salt."

"No."

She had the salt in her hand and she did not set it down.

"Sharon did that at Nora's birthday," I said. "Pat at the Y as well. Not the same. Something like it."

"Ruthie."

"Do not Ruthie me. What is it."

All summer I watched strangers step back off me and I never once asked one of them why. It took my own sister at my own stove.

Joyce put the salt down. Then she sat, which she never does with something in the oven.

She had her bag on the chair beside her, the one she has carried since 1987. She took something out of it and set it on the table between us.

Small. Wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She did not say one word about it.

"Do you want the nurse answer or the sister answer."

"I want whichever one nobody has given me."

"Then here it is. There is something." She turned her cup around on the table. "You have been right about that since February."

"I shower twice a day."

"I know you do."

"Then what."

"Things change on a woman past a certain age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go."

"Everybody knows that."

"Your skin also starts making something it never made before."

"What does it do."

"It has got a smell to it."

I sat there with that.

"I have never heard of that in my life."

"Nobody has. People do not talk about it."

"Joyce. He left me for a woman who was 5 months pregnant."

"I know it."

"So it was not that."

"I am not telling you why your husband went. I am telling you why a room does what a room does."

"Then what are you telling me."

"That you noticed something real. And then Rick taught you to explain it in the cruelest way there is."

I had to put my cup down.

"Then I will wash more."

"That is the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap does not take it off."

"Now you are being silly."

"Chop garlic tonight. Then wash your hands twice with your good soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"Garlic."

"Garlic. Your hands are clean and it stayed on you anyway. Soap has got nothing to take hold of."

Then she said the name of it, once. Nonenal. She said it the way people say a word they have heard a hundred times but never once had to write down.

I was doing arithmetic again, only this time it came out the other way.

Nora, who is 6 and climbs on everybody, going round a whole table on her own birthday to get up on somebody else.

And Meg. Meg in that hallway, saying the kindest sentence she could think of, with her voice down.

"22 years on that floor. And you stood at my stove and moved away from me."

"I did."

"And you never said it to me."

"No." She looked at the table. "I have got a list of women I never said it to, and my own sister is on it. There is no way to say it to somebody you love that does not come out of your mouth as an accusation. So none of us says it. And every one of us thinks we are being kind."

That is when I understood what my daughter had been being.

And the other thing, which took me until that night.

I had not imagined one bit of it. Every last thing I had counted up since February had actually happened.

I had just found the cruelest possible reason for it, and then I had gone and made the reason into who I am.

"So what takes it off."

She pushed the little parcel across the table at me.

"I have been sat here 20 minutes waiting on you to ask me for it."

I got the tissue paper off it.

"It is soap."

"Persimmon. It does not cover it up. It takes it apart."

I turned it over in my hand. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

I have smelled that before. I have smelled it 4 mornings a week since last spring, on a sidewalk, on a woman standing closer to me than anybody had stood in a year and a half.

"Diane," I said.

"I would think so." Joyce did not look up from her cup. "And she will not know why either."

"And it works."

"I sent women home off that floor with one for 15 years. I have used it myself since I was 58."

She wrote it on the back of my grocery list. Kaori.

"Order 2 while they have got them. They do it in small batches, so once a batch goes you are waiting on next year's harvest."

At the door she got her coat on and said the part I have thought about every day since.

"You did not let yourself go, Ruthie. You changed your face cream at 50 and never thought twice about it. You are still washing with what you used at 30. That is the whole of it."

It is a bar of soap. That is all it is. I am 61 years old, so I expected nothing at all from a bar of soap.

What I did that night was go round my own house and think about every person who has stood in it since February. The man who read the meter. The girl who brings the pharmacy order. The fellow who came about the gutters and talked to me from the step the whole time.

You cannot do that for long. I made myself quit and I ran the bath.

I used it because it was sitting there on the edge of the tub.

The next morning I caught the Kaori on my arm at the sink. It was still there at supper.

Thursday I went past the hall mirror, and then I stopped and went back and stood in front of it.

Not for any reason. Just standing there. Taller, somehow.

I had not looked at myself on purpose since February.

On the Friday I stood in the line at the Kroger right up behind the woman in front of me, the way a person stands in a line. I did not work out first where to put myself.

I have no idea how long I had been doing that.

Nora came for the weekend in October, the way she does when Meg and Tom go to somebody's wedding.

Saturday she fell asleep against me on the couch through the back half of a movie.

She is 6, so she has opinions on everything.

"You smell like the good store," she said.

I asked her which good store.

She said she did not know the name of it. Then she went to sleep on my arm.

I sat there with a dead arm through the end of that movie and most of the news after it.

I was not going to be the one who moved.

The second Thursday in October I went back to the 8 o'clock class. I had not been in that water since July.

I do not know what I thought was going to happen.

In the same changing room, at the same locker, Pat came round the end of the row with her towel.

"What is that," she said. "That is lovely."

"It is soap," I said. "Persimmon."

She shut her eyes for a second, which is a peculiar thing to watch a woman do in a changing room.

"My grandmother's back porch," she said. "In the summer. She has been gone since I was 19."

Then she picked her bag up.

"We are going over for coffee. Come."

In July I stood 6 feet from that table for 4 minutes waiting for somebody to make room for me.

This time Pat said come. So I did not ask her whether she meant it.

Meg had a Sunday at the end of October. Sharon was there.

She asked me how the swimming was.

I looked at Meg. She was cutting bread, so she did not look up.

She did not say one word about potatoes.

So I answered it myself.

I stayed until 9. I did not touch one plate.

At the door Meg held on to my arm a second longer than she needed to. I did not step back off her.

"You seem like yourself," she said.

That was 6 weeks ago.

I go Tuesdays and Thursdays now. Pat and I have got our own end of that table.

Bev called about New Year's and I got in first. 6 people. 20 years. My house.

Nora is coming to me for the whole week at Christmas, and Meg is the one who asked.

Somebody will ask me again whether I am seeing anyone. They always do.

I know what I am going to say this time. No.

Just the no. Nothing hung on the end of it.

Joyce texted me Thursday. Kaori is back on the website. Diane ordered 2. Pat from the pool ordered one.

Meg does a Sunday every other week now. The next one is this Sunday.

Nora has already asked if I will still smell like the good store at Christmas. I told her yes.

If everybody has been kind to you since the day your husband left.

If somebody in your family has ever explained you to a stranger while you were standing right there.

If you have started telling people you already have something on.

You do not need a man to want you.

You need to be underestimated one more time. So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the soap. Put the blouse on. Go on the Thursday.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

Every one of them was being kind to me.

Not one of them was right.

Your move.

body.text:
My husband said I was "getting too stale" at 55.
Four months later I walked into our grandson's birthday on another man's arm.
He choked on it. Still doesn't know how.

It started the night Greg came home from his buddy Dale's, three beers in, bragging about Dale's new girlfriend.

Half his age, he said. And the way she smelled. Like a woman who still bothered to take care of herself.

He told me that from his recliner, eyes already drifting back to the TV.

"You've gone a little stale, hon. That's all I'm saying."

Then he turned the volume up.

For ten years our evenings had looked exactly like that. Two recliners, two TV trays, the blue light of the television, and not one word between us.

The kids were grown and gone, and the house had gotten so quiet I left the kitchen radio on just for the sound of another voice.

And still, every morning, I made his coffee. Two sugars, by his chair.

I worked, I paid the bills, I ironed the shirts he wore to the bar without me, I cleared the plates he never carried to the sink.

Somewhere in those years he'd stopped seeing me. Stopped saying thank you. Stopped saying my name.

He hadn't always been like that. Somewhere under the recliner was the man who'd once driven through a snowstorm to bring me soup at the office. I'd just stopped being able to find him.

I told myself it was a rough patch. I'd been telling myself that for ten years.

I almost laughed. Stale. From the man who hadn't hauled himself off that recliner in two years. The man whose shirts I still ironed.

But the word crawled under my skin and stayed.

That comment wasn't really the reason. We'd drifted apart so slow I never saw the day it finished.

Two strangers under one roof. And I was tired. Bone tired of being the only one still trying.

It was my daughter Katie who finally said it out loud, both hands around a coffee mug at my kitchen table.

"Mom. You should have done this years ago. And I'll be right here."

So at fifty-five, I signed the papers on a Tuesday and walked out into a parking lot that smelled like rain, lighter than I'd felt in a decade.

I left Greg. He never left me.

The first weeks on my own were a strange kind of wonderful.

Biscuit asleep on the side of the bed that used to be off-limits. The kitchen painted the yellow Greg had vetoed for twenty years. Cereal for dinner, and nobody to answer to.

I called it freedom.

Freedom held up fine until about two in the morning. That's when I'd reach across the bed, find nothing but a cold sheet, and lie there in a house so quiet I could hear the clock in the hall.

I didn't want to grow old as the woman nobody reached for. I didn't want to die in that little house alone.

Greg didn't take it like a man.

He couldn't stand that I'd been the one to walk out, so he got on the phone before I could and poisoned every friend we had.

Poor Greg. Have you heard? She's falling apart. Couldn't last a month on her own.

Thirty years I kept his house and covered for him, and his parting gift was a whisper campaign. He made sure every word got back to me. That was the whole point.

For a while, God help me, I half believed him.

Then I got angry. Good and angry, for the first time in years.

I'd find a man who actually saw me. And I wanted Greg to choke on it.

Watch me, I thought.

Wanting it turned out to be the easy part.

Katie talked me into online dating, built the profile, hit save before I could lose my nerve.

I bought a new blouse for the first date and redid my lipstick at the mirror like a girl. I hadn't sat across a table from a strange man in thirty years.

He showed up twenty minutes late in a stained golf shirt, ordered for both of us without asking, and spent the whole dinner explaining his ex-wife was "clinically insane."

His photos had been fifteen years and forty pounds optimistic. I was home by eight.

The next one was better. Kind, funny, read actual books, asked questions and waited for the answers.

Three hours over coffee, and I caught myself thinking, maybe.

Then he mentioned, light as anything, that he still kept a key to his ex's place. "Just in case."

And just like that, the maybe was gone.

By the fifth date I stopped opening the app.

Some women just don't get a second act, I decided. I'd had mine.

The one person I finally told all of it to was my friend Sue.

Thirty years a nurse, sharp as a tack, seen everything twice.

We sat on her porch with iced tea, and I gave her the whole thing. The weird ones. The red flags. And finally, the word.

"Stale," I said. "Who says that to his own wife?"

Sue didn't laugh, and she didn't pity me. She just nodded, slow, like she already knew what I was about to say.

"Can I tell you something, and you won't take it wrong?"

"Go on."

"He was being cruel. But the smell part. He wasn't entirely wrong."

"Excuse me?"

"Hear me out. It matters more than anyone admits, with a man. And it shifts on all of us as we get older. Hormones."

"Sue. Are you telling me I stink?"

She laughed. "I'm telling you it's normal, and you'd never catch it on yourself. There's a name for it, even. Nonenal. We used to smell it on the older patients all the time."

"That is horrifying."

"It's chemistry, hon. Not character. Greg made it a verdict. It isn't one. It's about the only thing on your whole list you can actually fix."

"So I shower more."

"Regular soap doesn't touch it. It isn't made for that." She went inside and came back with a small wrapped bar called Kaori. "Here. We used to swear by this one on the ward. Persimmon. Do it for you, not for him."

I felt ridiculous even taking it. A bar of soap against thirty years of a man who'd stopped looking.

But that same night I looked it up. Glasses on, reading like I was buying a car. Turns out it's a real thing, properly studied. Persimmon is one of the only things that actually binds it, where regular soap just sits on top. That little Kaori bar is built on an old Japanese way of making it.

So I tried it. Not for Greg, not for anyone. Just for me. Ten quiet minutes at the sink every morning, a small ritual that was only mine. Taking care of myself, for once.

And after a while, I caught myself standing taller in the mirror. Shoulders back. Looking myself in the eye for the first time in years.

I didn't feel fixed. I felt like me, the one from before.

A week later Sue called. "Get dressed. Girls' night. There's a bar across town with a bluegrass band, and I'm not taking no for an answer."

She picked me up, took one look, and leaned in. "Well, look at you. You smell good." She grinned.

I went for the music. I'll have that on the record. I was finished with men.

The place was half empty, string lights over the bar, a trio tuning up in the corner.

And there was a man sitting right down on the floor by the fiddle player, eyes shut, grinning like it was the best thing that had happened to him all year.

When he came up for a beer he ended up on the stool beside me, and we talked clean through the second set.

Ray. Gardener's hands, dirt under one nail, a laugh that came easy.

At some point I realized an hour had gone by and I hadn't once braced for the catch. He just listened, laughed in the right places, and looked at me like the conversation was the best thing in the room.

Thirty years, and I'd forgotten what that did to a person.

The warmth up the neck. The little kick under the ribs. Butterflies, at fifty-five, in a half-empty bar.

He walked me to my car and didn't try a thing. Just asked, hands in his pockets, if he could call.

He was a kind man. The plain, real kind. Not pushy. Not playing games. I'd forgotten men like that were even out there.

So three days later, before I could talk myself out of it, I texted first.

We started slow. Long walks with my old dog. Suppers he cooked badly and proudly at my kitchen table.

On about the third one he stopped chopping, looked over, and said it like it was nothing. "You smell like citrus. I like that."

I had to turn back to the stove so he wouldn't see my face.

And slowly, the house began to change.

Muddy boots by my door now. Two coffee cups in the sink instead of one. My old dog losing her mind the second his truck turned into the drive.

The radio stayed off, because the quiet wasn't so heavy anymore. And the two-in-the-morning dread, the one I'd carried for years, just stopped coming.

I was a little bit in love. At my age, I'd long stopped believing that could happen again.

Then, four months after Greg told me I'd gone "stale," our grandson turned five.

The whole family came to my son's backyard for the party. Greg too, in a lawn chair by the cooler.

This time I didn't walk in alone. I walked in on Ray's arm, in a red dress I'd bought myself that morning.

Our grandson spotted him first and came tearing across the grass, and Ray scooped him up like he'd done it a hundred times.

The boy had taken to calling him "Bumpa," and he hollered it now so the whole yard could hear.

"BUMPA, come see the frogs!"

My son watched them go, then put a hand on my shoulder.

"I like him, Mom," he said. "And you. You seem happy. Properly happy."

Across the patio, Katie caught my eye and didn't say a word. She didn't need to.

The same friends Greg had told I was falling apart watched me come in glowing, a good man's hand at the small of my back.

Nobody was using the soft, careful voice now.

And Greg looked up from his chair, saw the man, saw my face, and the hello died in his throat.

He never got the word out.

That was the choke. The one I'd wished on him, alone on the cold side of that bed. He still doesn't know how I did it.

I didn't go over and smooth it for him. I'd done that my whole marriage. Not this time.

He'd called me stale, four months and a whole life ago. He had it exactly backwards.

Ray and I are driving up to a little cabin this weekend. Just the two of us.

Sue called this morning.

"Well?" was all she said. She could already hear the answer.

"I'm going to need more of that bar," I told her.

"Order a few while you're at it," she said. "They sell out fast. And tell the other women."

So that's what I'm doing.

Those ten quiet minutes at the sink became the first kind thing I do for myself all day. I can't start a morning without them now.

So I left the link below. It's a little persimmon bar called Kaori.

If you wake up tired, half sure the best part's behind you, it's a good place to start.

And if someone you love has gone quiet, and you can't work out why.

Maybe you don't need to prove anyone wrong. Maybe you just need a better bar.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.
Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.
One bar of it cost me my doctor of eleven years.

I have never told anybody what I paid for that bar.

Now I'm putting it on Facebook.

If you already bought a persimmon soap but got nothing out of it, this is for you. Please read the whole thing.

It's long. You're busy. I know.

It started in September.

I'm 67. Dr. Mercer knew my knees, my blood pressure, the year my mother died.

At the end of my checkup she put her pen down.

"One more thing, Diane. Our skin changes as we get older. It can carry a smell it didn't used to, and nobody ever mentions it."

Then two words. "Persimmon soap."

She said it kindly. She said it once. It wasn't on any of the papers she gave me.

Doctors never said anything. Mine did.

I'd been seeing those ads for weeks. I scrolled past every one. But they made me kind of doubt myself.

For about a year, my daughter Sarah's Sunday visits had been ending a little quicker at the door. No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

I'd asked her once, straight out, because I couldn't tell on myself. "Do I smell like an old lady to you?"

"Mom. You're fine."

My daughter's real frank about things and outspoken. I would've thought she would have told me if I needed it. But you never know.

An ad is one thing. Eleven years of Dr. Mercer is another.

I decided to buy it and not tell my husband the price.

That night I ordered the first one that came up on my phone. $18.99, plus $5.99 to ship it.

It came in a small box with a persimmon printed on it.

The box didn't say much. So I used it like any soap. Every morning, in the shower, down to a sliver I could barely hold.

It was nice but I wasn't sure if that solved the problem.

After, I'd put my nose to the collar of my robe anyway. The sniff test.

Every morning it told me the same thing. Nothing.

The first Sunday, Sarah hugged me at the door with her car keys already in her hand.

The second Sunday, the same.

The third Sunday I said it before she could. "Go on. Beat the dark." She was on her feet before I'd finished.

Fourth Sunday. Keys.

Fifth Sunday, I'd used the last of the bar that morning. Keys.

I wondered if it was just another soap.

My husband Don found the empty box in the bathroom cabinet. "That the fancy stuff?"

"It seems like voodoo," I said. "Not a clue if it is effective."

I didn't tell him what I'd thought every one of those mornings. What Dr. Mercer smelled on me in that exam room. For nothing.

My blood pressure check was a Thursday in October.

Dr. Mercer wrapped the cuff around my arm. "How did you get on with the soap, Diane?"

I waited until I had my coat back on.

Then I said, "Next time, keep your two words to yourself."

At the front desk I asked Patty for the form to have my records sent somewhere else.

"Are you sure, Diane?"

Dr. Mercer stood in the hall with my chart. She didn't say a thing.

I signed it.

That Sunday Sarah got up at a quarter to four.

"You okay, Mom? You're quiet."

"Just tired," I said.

At the door I got the side hug. The back arched and the behind hanging out creating distance between the hugger and the hugged. Her keys were already in her hand.

I knew that hug. I used to give it.

My mother lived alone her last six years, forty minutes from me. Every other Sunday I drove over. Every other Sunday I hugged her at her door exactly like that, with my keys in my hand.

I remember the smell of my mother and my grandmother and just thought it was old people smell.

"Leaving already?" she'd say.

"Traffic, Mom."

I never said a word to her.

That night I lay next to Don with the clock on 11:40.

Five weeks. $24.98. Eleven years.

"Why didn't it work?" I said. Out loud.

Don said, "Hmm?" He rolled over.

Nobody answered.

My hugs had started declining. I noticed but figured it is what it is.

I was an idiot paying so much for soap.

So I stopped. No more sniff test, no more asking Sarah. I didn't go looking for another bar.

Ten days later the phone rang at suppertime.

"Diane, it's Dr. Mercer." A pause. "Not the office. Me."

I nearly hung up.

"I'm not calling to get you back," she said. "I'd like to see what you bought. The box, if you still have it."

"Why?"

"Because I'm the one who sent you to buy it."

I figured she'd be nice to me right up until I bought something.

But she was asking me to bring her the proof she was wrong.

I put the empty box in my handbag. I went to be proved right.

She saw me after her last patient, in her own office.

There were six boxes on her desk. Different names. A persimmon printed on every one.

I wasn't the only one she'd rung.

I set mine down with the others. She looked at them a long time.

"Twenty years I've been saying those two words to women," she said. "I never once told anybody how to choose one."

"So it's a fad."

"How do you know?"

"I really didn't notice a difference."

"When you come home from a week away, what do you smell?"

"The house. Coffee, and Don's old jacket by the door."

"And the next morning?"

"Nothing. It's just the house."

"Where did it go?"

I didn't answer. She waited.

"Nowhere," I said. "I stopped noticing it."

"The brain tunes out a smell that never leaves you. Mine does too."

"Every morning for five weeks I smelled my own collar," I said. "I probably wouldn't be aware of any difference. Either way."

"You weren't a fool, Diane."

"Then who would know?"

"Who did you ask?"

"Sarah. She said I was fine."

"Would she tell you?"

I thought about my mother's front door.

"No," I said. "I never told mine."

"Then how was I supposed to choose one?"

"Now I'm telling women to find a maker who says who it's made for," she said. "One who tells you where to wash with it. Behind your ears, around your neck, your chest, across your back."

"Mine never said."

"Neither did I. You didn't do one thing wrong."

She touched the nearest one. "But that's still only a box talking. It can't tell you whether it works."

"Only Sarah can," I said. "At the door."

"Which one do you use?"

She opened her desk drawer. A bar, still in its paper.

"This isn't a prescription," she said. "It's made only for women over sixty. I'm 64, and it's what I wash with."

The paper said Kaori.

I held it to my nose. "Citrusy."

"Don't ask me if it works. I'd be the last to know."

I knew how I looked. A woman my age, being handed soap across a desk.

Not sure if I was investing in another scam. Always thinking it would be one more thing I'm wasting money on.

"Why that one?" I said. "Any of these would do."

"Maybe. I can't tell them apart, and I've tried. So I take the one where somebody else pays if it does nothing for me."

"I'm not buying another one."

"I'm not selling you anything." She pushed it over to me. "Ring me. Whatever happens."

I drove home with it on the passenger seat. I put it in the shower where the last one had been. I didn't tell Sarah. I didn't tell anybody.

I washed where Dr. Mercer had said, every morning. I didn't do the sniff test once.

The first Sunday on her bar, Sarah hugged me at the door with her keys in her hand. Same as always.

Voodoo, I thought. Again.

That night I nearly put it back in its paper.

The second Sunday it was dark by five. The porch light came on when we stepped out. There were wet leaves all over the step.

Sarah had her coat on. Her keys were still in her bag.

She hugged me with both arms. Her chin on my shoulder, the way she did when she came home from college.

She stood there long enough for the porch light to click off.

I don't know which of us let go first.

Neither of us mentioned it. I didn't ask her. I'm not going to.

Nobody said a word when Sarah started leaving early. Nobody said a word on Sunday either.

My mother never found out. I nearly didn't.

On Monday I rang Dr. Mercer. My turn. She answered on the first ring.

"Well?" she said.

"She didn't get her keys out till she was at the car."

The line went quiet for a second.

"Can you put me back on your list?"

"I never took you off it."

Dr. Mercer can't put any of this on Facebook. I can.

So please. Don't buy persimmon soap to find out with your own nose. Mine told me nothing for five weeks.

Don't ask your daughter either. She'll tell you you're fine.

If you buy one more bar, give it two weeks. Then watch how the people you love say goodbye.

I'm just Dr. Mercer's patient. Nobody pays me a cent for any of this.

The one she gave me is Kaori. One bar is $19.95. Six bars are $60.

If it does nothing for you, they give you your money back.

Sarah's coming Sunday.

Diane

P.S. Don read this over my shoulder. He says he never knew what I paid for that first bar. He also says I can't write all this without saying where to get the other one.

I left it out on purpose. I didn't sit down to sell anybody soap. But he's right, it saves you looking.
