body.text:
My friend Bonnie paid six hundred dollars to get me out of my own house for four days. She called after she booked it. "You're going. It's paid for. Don't start."

I did not want to go anywhere.

I am going to tell you why she made me.

Bonnie and I have been friends forty years. Her sister Louise keeps two rooms in her house outside Boone for people who come up for the leaves. Bonnie has gone down every October for nine years.

She had asked me along twice. This time she did not ask.

Here's what 58 looked like before I went.

Wayne and I have been married thirty-one years.

He used to take my hand walking out to the car. Neither of us ever decided that. It stopped somewhere in the last two years. I could not tell you the month.

He moved into the back bedroom fourteen months ago. His back. That mattress is firmer.

Pam and Sheila used to call on a Thursday about cards. Now I hear about the Thursdays afterwards.

Marcy across the street used to sit at my kitchen table on a Saturday. Now she stands on the step. She says she's sweaty from the walk.

Every one of those has a reason on it. Every reason is true.

Then in August Wayne's mother called me.

Jeanette is eighty-four. She calls Wayne on Sundays. In thirty-one years she has never once called me.

She said she was just checking in. She asked me twice how I was doing. Not how we were doing.

I said we're fine, and asked her about her knee.

I stood in the kitchen afterwards with the phone still in my hand. Somebody outside this marriage had been told something about it. I was the last one in the house to find out what.

I didn't tell Bonnie. I didn't tell anybody.

Kyle flew up over Labor Day for a wedding in Delaware. He lives in Charlotte now. We had him two nights, so I got the good coffee in on the Friday.

He booked a room at the Hampton out by the interstate.

"It's a six o'clock flight out of Columbus, Mom. I'd have you up at four."

His bed in that house has been made up since 2019. I told him that was smart thinking, then I put the sheets back in the closet on the Tuesday.

We had a nice supper. He hugged me out by the car and then he got in it.

Two weeks later I ran into Pam by the eggs at Kroger. She held onto her cart with both hands. She said the summer had gotten away from everybody. She said she would call me about a Thursday.

She was warm the whole time. She has known me twenty years. She did not call.

So I stopped putting things forward. If I don't suggest the Saturday, nobody has to tell me they can't do the Saturday. It is easier on everybody, so I didn't think of it as anything at the time.

None of it started with his mother's phone call. I had asked Wayne back in March whether something was wrong. He said no. I took the no. That was the whole conversation, so we have not had another one.

If I ask for a hug, he gives me one very briefly. It makes me want to cry. I have never said that out loud to a living soul.

One night in the spring I cried and begged for a hug. A kiss. Anything. He stood there at the sink and said okay, okay. Then he went to bed.

You're not just living with no physical affection. There's no emotional affection either. That is what two years of it is, and nobody in that house has ever once been unkind to me.

At least we're still here, I used to say in the car. At least we're still here.

I told myself I could cope and things would improve. They didn't.

In September I said one thing about it to Bonnie, while she was pulling weeds out of my front bed. That Wayne had been run down, and the house had gone quiet.

She didn't sit back on her heels. "It's just age. This is what happens." Her Dwight went the same way at sixty, she said.

She was kind, so I put the question down.

Then in October she booked the four days.

I packed the night before. Four days of somebody else's towels so Bonnie could feel like she had done something for me. I did not say that to her. I said thank you.

We drove down on a Tuesday. Almost seven hours, and Bonnie talked for five of them.

Somewhere past Wytheville she said, "Is everything all right with you and Wayne?"

"He's been run down," I said. "Is Louise still doing the porch in the fall?"

She let it go. Forty years, and she let it go, because I asked her to without saying it.

We stopped at a Hardee's. She paid for that too. Four days of being handled, I thought. I ate the biscuit.

Louise's house sits up a gravel road with a porch across the whole front of it. There's a hickory that drops on the roof at night and makes you sit up in bed. She's seventy-one. She cooks for whoever is in it.

She came out to the car and had my bag off me before I got the door shut.

"You'll be in the back," she said. "It's the cold one. There's another quilt in the chest."

Bonnie carried the wine in like she owned the place. She has her own hook by the door for her coat, with her name on a piece of tape underneath it.

There was a wood stove going in the kitchen and something with apples in the oven.

The back room has a sloped ceiling and a window that looks at the hickory.

There's a small bathroom off that room with a shelf over the sink. On the shelf there is a dish with a bar in it and nothing else in it.

I washed with it before dinner because I was a guest and it was what was there.

We ate at the kitchen table, the three of us and a pan of cornbread. I was in bed by nine.

Wednesday morning I washed and came down. Louise had the coffee going.

A man named Dale came at ten to look at her gutters. When he was done he took a coffee, pulled out the chair across from mine at that kitchen table and talked to me about gutters for ten minutes.

I want you to understand how small a thing I was noticing.

That afternoon Faye from the next place down came over for coffee. There were four chairs on that porch. She took the one touching mine.

Wednesday night Bonnie hugged me in the hallway, but I was the one who stepped back first. It took me until the next morning to work out why that was strange.

Thursday I washed, took my coffee out to the porch and said it out loud to Bonnie.

"It's the air up here," I said. "It's sleeping in a room with no clock in it. It's four days of not having to be anything for anybody."

Bonnie said it was probably all three.

Louise was carrying a bowl past us and said nothing at all, which from her is a speech.

That afternoon Bonnie drove into town for gas. I found Louise on the back step with a colander of beans.

"Louise. What is it about this house?"

"What do you mean, honey."

"People keep coming and sitting down next to me. That has not happened to me at home in two years and it has happened three times since Tuesday." I sat down on the step below her. "And don't tell me it's the air. I've been telling myself it's the air since Wednesday and I've quit believing it."

She kept snapping beans.

"Bonnie let go of you first on Tuesday," she said. "At the door. She's done it for years and she doesn't know she does it. Last night you let go first."

"How would you notice a thing like that?"

"I've had people in this house twenty-two years. Noticing is most of the job."

She put a handful in the colander.

"You're right that something's different about you since Tuesday. You're wrong about what did it."

"I shower every day. I showered at home too."

"I know you do."

"Then what."

"I'm seventy-one," she said. "Things change and none of it is anybody's fault. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin dries out on you."

"You color it. You get the glasses."

"That's right. Your skin also starts making something it never made before. Some kind of compound. It has a smell to it. Not a nice one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't say it out loud."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set the colander down on the step.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off you."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"You chop garlic," she said. "Then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell," I said.

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed on them anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't take hold of."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works the same way."

I sat there on that step with the beans between us.

"Then what gets rid of it."

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

She wiped her hands on her apron.

"You've been using it since Tuesday."

I looked at her.

"The bar in the dish in your bathroom. There's nothing else in that dish and there hasn't been for six years. Everybody who sleeps in that room uses it, and not one of them has ever asked me what it is."

Dale sitting down at that table. Faye taking the chair against mine. Bonnie's arms still around me while I was already stepping back.

Three days, and nobody had said one word to me.

"It's soap," she said. "Made out of persimmon."

"Soap."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And that works."

"A woman who stayed here left one behind about six years ago with a note about it. I was rude to her in my head for a week."

She picked the colander back up.

"One morning that winter I noticed I'd quit turning my cheek when people came in to hug me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori," she said. "Go in the hall closet before you leave and take one home."

"Louise."

"They make it in small batches and this one's nearly out. When a batch goes you wait months for the next."

We drove home Saturday morning with a bar out of Louise's hall closet in my bag, wrapped in one of her dish towels. I felt like a fool about it for the first hour.

Thirty-one years of a marriage, and the answer is a bar in a dish in somebody else's bathroom. Say that out loud in a car and listen to it.

Then I turned it the other way round. Nobody told me one thing until Thursday afternoon. By Thursday afternoon it had already happened. Whatever it was, it had done the whole of its work while I was still crediting the mountain.

An hour out of Boone, Bonnie said, "You've been different since Wednesday." She had her sunglasses on. "I thought it was just getting you out of that house."

"So did I," I said.

We got back the last Saturday in October.

The second week, Wayne took my hand in the parking lot at Kroger. Coming out, both of us carrying bags. He didn't say anything, so neither did I. We walked to the truck like that.

The door of the back bedroom stands open now. It has stood open since the first week of November. I have not asked him about it and I am not going to.

Pam called on a Tuesday. Not about a Thursday. About nothing at all. She talked forty minutes about her son's kitchen. I sat down on the floor by the refrigerator and let her.

Marcy came in the side door two Saturdays ago, pulled out a chair at my table and sat in it the way she used to.

Then she stopped in the middle of what she was saying.

"What is that scent, what's it called?"

"It's a bar of soap."

"You smell like somebody's been peeling oranges in here." She got her phone out. "Write it down for me before I forget."

"Kaori."

He still takes his coffee out to the truck by himself at ten past five every morning. That one has not come back. I don't expect it to now.

Last Sunday I was at the sink doing the pans. He came in and stood next to me instead of in the doorway.

"Good to have you back," he said.

I was gone four days.

I have never told him what changed. He has not asked me. He isn't going to, so I have stopped needing him to.

Louise called Bonnie in November. There's a new batch and it's already most of the way gone. Bonnie ordered two. I ordered three.

Kyle is coming at Thanksgiving. He asked me on the phone whether his bed was still made up.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.

Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.

My name is Dr. Margaret Ellis. I'm a geriatrician and I've been doing this for 22 years

I want to be clear about something before I say anything else. I don't recommend products. My patients will tell you that. When I finally do tell someone to buy something, it's because I've watched it work, over and over, for years.

Which is why what happened last year bothered me so much. But let me start from the beginning.

I did part of my training at a geriatric hospital in Japan.

Part of the reason why I went to Japan was to find out why they live so long.

What I found was, a big part of that is that they are extremely comfortable and confident with aging, you would love to see how most of them go so confidently into their 90's

And this isn't just a feeling. There's real research behind this.

How you feel about aging changes how you age.

In the most famous study, people with a positive view of getting older outlived the people who feared it by around seven and a half years.

Which is exactly why the next thing I learned in Japan stuck with me. Because there is one thing that can quietly take all that confidence away

That's where I first heard a word we don't have in English.

Kareishu.

Aging odor.

In Japan, nobody pretends it isn't real, it's common sense there, the way gray hair is common sense.

Everyone knows that around sixty, your skin starts making a compound called 2-nonenal. Everyone knows what it smells like. And everyone knows what to do about it.

Because they've been dealing with it for centuries.

The answer there has always been the same.

A soap made from fermented persimmon. They call it kakishibu.

Unripe persimmons, pressed, then left to ferment for months, until they're full of tannins.

And tannins are one of the only things that actually grab onto nonenal

At the hospital, nurses handed those bars to patients the way we hand out blood pressure pamphlets.

Then I finished my training, came home, and learned something strange. Here, none of this existed.

No word for it. No pamphlet. In 20 years of practice, not one patient has ever brought it up with me first.

But I would watch what it did every single week.

One of my patients taught second grade for 41 years. Then one September the school gave her class to a teacher half her age and called it restructuring.

It took her months to get the real reason out of her principal. Parents had complained about a smell.

Patients noticing their grandson's hugs getting shorter.

Family becoming more and more distant.

So I did the only thing I could.

Quietly, in my office, I started telling people about persimmon soap. I've been doing it since the year I opened my practice.

Back then my patients had to order it from tiny importers and wait weeks for it. But it worked, over and over, right in front of me.

For twenty years it was the one product I broke my own rule for.

Then, about a year ago, everything changed. Persimmon soap was suddenly everywhere.

Suddenly, patients were asking me about it.

People walked into my office holding their phones, showing me ads.

After twenty years of explaining kakishibu from scratch, I didn't have to convince anyone anymore.

You have to understand what that means in my office. Telling a patient about aging odor is the most delicate conversation I have.

I am telling someone they carry a smell they cannot smell.

So when patients started bringing it up themselves, it honestly felt like a relief.

Last year alone, sixty-one of my patients bought a bar on my recommendation. I know the exact number, because I keep track of everything I recommend.

Then the calls started.

"Be honest with me, doctor. Was this supposed to do anything at all?"

By the end of the year, nineteen of those sixty-one patients had left my clinic. A few told my receptionist why. Most just stopped booking.

One woman had been with me for eleven years. On her way out she said she didn't need "this old people smell nonsense." Eleven years, gone.

And I had no answer.

Same soap, as far as I knew. Same instructions I'd given for two decades. It had never failed like this.

So I did something I've never done in my career. I started calling the ones who would still take my call, and I asked them to bring me what they had bought.

The first bar arrived on a Monday morning. A patient named Ruth set it on my desk, still in its box.

And the moment I put my eyes on that bar I knew something was wrong.

That bar was bright orange, looked like a block of cheddar

The Kakishibu I knew from Japan was nothing like that.

So I did the test the nurses in Japan taught me.

I carried her bar to my office window and held it up against the light. The light hit it and stopped. Nothing came through.

Real kakishibu is translucent. Hold it to a window and the light passes straight through it, and it glows amber, like honey held up to a lamp.

The next day I brought my own bar from home and held them side by side at the same window and sent her a photo.

Mine glowed. Hers might as well have been a brick.

Two more patients brought theirs in that week. Different brands, different boxes.

Same brick.

Not one of them had ever touched the thing I was recommending.

Here's what they'd actually bought. Juice soap. Ripe persimmons pressed for juice, stirred into an ordinary soap base, dyed orange.

And juice has none of the tannins.

The tannins come from fermenting the unripe fruit for months. Skip the fermentation and you have a bar that smells nice, looks the part, and does absolutely nothing about nonenal.

That glow isn't a color anyone can add. It's the material itself. Which is why no dyed bar can fake it.

My patients had been washing with orange dye for months. And here is the part that made me genuinely angry. It's completely legal.

Juice, dye, a persimmon on the label, and the box gets to say persimmon soap.

Nineteen people trusted me, scrubbed every day with colored soap base, smelled exactly the same, and decided I was a fool. And honestly, they were half right.

Because I'd been saying "persimmon soap" for twenty years, when I should have been telling them exactly what to look for.

So I started doing the research I should have done a year earlier.

Out of everything sold online, there were only two brands that looked like they produced real kakishibu.

One of them is the famous one, The girl that owns it has been on shark tank.

It looked like something I could actually trust, but I'd already lost nineteen patients to a label. I wasn't going to risk a twentieth.

So I dug deeper.

On that Shark Tank episode, the founder said each bar costs about a 1.85$ to make.

AND they sell it on a subscription, every month, all year round. And it has never, as far as I can tell, been out of stock.

Not once.

Now remember what kakishibu is. Persimmons ripen once a year. The unripe fruit gets pressed and then ferments for months. There is only ever as much real kakishibu as the last harvest gave.

A dollar eighty-five, unlimited supply, forever, from a once-a-year fruit. I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm telling you I cannot make that math work.

That was enough for me to keep looking.

So I ordered a bar from the other brand, shipped to my clinic. This time I was going to test it myself before it went anywhere near a patient.

The bar arrived two days later, from a small brand called Kakiyu.

I took it straight to the same window where Ruth's orange bar had failed, and held it up.

The light went straight through it. That deep amber glow, exactly like the bars the nurses handed out in Japan.

My receptionist asked me why I was smiling at a bar of soap.

It looked like a scene coming out of a Indiana Jones movie

Then I took it home and used it for two weeks, because a glow isn't a result.

It was the first bar I'd held in a year where everything matched: the color, the light, the one-harvest story, even the fact that it kept selling out while I was researching it.

And it held up.

So I went back to their site and ordered nineteen more.

All nineteen bars went out the same week, to their homes, each with a handwritten note.

I kept the note short. The soap was real. The bar you bought was not. Hold this one up to a window and you'll see the difference for yourself. Then call me.

The first call came nine days later.

It was Ruth. She didn't say hello. She said, "My daughter hugged me goodbye yesterday, and she didn't rush it."

Then she went quiet, and we stayed on the phone like that for a moment, and I didn't mind one bit.

Within two weeks, my front desk had heard from fourteen of the nineteen.

One man told me his wife had started sitting on his side of the couch again.

Another patient said her grandkids stayed the whole sunday afternoon, and nobody found a reason to leave early.

Here's the thing about this problem.

Nobody ever announces the change, in either direction. Nothing gets said when people drift away, and nothing gets said when they drift back. They just lean in again.

But you can see it. My patients walk into my waiting room differently now. Straighter. They linger at the front desk to chat.

That confidence I saw everywhere in Japan, the one the research says is worth seven and a half years, I watch it come back one appointment at a time.

I now tell every patient the same thing.

If you're going to try persimmon soap, you have exactly one job. Make sure it's real kakishibu. Hold the bar up to a window.

If the light passes through and it glows amber, it's real. If the light stops, you're holding dye.

Kakiyu is the only bar I've found that passes every test I know how to run. I don't get a cent for saying that, and they have no idea I'm writing this

There's a sixty day guarantee, so the test costs you nothing. Use it for two months. If nobody around you moves closer, send it back. I only wish the nineteen orange bars had come with those terms.

So this is me, asking you the same thing I asked at the start. Please don't buy persimmon soap. Buy the real thing once, or don't buy anything at all.

Twenty-two years, and this is the first time I've ever written something like this about a product. But I watched nineteen people spend months getting quietly written off by the people they love, over a bar of dyed soap.

If this reaches even one person before they buy another orange bar, it was worth writing.

PS. A few people asked me to put the link here. I didn't include one when I first wrote this, I was writing a warning, not an advertisement. But you're right that it saves you searching, so here it is: https://kakiyucare.com/products/kakiyu-persimmon-soap

PPS. Since posting this, I've had people tell me they went looking for Kakiyu on Amazon. Please don't. Kakiyu doesn't sell there, and what comes up when you search the name is exactly the orange soap this whole letter is about. The real bar exists in one place, their official website. Use the link above and nowhere else.

We bought 12 persimmon soaps sold for "old person smell" and read every ingredient list. Here's what we found:

❌ 7 of 12 don't contain persimmon at all — the orange is food colouring (CI 15985)
❌ Several say "persimmon extract" on the front and never name it on the back
❌ Almost none use kakishibu, the fermented unripe fruit, which is the part that binds the oil
❌ The doses that are listed are too small to do anything measurable

Only 3 of the 12 passed.

The #1 pick is the only one using fermented kakishibu at a strength you can actually read on the label — Diospyros Kaki Fruit Extract, named on the INCI, not hidden inside "fragrance". Kakishibu is unripe persimmon pressed and left to ferment for months. The tannin binds the oil instead of trying to rinse past it. No dye. No masking fragrance. No subscription to cancel.

If you shower twice a day and it's back by three… if you've caught it in the car and not on yourself… if your pillowcase smells before your skin does… if you've already bought a persimmon soap and felt nothing — this is why. The soap was fine. There was just no kakishibu in it.

body.text:
Please stop buying the orange ones. I know that sounds odd. Every box in the category is orange. Every listing has persimmons photographed on it. The orange is the whole reason you recognise it as persimmon soap in the first place.

It looks logical. Persimmons are orange, so persimmon soap is orange. Basic sense.

Except it's backwards. And the reason it's backwards is the entire difference between a bar that works and £22 in the bin.

Women aren't failing with persimmon soap because persimmon soap doesn't work. They're failing because of which fruit is in the bar.

Buying a dearer orange one doesn't fix that. It just costs more.

Here's what's actually going on. Because nobody selling these will ever explain it to you.

There are two completely different materials being sold under one word.

Kakishibu is fermented persimmon tannin. Unripe astringent persimmons are picked green and hard - at the stage where biting one shuts your mouth up - then pressed, and left in a vat to ferment for months. What comes out is dark, thick and nearly black. Japan has used it for four hundred years, on paper, on fabric, on wood and on skin.

Persimmon juice is the pressed ripe fruit. It's cheap, it's orange, and it photographs beautifully in a bar of soap.

Both are legally allowed to print the word persimmon on the front of the box, in the same size type.

Now here's why the difference decides everything.

The compound behind aging odour is called 2-nonenal. Japanese researchers identified it in 2001. It is not sweat, it is not bacteria, and it has nothing to do with hygiene.

It's an oil. Which is why ordinary soap cannot lift it - soap is a detergent built for sweat and water-soluble dirt, and oil and water don't mix. You already know that from a roasting tin.

What lifts it is the tannin. Tannins are polyphenols; they carry several binding sites that latch onto the molecule and carry it off with the rinse water.

And the tannin is concentrated in the unripe fruit. It is what makes the green one astringent. As the fruit ripens and sweetens, that astringency goes - which is the same thing as saying the tannin goes.

So the glossy orange persimmon on the front of the box is not a decorative choice.

It's the wrong fruit, photographed.

That escalating feeling - that you've tried this and it doesn't work on you, that you're somehow the exception - isn't in your head. It's real. But it isn't what you think it is.

Now here's where it gets worse.

You cannot smell this on yourself. Your own nose adapts within days and you go completely blind to it - not "hard to detect", impossible.

Which means you cannot evaluate a bar of soap. You use one for three weeks, you notice nothing, and you have no way on earth of telling the difference between "this bar is dyed glycerin" and "this bar is working perfectly and I simply cannot tell."

Buy the wrong fruit. Feel nothing. Get no feedback. Conclude the idea is nonsense. Give up on the one thing that was going to help.

That is the loop this whole category runs on, and it is why so many women have three of these in a drawer.

This is why nothing has worked.

"Persimmon fruit extract" on a panel is the ripe fruit. A trace of it, usually below the fragrance.

"Persimmon" on the front of the box and nowhere in the ingredients means there is no persimmon in the bar at all.

CI 15985 is an orange food colouring. It is the reason the bar is orange and it is doing no work whatsoever.

A Japanese-looking font is not a Japanese product. One of the bars I was shown had Japanese characters on the front and Guangdong on the bottom, in six-point type.

And four and a half stars from two thousand people means two thousand people found it pleasant in week one. It does not mean it worked, because none of them could have known.

And the price tells you nothing either.

That is worth saying on its own, because it is the trap almost every woman falls into. The first bar does nothing, so you buy a dearer one — which is the correct instinct in every other category and is worthless in this one.

Price has no relationship to which fruit is in the bar. I have seen dyed glycerin sold at thirty pounds and I have seen a genuine fermented bar sold for less than that. The cheapest real one costs a little more than the dearest fake, and that is the whole of the relationship.

Nor does the country on the front. Two bars I was shown had Japanese characters printed across them. One said Guangdong on the base, in six-point type, where nobody would look.

Nor do the reviews, and this is the one that costs women the most. Four and a half stars from two thousand people means two thousand people found a bar pleasant in its first week. Not one of them could have known whether it worked, because none of them could smell it on themselves. Those reviews are honest. They are simply measuring the wrong thing.

The label has been the only real evidence the entire time. And almost nobody turns the box over.

Except there is one thing that cannot be faked, and it takes ten seconds.

Hold the bar up to a window. Fermented kakishibu is translucent amber and the light goes straight through it, like a piece of resin. A dyed bar is opaque all the way through.

Then look at the panel for two words: Diospyros Kaki.

That's it. That's the whole test.

I grew up with the real thing in my grandmother's bathroom in Mino, in Gifu, which is where it has been made for centuries, and I have written down exactly what I check. Including:

• Where on the ingredient panel it has to sit before the amount means anything - which matters far more than whether the word is there at all.

• The window test, and the one lighting condition where it will fool you.

• What "fermented" is allowed to mean on a British box, and what it usually means.

• Why the bar being unscented is the thing I'd check second, and what a fragrance in this particular product is almost always covering.

Read it before you buy another one - from us or from anybody 👇

body.text:
After my divorce my best friends lied about excluding me from Italy. But they missed my ex-husband more. So I booked the flight and took care of that.

Cassie and I have been best friends for 20 years.

She and Greg. Mike and Pam. Dave and Rachel. Three couples, plus Mark and me.

Every September for 16 years, the 8 of us traveled together.

I researched the towns. I found the excursions. I booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics.

For 16 years this was the best week of my year.

Then Mark and I divorced. 14 months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, sweetheart, we thought you needed a little time for yourself. After everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And it's close quarters over there. One apartment, six of us, the heat in August. Ever since the divorce you just haven't been yourself, Susan."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing Amalfi in September. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing."

I said, "Sure, Cassie. I'll put something together."

Then I hung up. I sat in the kitchen for an hour.

Why did I say yes.

That's the part I kept going back to. She left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. And I said sure. Like it was nothing.

Maybe I was being unfair to her. It really could have been last minute. Cassie has not been cruel to me one day in 20 years.

Or maybe I said yes because it was the only thing they still wanted me for.

I sat there a while longer. Then I got the laptop.

I started planning it. Spent weeks on it.

Found a private lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through the terraces that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE. You're amazing. This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house. "Just a little get-together," she said. "Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out. Candles lit. All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in. The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about September."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Mark and Brittany took your spot this year."

Mark.

And Brittany.

The woman he left me for. She was 34. She'd been in his life for two years, one of them while he was still married to me.

"Mark reached out," Cassie continued. "He and Brittany just got engaged. And honestly, we've all known Mark for 20 years. It felt wrong to exclude him forever."

Exclude him.

The man who cheated on me for a year. Who left me for a woman half my age. Who kept the house in the settlement because I couldn't afford to fight him for it.

He's the one they were worried about excluding.

"Susan, we love you. You know that. But nothing has changed since we talked on the phone."

Close quarters. The heat. I just hadn't been myself.

She looked around the table. Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way. You have to understand."

You have to understand.

I looked at Cassie. At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get. Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass. Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry. I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

She wasn't wrong. That was the part I couldn't put down.

The next morning I drove over to Nora's. My sister. 28 years a nurse, most of it on a geriatric floor. She lives 20 minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her everything. The photos from Florence. The "you're so good at organizing" call. The dinner. Cassie's voice. "Ever since the divorce."

And the part I could barely say out loud: that Mark and Brittany were taking my spot. On the trip I planned.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She didn't say a word about it.

"They're right that there's something," she said. "They're wrong about what it is. Those two aren't the same thing."

"Nora, what is this about?"

"28 years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then that's not me. I'm a clean person, Nora. I always have been. I buy the good body wash."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"And people notice it," she said. "Not that they know what they're noticing. They couldn't tell you. They just start standing a little further back, and they make up a reason for it afterward."

"Nora."

"You didn't do anything, Susan. Nobody did this to you. Your skin changed at 60 the same way your eyes changed at 45, and nobody sent you a letter about either one."

"So it was never me."

"It was never you."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my floor home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

I picked it up and held it to my face. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It's called Kaori. I'm down to two bars myself."

I was at the door when she said the other thing.

"Book the flight, Susan. Go on your own."

"Cassie isn't going to un-invite Brittany."

"I'm not talking about Cassie. You found that grove because you wanted to see a grove. You got that table because you wanted to sit at it."

She held the door open.

"So go sit at it."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That afternoon I ordered two more. Then I booked the trip.

Same week. Same coast.

Their hotel. One floor up.

Paid for with the money from my half of the retirement account. The only thing I got in the divorce that was actually mine.

And I told no one.

September on the Amalfi Coast is hotter than people think.

I was on the hotel terrace with a glass of prosecco when I saw them come up from the road below. Cassie fanning herself with a folded map. Brittany walking ten feet behind Mark, not talking.

Twenty minutes later Cassie appeared on the terrace. Flushed. Hair coming undone.

She froze.

"Susan? What are you doing here?"

"Same week. Same coast."

She stared a second too long. Then she went to her room without saying anything else.

I didn't move. I had nowhere to be. And a very good glass of prosecco.

Day three. The lemon grove.

Twelve spots. I'd booked one for myself. The group had the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I got there first. Signora Rossi walked me up through the terraces and showed me how they wrap the lemons in cloth for the winter.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi looked up and waved at me across the terrace.

"Susan. You are the one who wrote to me. In Italian."

The whole group turned around.

Mark saw me. He stopped.

"Susan? You're on this tour?"

"I found this tour, Mark."

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked at Brittany.

Brittany adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

There was a woman on the tour with her daughter. About my age. She ended up next to me at the wall while Signora Rossi was talking.

She leaned in slightly. Then leaned back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearing something? I've been trying to place it since the van."

"It's a soap."

"It smells so good. Like citrus. Fresh." She laughed at herself. "Sorry. I've been behind you for twenty minutes trying to work out what it was."

"It's called Kaori."

She typed it into her phone right there against the wall.

Cassie was three feet away with her hand cupped over her eyes against the sun.

She didn't say anything.

I thought about that on the walk back down.

We've been talking, all of us. That is what Cassie said at the table.

All of them. Talking. And not one of them ever talked to me.

I think I understood now.

That evening the group was at the bar on the hotel terrace. I was two tables away with a book.

Dave came over. The quietest of the husbands. He sat on the edge of the chair next to mine.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip," he said. "And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar. Then he got up and went back to it.

I didn't read another page.

Night four. The dinner Cassie had booked for the group.

I came down at eight.

Cassie was already seated, fanning herself with the menu. Brittany's shoulders were burned across the top. She kept shifting in her chair.

Mark looked up when I walked in.

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-50s. Elegant. Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But I have to ask what you're wearing."

"It's a soap."

"A soap." She put her hand on her chest. "I write for a travel magazine. I've been trying to place that since you sat down. It isn't perfume. It's citrus, and it's fresh. It's lovely."

"Kaori. My sister gave it to me."

"Can I get it here?"

"They only make it when the persimmons come in," I said. "Once a year."

She wrote it in the journal anyway.

Brittany leaned over and said something to Mark. He didn't answer her.

Cassie watched all of it.

The woman with the journal. The pen.

She picked up her wine glass. Took a long sip. Set it down. Looked straight ahead.

Brittany had stopped shifting in her chair.

Mark was watching me. Not Brittany. Me.

Day seven I ate alone at the cliffside table in Positano. The one I'd booked three months earlier, for them.

They had tried for it that morning. Fully booked, the restaurant told them.

Last night. Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the terrace afterward. Water black. Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Greg hasn't left the room with the air conditioning since Tuesday," she said.

"That's a shame."

"Brittany's shoulders are blistering. She had to wear a shawl to dinner."

"I noticed."

She looked at me.

"People keep asking about you."

"They do."

"The woman with the journal. The girl at the front desk asked me what my friend uses."

Silence.

"Where did you get it?"

I looked at her.

"Kaori," I said. "But they only make it when the persimmons come in. That batch is gone."

She looked down.

"Of course it is."

"They restock when the fruit comes in. If you wait, you wait a long time."

She nodded.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my room without looking back.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

They left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. Apparently I'm capable enough to find a restaurant with a three-month waitlist. Just not capable enough to sit at one.

"We thought you needed a little time for yourself."

"Ever since the divorce, you just haven't been yourself."

Not one of them ever told me what they actually meant.

My sister did. In her kitchen, in about ten minutes.

Nora called last week. Kaori has a new batch up. It's already most of the way gone.

They're doing September again next year. Sicily, someone said.

Nora has already asked whether Sicily has lemon groves.

I told her yes.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost yourself.

You don't need to be replaced.

You need to be underestimated one more time.

So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the Kaori. Run the bath. Go anyway.

It costs less than fifty cents a day. Less than the coffee I drink while I plan other people's trips.

They only make it when the persimmons come in. Once a batch goes, you wait months.

Cassie asked where I got it. I told her it was sold out.

She's waiting until next year.

I was already home.

Your move.

She got pulled over in the pouring rain and the officer wouldn't believe the license was hers. He said the woman in this photo is fifty-five and that is not you.

She told him it is her, she's fifty-five, and she's on the job too — then showed him her badge. That made it worse. Now he thought she was carrying a fake ID and impersonating a cop. He put her over the hood of the patrol car in the rain and cuffed her while she stood there calm and soaked, telling him both were real.

body.text:
For twenty years my husband called me baby, honey, love. Never my name. Maybe that's why I didn't notice when it stopped.

He started saying my name the way a stranger would. No warmth. No breakfast. No kiss at the door. And then one day he introduced me as his sister in front of the girl he'd told me not to worry about. I smiled and said nothing. Twenty-one years of marriage, and that's where we'd arrived.

I didn't blame him. I did what women do — I blamed the face looking back at me. My skin had changed and everything I put on it just sat on top and lied. Creams, serums, every product I could find. So I stopped going out. Stopped answering the phone. Some nights I'd get ready hoping he'd look at me, and he never did.

Then my Korean aesthetician friend came over, took one look at me and said sit down. This isn't your age. This is what the wrong products do to you.

He told me Korean dermatologists spent years on this one, tested in their own labs, formulated for skin that's actually been through something — not twenty-five-year-old skin sold to women like me in different packaging.

He squeezed a drop onto my hand and it came out almost white and I told him that's never going to work. He said give it a second. And it found my exact shade right there on my skin. He did one side of my face and left the other, and one side was everything I'd been hiding behind for years. The other side was me.

A month later the laugh came back. The walk came back. And when I drove past his lunch spot and saw them together, I didn't stop and I didn't cry. I just kept driving with the music on.

He texted that night saying he'd made a mistake. I read it, put my phone face down, and kept living.

body.text:
I recommended persimmon soap to 61 patients last year. 19 of them ended up leaving my clinic

My name is Dr. Margaret Ellis. I'm a geriatrician and I've been doing this for 22 years

I want to be clear about something before I say anything else. I don't recommend products. My patients will tell you that. When I finally do tell someone to buy something, it's because I've watched it work, over and over, for years.

Which is why what happened last year bothered me so much. But let me start from the beginning.

I did part of my training at a geriatric hospital in Japan.

Part of the reason why I went to Japan was to find out why they live so long.

What I found was, a big part of that is that they are extremely comfortable and confident with aging, you would love to see how most of them go so confidently into their 90's

And this isn't just a feeling. There's real research behind this.

How you feel about aging changes how you age.

In the most famous study, people with a positive view of getting older outlived the people who feared it by around seven and a half years.

Which is exactly why the next thing I learned in Japan stuck with me. Because there is one thing that can quietly take all that confidence away

That's where I first heard a word we don't have in English.

Kareishu.

Aging odor.

In Japan, nobody pretends it isn't real, it's common sense there, the way gray hair is common sense.

Everyone knows that around sixty, your skin starts making a compound called 2-nonenal. Everyone knows what it smells like. And everyone knows what to do about it.

Because they've been dealing with it for centuries.

The answer there has always been the same.

A soap made from fermented persimmon. They call it kakishibu.

Unripe persimmons, pressed, then left to ferment for months, until they're full of tannins.

And tannins are one of the only things that actually grab onto nonenal

At the hospital, nurses handed those bars to patients the way we hand out blood pressure pamphlets.

Then I finished my training, came home, and learned something strange. Here, none of this existed.

No word for it. No pamphlet. In 20 years of practice, not one patient has ever brought it up with me first.

But I would watch what it did every single week.

One of my patients taught second grade for 41 years. Then one September the school gave her class to a teacher half her age and called it restructuring.

It took her months to get the real reason out of her principal. Parents had complained about a smell.

Patients noticing their grandson's hugs getting shorter.

Family becoming more and more distant.

So I did the only thing I could.

Quietly, in my office, I started telling people about persimmon soap. I've been doing it since the year I opened my practice.

Back then my patients had to order it from tiny importers and wait weeks for it. But it worked, over and over, right in front of me.

For twenty years it was the one product I broke my own rule for.

Then, about a year ago, everything changed. Persimmon soap was suddenly everywhere.

Suddenly, patients were asking me about it.

People walked into my office holding their phones, showing me ads.

After twenty years of explaining kakishibu from scratch, I didn't have to convince anyone anymore.

You have to understand what that means in my office. Telling a patient about aging odor is the most delicate conversation I have.

I am telling someone they carry a smell they cannot smell.

So when patients started bringing it up themselves, it honestly felt like a relief.

Last year alone, sixty-one of my patients bought a bar on my recommendation. I know the exact number, because I keep track of everything I recommend.

Then the calls started.

"Be honest with me, doctor. Was this supposed to do anything at all?"

By the end of the year, nineteen of those sixty-one patients had left my clinic. A few told my receptionist why. Most just stopped booking.

One woman had been with me for eleven years. On her way out she said she didn't need "this old people smell nonsense." Eleven years, gone.

And I had no answer.

Same soap, as far as I knew. Same instructions I'd given for two decades. It had never failed like this.

So I did something I've never done in my career. I started calling the ones who would still take my call, and I asked them to bring me what they had bought.

The first bar arrived on a Monday morning. A patient named Ruth set it on my desk, still in its box.

And the moment I put my eyes on that bar I knew something was wrong.

That bar was bright orange, looked like a block of cheddar

The Kakishibu I knew from Japan was nothing like that.

So I did the test the nurses in Japan taught me.

I carried her bar to my office window and held it up against the light. The light hit it and stopped. Nothing came through.

Real kakishibu is translucent. Hold it to a window and the light passes straight through it, and it glows amber, like honey held up to a lamp.

The next day I brought my own bar from home and held them side by side at the same window and sent her a photo.

Mine glowed. Hers might as well have been a brick.

Two more patients brought theirs in that week. Different brands, different boxes.

Same brick.

Not one of them had ever touched the thing I was recommending.

Here's what they'd actually bought. Juice soap. Ripe persimmons pressed for juice, stirred into an ordinary soap base, dyed orange.

And juice has none of the tannins.

The tannins come from fermenting the unripe fruit for months. Skip the fermentation and you have a bar that smells nice, looks the part, and does absolutely nothing about nonenal.

That glow isn't a color anyone can add. It's the material itself. Which is why no dyed bar can fake it.

My patients had been washing with orange dye for months. And here is the part that made me genuinely angry. It's completely legal.

Juice, dye, a persimmon on the label, and the box gets to say persimmon soap.

Nineteen people trusted me, scrubbed every day with colored soap base, smelled exactly the same, and decided I was a fool. And honestly, they were half right.

Because I'd been saying "persimmon soap" for twenty years, when I should have been telling them exactly what to look for.

So I started doing the research I should have done a year earlier.

Out of everything sold online, there were only two brands that looked like they produced real kakishibu.

One of them is the famous one, The girl that owns it has been on shark tank.

It looked like something I could actually trust, but I'd already lost nineteen patients to a label. I wasn't going to risk a twentieth.

So I dug deeper.

On that Shark Tank episode, the founder said each bar costs about a 1.85$ to make.

AND they sell it on a subscription, every month, all year round. And it has never, as far as I can tell, been out of stock.

Not once.

Now remember what kakishibu is. Persimmons ripen once a year. The unripe fruit gets pressed and then ferments for months. There is only ever as much real kakishibu as the last harvest gave.

A dollar eighty-five, unlimited supply, forever, from a once-a-year fruit. I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm telling you I cannot make that math work.

That was enough for me to keep looking.

So I ordered a bar from the other brand, shipped to my clinic. This time I was going to test it myself before it went anywhere near a patient.

The bar arrived two days later, from a small brand called Kakiyu.

I took it straight to the same window where Ruth's orange bar had failed, and held it up.

The light went straight through it. That deep amber glow, exactly like the bars the nurses handed out in Japan.

My receptionist asked me why I was smiling at a bar of soap.

It looked like a scene coming out of a Indiana Jones movie

Then I took it home and used it for two weeks, because a glow isn't a result.

It was the first bar I'd held in a year where everything matched: the color, the light, the one-harvest story, even the fact that it kept selling out while I was researching it.

And it held up.

So I went back to their site and ordered nineteen more.

All nineteen bars went out the same week, to their homes, each with a handwritten note.

I kept the note short. The soap was real. The bar you bought was not. Hold this one up to a window and you'll see the difference for yourself. Then call me.

The first call came nine days later.

It was Ruth. She didn't say hello. She said, "My daughter hugged me goodbye yesterday, and she didn't rush it."

Then she went quiet, and we stayed on the phone like that for a moment, and I didn't mind one bit.

Within two weeks, my front desk had heard from fourteen of the nineteen.

One man told me his wife had started sitting on his side of the couch again.

Another patient said her grandkids stayed the whole sunday afternoon, and nobody found a reason to leave early.

Here's the thing about this problem.

Nobody ever announces the change, in either direction. Nothing gets said when people drift away, and nothing gets said when they drift back. They just lean in again.

But you can see it. My patients walk into my waiting room differently now. Straighter. They linger at the front desk to chat.

That confidence I saw everywhere in Japan, the one the research says is worth seven and a half years, I watch it come back one appointment at a time.

I now tell every patient the same thing.

If you're going to try persimmon soap, you have exactly one job. Make sure it's real kakishibu. Hold the bar up to a window.

If the light passes through and it glows amber, it's real. If the light stops, you're holding dye.

Kakiyu is the only bar I've found that passes every test I know how to run. I don't get a cent for saying that, and they have no idea I'm writing this

There's a sixty day guarantee, so the test costs you nothing. Use it for two months. If nobody around you moves closer, send it back. I only wish the nineteen orange bars had come with those terms.

So this is me, asking you the same thing I asked at the start. Please don't buy persimmon soap. Buy the real thing once, or don't buy anything at all.

Twenty-two years, and this is the first time I've ever written something like this about a product. But I watched nineteen people spend months getting quietly written off by the people they love, over a bar of dyed soap.

If this reaches even one person before they buy another orange bar, it was worth writing.

PS. A few people asked me to put the link here. I didn't include one when I first wrote this, I was writing a warning, not an advertisement. But you're right that it saves you searching, so here it is: https://kakiyucare.com/products/kakiyu-persimmon-soap

PPS. Since posting this, I've had people tell me they went looking for Kakiyu on Amazon. Please don't. Kakiyu doesn't sell there, and what comes up when you search the name is exactly the orange soap this whole letter is about. The real bar exists in one place, their official website. Use the link above and nowhere else.

body.text:
There's a box on my pantry shelf that my daughter is never to sell, never to give away, and never to let a stranger price.

It has been up there since September. It cost less than the groceries I bring home on a Thursday. And I need to tell you how a stranger's estate sale put it there, because the woman who told me what belongs in a box like that was standing over her own mother's, and what she said to me on that porch changed how my family does Sundays.

It was a Saturday morning in August. One of those white farmhouses out past the fairgrounds.

The ad said TOOLS, FURNITURE, HOUSEHOLD.

Doug wanted the ladder. I wanted the white platters. I still don't know what I wanted them for.

The whole place was priced to go. Furniture tagged. Dishes in dollar boxes. Sixty-some years of a woman's life out on folding tables in wet grass. It wasn't nine o'clock yet.

Except for one.

Up on the porch, two steps above all of it, somebody had put a box on a kitchen chair, the way you'd sit a person down. The flaps were folded shut. There was an index card taped to the top. On the card, in marker: NOT FOR SALE.

I stood at the bottom of those steps longer than I meant to.

"You can stand there as long as you want." A voice behind me. "That's the one thing out here you can't have."

She was about sixty-five. Gray hair pinned up, a cardigan on in August, a roll of green price stickers in one hand.

"Sorry," I said. "Everything else out here has a tag on it. That one doesn't. What's in it?"

"Something that gets used up." She put her hand out. "Ruth."

"Diane," I said. "Used up?"

"That's right."

I should have said thank you and gone to look at the dishes.

Before I tell you what I said instead, I have to tell you about the year I'd had.

I'm 62. Doug and I have been in this house 31 years.

Rachel is our only one. She's 37. She and Scott have Owen, 11, and Nell, who was six then.

For twenty years Sunday was at my house.

I did the roast. I did the table.

Then last September Rachel and Scott bought the house on Delaware Street. A kitchen twice the size of mine. They'd been saving for it since Owen was born.

That's when Sunday moved.

The first Sunday there, I came to the door with a pie, because I brought the pie now.

Bonnie was already inside. Bonnie is Scott's mother. She has been at every one of these for eleven years.

Nell came down the hall at a run. She went to Bonnie, both arms around her, hanging off her the way they do.

Then she came to me. She said hi Grandma, so I got the one arm. She let go first.

Same hallway. Same afternoon.

I told myself she's six, they get like that, she'd been up since five thirty.

We sat down to eat and there was a bag on the chair beside her. Somebody's tote bag with a swim towel in it.

I sat down at the other end, next to Scott.

The bag was there the Sunday after. And the one after that.

Nobody ever put it there while I was in the room. It was just already on the chair, every week.

In November I came in out of the rain and Scott took Bonnie's coat off her shoulders and hung it in the closet.

I had my arm half out of mine.

"Keep it on, Mom, we're not fussy in here."

So I kept it on. I ate my dinner in my coat. I thanked him for it.

By February the children were being sent in to say hello.

Rachel would call down the hall. They'd come stand in the kitchen doorway and say hi Grandma. Then they'd go. Then the TV would come back on.

Twelve seconds. I counted it once. I wish I hadn't.

I didn't say a word to anybody. Not to Doug. Not to my sister Peggy in Ohio. I tell Peggy everything.

What was I going to say. My daughter bought a house. My granddaughter is six years old. Nobody had been anything but nice to me.

There was one night in March I lay there and wondered whether Nell just didn't like me. Not something I'd done. Me.

I got up and made tea. I did not think it again.

So I settled on my age, because it was the only thing on the table. I'd tell myself in the car on the way home, while Doug hunted up the ballgame.

You move out of the middle of the family and over to the edge of it. That's how it goes. That's how it's supposed to go. At least I'm still here to watch it.

In April, Rachel walked me out to the car.

"We're just going to keep doing Sundays here from now on," she said. "It's so much easier for you, Mom. You've done twenty years of it."

She meant it kindly. Rachel has never once been unkind to me in her life.

"That's a good idea," I said.

And it is a good idea. I have not offered to host since.

I could not find one thing that anybody had done wrong. That's the part I couldn't put down. Not knowing what it was, that was worse than the rest of it.

That was the year.

So I stood there in the grass and asked Ruth about the house instead of the box.

"You grew up here?"

"My mother did. Then I did. Then I came back." She looked out at the tables. "I had her here the last four years. I know where every one of those spoons goes."

"That's a long four years."

"It was a good four years." She peeled a sticker off the roll and put it on the arm of a chair without looking. "Where's yours?"

"Delaware Street. Twenty minutes."

"You do Sundays?"

"Sundays are at hers now," I said. "She's got the room for it."

Ruth stopped with the roll of stickers halfway to the next chair.

"Who takes your coat?" she said.

"I'm sorry?"

"At your daughter's. You come in with a coat on. Who takes it off you."

I stood in the wet grass with my pocketbook over my arm.

"Nobody," I said. "They tell me to keep it on. They're not fussy in there."

"And you thank them for it."

"I thank them for it."

Ruth put the stickers in her cardigan pocket.

"My mother thanked them too," she said.

"How would you know a thing like that?"

"Because I stood in that kitchen four years watching people do it to her, and it took me two of them to work out what I was looking at." She glanced at the screen door. "I've said this out loud to two people in my life, and one of them doesn't speak to me now. Tell me to go price my chairs and I'll go price my chairs."

I didn't tell her that.

Doug came across the grass with an extension ladder on his shoulder. Doug can find the one conversation in the county he has no business in.

"Twelve dollars," he said. "For a ladder."

Ruth waited until he'd set it down.

"I've never met your daughter," she said. "I'll tell you the true part anyway. Nobody in your family has done a thing to you. You're sixty-some?"

"Sixty-two."

"Things change at sixty-two. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin dries out on you."

"Nobody's fault," I said. "You color it. You get the glasses."

"That's right. Your skin also starts making something it never made before. Some kind of compound. It has a smell to it. Not a nice one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

Doug was looking at the side of my face.

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong. Ordinary soap won't take it off you."

"Soap's soap," Doug said.

"All right." She turned to him. "You chop garlic. Then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

Doug didn't say anything.

"And?"

"They still smell," I said.

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed on anyway."

"Garlic leaves something behind that the soap doesn't take hold of."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same."

I stood there with that.

Twelve seconds in a doorway. A bag on a chair. Keep it on, we're not fussy.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

Ruth went up the two steps and put her hand flat on the box.

I heard myself say it before I'd worked it out.

"That's your mother's," I said. "I can't have your mother's box."

Her face changed. This was the question she'd been walking me toward from the minute she asked about my coat.

"No. You can't. That one's hers, and it stays shut."

She went in through the screen door anyway and came back with something small in tissue paper, orange showing through the fold.

"I buy three at a time. I have since the spring before she died. This one's mine."

She put it in my hand.

"It's soap," she said. "Made out of persimmon."

"Soap."

"It doesn't cover anything over. The tannins take it apart."

"What happened with your mother?"

Ruth looked out at the yard.

"Same as you. The girls stopped coming past the doorway. My brother took to dropping them off and driving away."

"Nobody said anything to her?"

"Not one word, to her or to me. I'd have taken a fight over it. Honest to God, I would have."

"And then?"

"Then I started washing her with it. That's the whole of what I did."

"You never told her why?"

"What do you say." She folded her arms. "By Christmas my brother's youngest was up on the arm of her chair with her feet in her lap. Nobody told that child to do that."

Doug had gone quiet behind me.

"That fixed it," he said. "A bar of soap."

"It didn't fix her family," Ruth said. "There was never anything the matter with her family."

Doug picked the ladder up, then he put it down again.

"She told me one thing that spring I've never got out of my head," Ruth said. "She said she'd stopped getting ready to be let go of."

"Where do you get it?"

"You order it. It's called Kaori." She wrote it on the back of a green sticker and pressed it onto my sleeve. "Get more than the one while you can. They make it up in small batches, and when a batch goes you're waiting months on the next."

Doug paid his twelve dollars. I bought my platters.

We were most of the way home before either of us said anything.

"That woman was very sure of herself," Doug said.

"She was."

He didn't turn the radio on.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward feeling like a fool, taking advice off a stranger at a yard sale. Then I ordered six of them before I went to bed.

The next Sunday, nothing. Nothing at all. I felt foolish the whole way home.

The box came the second week of September. I put it on the pantry shelf behind the flour. I showered with the Kaori before I went.

The Sunday after that I came in and Scott took my coat off my arm and hung it up. He did it the way you do something you've always done. I don't think he knew he'd done it.

The bag wasn't on the chair beside Nell. It was on the floor under the window with the rest of the bags. Nobody moved it while I was watching. It was just where bags go.

Nell got down out of her chair halfway through the meal, came around the table and leaned on me. She stayed there for the whole of the pie. She said I smelled like the orange kind.

In October Rachel called on a Tuesday to ask if I'd want to do Sunday at mine again. Nell keeps asking about the roast.

I said I'd have to look at my calendar. Then I sat in my kitchen and laughed at myself, because there is nothing on my calendar.

I never said one word to any of them. Not to Rachel. Doug and I have not talked about it once. There was nothing to say. Nobody had done anything.

Sunday is at my house again now. Not every week. Two out of the four, so I want to be careful how much I'm claiming. It's a Sunday. It isn't a happy ending.

But there's a box on my pantry shelf behind the flour. It's the one I told you about at the start. That's why the instructions exist.

I gave them to Rachel in my kitchen the week before Thanksgiving. Not the whole of it. Just that the box stays on the shelf, that she is never to sell it, never to give it away, and never to let a stranger price it.

"Mom," she said. "It's soap."

"I know what it is," I said.

I still have the green sticker. It's in my wallet behind my library card.

Two of the six went in the mail to Peggy in October. She didn't ask for them and hasn't stopped talking about it since.

Sunday's at mine this week. Rachel is bringing the pie.

Nell has already asked me which she gets on Sunday, the roast or the orange kind. I told her both.

If your family moved something and told you it was easier for you.

If nobody takes your coat any more and every one of them has a reason.

If the little one goes to somebody else first, in the same hallway, on the same afternoon.

You don't need to have it out with your daughter. You don't need anybody to finally tell you what you did.

You need one thing taken off you that nobody was ever going to name.

Get the soap. It's called Kaori. Take the shower. Go to Sunday.

They make it in small batches. When a batch goes you wait months on the next, which is why I ordered six and not one. The link's below. A bar is $19.95, six are $60. If it does nothing for you they give you your money back inside sixty days.

It's my Sunday again.

Nobody was told anything. Nobody had to be.

There's just a box on the shelf that my daughter knows better than to touch.
