body.text:
My husband said I was "getting a little stale" at 63. Then he showed up uninvited to my girls trip in Tulum. He lasted three days.

Mark and I have been married for 26 years.

We met when I was 36. He was 40. Both working in tech in Dallas.

We got married a year later. Had two kids. Emma and Jake. Both grown now. Emma's in Seattle, Jake's in Denver.

For the first nineteen years, things were good.

We traveled. We hiked. We went to concerts.

Then Mark retired early. Two years ago. Sold his company. Made enough that we're comfortable.

That's when things changed.

He started playing golf five days a week. Long lunches with the same four men. His whole life became tee times and the clubhouse.

Most of the men he plays with are on their second wives. Younger. A lot younger.

And Mark started noticing things out loud.

Never about me. Just… out loud.

"You walk past Dave's wife and the whole room smells like a hotel lobby."

He'd say it in the car on the way home. Then he'd talk about the traffic.

I told myself he was just making conversation.

Then Thanksgiving.

Ray hugged me at the door and I felt him turn his head.

Ray has been Mark's closest friend since before I met either of them. He comes every year.

Later he was in the kitchen with Mark a long while. The water running the whole time.

That night, in our bedroom, Mark said: "I asked Ray about it today."

"About what?"

"He said he'd noticed it too. That you smell different than you used to. Older, maybe."

He said it gently. Like he was handing me something helpful.

"It's not a big deal."

It's not a big deal.

Twenty-six years and he never once said a word about it to me.

One afternoon in my own kitchen, and by ten o'clock he had.

A few weeks later, at the neighbors' barbecue, I sat down next to him on the wicker couch.

After a minute he stood up. "Going to get another beer."

He came back. He didn't sit down again.

By January he was stopping in the doorway of our bedroom.

Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold.

"Becca, you've gotten a little… stale. I don't know how else to put it. Maybe look into something. For yourself."

For yourself.

He smiled like it was a joke. Like he was being thoughtful.

I didn't laugh.

In February I got a text from four women I went to the University of Texas with. We'd stayed close for over thirty years.

"Girls trip. Tulum. Five days. March. Who's in?"

I said yes before I put the phone down.

When I told Mark over dinner, he put down his fork.

"Five days? In Mexico?"

"Yes."

"Becca, you sure that's a good idea?"

"Why wouldn't it be?"

He looked at me carefully. "Just… five days in close quarters with four other women. Heat. Sun all day. I'm just thinking about you."

I'm just thinking about you.

"I'm going."

"Of course. Just pack accordingly. Bring whatever you usually use. Maybe more of it."

I left the table before I said something I'd regret.

I didn't pack for a month. Every time I thought about the suitcase I heard him say bring more of it.

Two days before the flight I drove over to Carol's.

Carol's sixty-nine. Twenty-eight years on a geriatric ward before she retired. She lives ten minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her about the doorway. About the wicker couch. About getting a little stale.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon-orange. Characters on the front I couldn't read.

She didn't say a word about it.

"He's right that there's something," she said. "He's a liar about what it is. Those two aren't the same."

"I shower every day."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"Twenty-eight years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes, your eyes go, your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my ward home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. Order more while you can. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone. Once a batch sells out you're waiting months."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That night I finally packed. Mark came into the bedroom. Stopped at the threshold like always.

"That's all you're bringing?"

"That's all I need."

"You sure? You should bring extra stuff. For the heat. You know how you get."

I zipped the bag.

"I'm sure."

The morning of the flight I called an Uber. Mark was making coffee.

"You sure you don't want me to drive you?"

"I'm fine."

"Alright. Have fun. Try not to overdo it."

I left.

The Uber dropped me at the terminal.

I walked in.

And I saw him.

Mark.

Standing at the check-in counter. With two suitcases.

He turned and saw me.

"Surprise," he said.

I just stared.

"What are you doing here?"

"I couldn't stop thinking about it. You going all that way alone. I got worried."

"Mark. I'm going with my friends."

"I know. But still. I just want to make sure you're okay. I booked the same flight. I'll stay at a different resort. Do my own thing. Just be nearby in case."

He said it like he was doing me a favor.

"You booked the same flight without telling me."

"I wanted it to be a surprise."

The agent behind the counter was watching us.

Both his bags came out overweight. $75 each. He paid $150 in fees while I walked to the next counter.

"Just the one bag?"

"Just the one."

At security, Mark got pulled aside. Shoes. Belt. Watch.

I went through and walked to the gate.

We landed in Tulum. I met my friends at the rideshare pickup.

"Is he really here?"

"He's really here."

"What is he thinking?"

"He thinks I need supervision."

I checked into the resort. Unpacked in five minutes. Showered with the bar.

When I came out into the suite my college roommate Maya was sitting on the bed.

She tilted her head slightly.

"You smell incredible. What is that?"

"Soap."

"From where?"

"A friend gave it to me."

She kept her eyes on me a second too long. Then she smiled. "Send me the link when you get home."

I changed into my swimsuit and met my friends at the pool.

An hour later, Mark showed up. At our resort.

Sunburned already. Forgot sunscreen. Same shirt from the plane.

"There you are," he said. "I checked into my place down the road. Just wanted to make sure you got here okay."

My friends stared.

"I'm fine, Mark."

He stood there. Awkward.

That night my friends and I went to dinner. Mark texted: "Where are you guys eating?" I didn't answer it.

Day two. Mark at our pool again. Still sunburned. Wearing a gift-shop T-shirt that said "Tulum."

"One of my bags is still missing."

We went out snorkeling. Mark didn't come. "Too tired."

Day three. Lunch at the beachside restaurant.

A woman in her thirties went past our table. Stopped. Came back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "You smell incredible. Can I ask what you're wearing?"

She laughed at herself.

"Sorry. I've interrupted your lunch. It just stood out to me."

"It's a bar of soap."

"What's it called?"

"Kaori."

She typed it into her phone. "I'm going to find this. Thank you."

She walked away.

Nobody at our table said anything for a moment.

Then Maya: "Becca. That happened yesterday too."

"What?"

"At the front desk. The girl checking us in. She kept leaning in slightly while you were talking to her. I noticed. I just didn't say anything."

Mark was at the next table over. He'd watched the woman come over. He'd heard all of it.

He looked at his lunch and didn't look up.

I sat there a moment. Watched him not looking up.

And I thought about Ray at Thanksgiving. About the hug at the door and his head turning.

About my husband walking into the kitchen to ask his oldest friend whether his wife had started to smell old.

Neither of them ever said it to me. They said it to each other.

I think I understood now.

Day four I posted photos from the snorkeling trip.

Me and my friends. Tan. Smiling. Looking healthy.

Within an hour the comments came in.

My sister: "You look AMAZING."

Emma: "Mom!! This is so cool!"

Then Mark's phone started buzzing. He was at the pool near us.

I could see his face changing as he read.

Dave: "Bro, Becca looks incredible. What are you doing at home?"

Tom: "Your wife's living her best life."

Steve: "Dude. When did Becca get so fresh?"

Mark put the phone down. Looked at me.

"You were right," he said quietly.

"About what?"

"About this trip. About me being wrong."

My friends were pretending not to listen.

"I think I should head home," he said. "Let you finish this with your friends. I'm sorry."

He left that afternoon.

We spent the last two days on the beach. No interruptions. Nobody hovering.

When I got home he was sitting in the living room with the lamp on.

"I don't want us to keep going the way we've been going," he said.

"Neither do I."

"I watched you walk into that lobby in Tulum," he said. "And you looked like you'd outgrown me. That's what scared me. So I made you smaller instead of getting bigger."

"You did."

"I know. I don't want to be that."

We talked until two in the morning. Actually talked, which we hadn't done in about three years.

Carol called last week to ask about the trip.

I told her all of it. The airport. The woman at the restaurant. What Mark did when I got home.

She laughed for a long time.

Then: "They opened a new batch. It's already most of the way gone. Once it's out you're waiting until next year."

I ordered two that night.

Here's the part I keep coming back to.

I didn't win an argument. I didn't say one clever thing to him. I never once told him he was wrong.

I bought a bar of soap. I stood up for myself.

That was the whole of it.

And you've already done the hardest part. You've spent a year noticing something was wrong and being told it was nothing.

All that's left is the shower.

It's called Kaori. The link's below. It costs less than fifty cents a day.

They make it in small batches. When a batch goes you wait months for the next one.

Order the bar. Take the shower. Let them come to you.

If somebody you love has been quietly stepping back from you and you can't figure out why.

Maybe you don't need to win an argument.

Maybe you just need a better bar.

body.text:
I bought the persimmon soap the internet keeps telling women my age to buy.
I used it every day for 3 weeks, morning and night, the whole bar.
My husband is still sleeping in the spare room.

I am 61. Ron and I have been married 34 years. He retired last September after 38 years at the county.

He was still in our room at Christmas. I want to be accurate about that, because I have gone over the order of it more times than I can tell you.

This is what happened in between, and what it cost me to find out.

By January he had stopped coming into our bedroom.

He would stand in the doorway with his coffee and tell me about the gutters from there. Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold like a man delivering something.

In March he moved his pillow into the spare room. He said it was his back, and that the mattress in there was firmer, and that he was sorry, and he was sorry the way you are sorry when you have already decided.

I bought him a mattress topper in April. The expensive one, the one the man in the store said was for people with backs.

In June I went in there for the window fan and I found it behind the door. Still in the plastic. The tape had not been broken.

I stood there holding a mattress topper for a long time.

He had not been sleeping badly. He had been sleeping somewhere else, and he had found a reason for it that I could not argue with, because you cannot argue with a man's back.

Kate is our daughter. She is 33 and she is 40 minutes away, and she is the kind of daughter who calls on the drive home.

She had been putting the window down in my car since about February. Two inches. Then she would say something about the heat, in February, in Ohio.

In May she drove us both to my sister's and she had the air on the whole way with the windows cracked, and when I asked her she said she gets carsick if it is stuffy. She has never been carsick in her life.

In April, at my own table, she suggested we eat out on the porch. It was 48 degrees. We ate out on the porch, all of us, in coats, and everybody said what a lovely idea.

I want to be fair to them. Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not once. Not one word.

They just kept finding reasons, and the reasons were all good ones, and there were a lot of them.

The night I found the topper I sat up until 2 in the morning with my phone, typing things into it I would not have said out loud in an empty house.

I will not write out what I typed. Any woman my age who has done it knows what I typed.

I found women saying the same 3 words to each other on a page I will not name. Persimmon soap. That was all of it. Nobody said why it was persimmon and I did not care why.

I ordered a persimmon soap that night. 9 dollars, an orange bar, persimmons all over the box, a bit of Japanese on the front. It came on the Thursday.

I used it every day for 3 weeks.

I want to tell you exactly how careful I was, because I need you to understand what it did to me when nothing happened. Every morning. Every night. The whole bar.

Ron stayed in the spare room.

Kate put the window down in July.

And I stopped, because there is only one thing left to think when the answer does not work. It is not the answer that is wrong. It is you. And you are not fixable.

I put the wrapper in the bin and I did not tell one living person I had bought it.

In August I went into the pharmacy on Harrison for Ron's back. That is the part I still cannot get over. I was in there buying a heat patch for the back he does not have a problem with.

Maggie has been behind that counter 17 years. She did my mother's blister packs for the last 2 years of her life and she never once made me feel like I was asking too much.

She rang up the heat patches and she said, "How is he doing?"

And I said, "He's fine," and then I stood there and did not move away from the counter.

There was nobody behind me. She waited.

"Maggie, can I ask you something that isn't about him."

She put the patches in the bag and left the bag on the counter.

"Is there something about me. A smell. I have thought about it every day since March and I cannot ask anybody in my own house."

She did not look surprised, which was the first kind thing that happened to me all year.

"There's something," she said. "You're not imagining it. But it isn't what you think it is."

"I shower every day. I have showered every day of my life."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"I've stood here 17 years. Things change for women our age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She leaned on the counter.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"That can't be right."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I put my hand on the counter.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

"Persimmon. The tannins take it apart. It doesn't cover it."

And I heard myself say it out loud in a pharmacy at 20 past 4 in the afternoon.

"I bought that. I bought a persimmon soap in June. I used it for 3 weeks and nothing happened, so I stopped."

She did not say anything for a second.

Then she said, "Have you still got the box?"

I said it was in the bin in June.

"Then buy another one and bring me the box before you use it. Any of them. Whichever one you like the look of."

I did. I brought it in the following Tuesday in my purse.

She turned it over on the counter and put her finger on the list on the back and read it to me out loud, the way she reads a label to somebody's mother.

Water. Palm oil. Glycerin. Fragrance. A color, with a number on it.

She got to the bottom of the list and stopped.

"Now find me the persimmon."

It was on the front of the box 4 times. It was in the name of the product. There was a photograph of one on it.

It was not in the list at all.

"That's what you bought in June," she said. "You didn't try persimmon soap. You tried an orange soap that had been told to look like one."

I stood in that pharmacy and my eyes went, which I had not done in front of anybody all year, including in the spare room doorway in March.

"So it was never me."

"It was never you. And it wasn't even your judgment. It was one line on a label that nobody has ever told you to read."

She reached under the counter for her handbag, which is a thing I had never seen her do, and she took out a small parcel wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon orange. Characters on the front I could not read.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"I can't take yours."

"I buy 3 at a time. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone, so I've learned."

"Does it work?"

"I've used it 6 years. One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped standing a bit back from people. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. I can't sell it to you. That is more or less the point of it."

I used it that night. It is a bar of soap. I did not expect anything, because I had already been here in June.

The first week I could not tell.

The second week Kate drove me to my sister's again and we had the windows up the whole way and she talked about her job the entire time and I do not think she noticed she was doing it.

At the end of August, Ron came into our bedroom to get a book off his own shelf, which he had been doing from the doorway since January.

He came in. He sat on the end of the bed while he found his place in it. He stayed about 20 minutes.

He did not say anything and neither did I. I have learned something about what does not get said in that house.

In September a woman waiting for her prescription behind me at Maggie's counter said, "I'm sorry, what is that? It's citrus. It's lovely."

I said it was a bar of soap.

Maggie did not look up from her computer. She said, "Isn't it."

Ron came back into our room on the 4th of October. He carried his own pillow in and put it down and said, "I've been sleeping badly in there."

I said, "Have you."

That is as close as either of us is going to get, and after 34 years I find I do not need the rest of it.

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

I was right in June. I had the right idea in the middle of the night on my own phone, and I paid 9 dollars for it, and it did nothing, and I decided that meant there was something wrong with me that could not be fixed.

It was the bar. It was only ever the bar.

Maggie texted me last week. Kaori is back on the website. She has ordered 3, because that is what she does.

Kate is driving us both to my sister's for her birthday on the 2nd.

She has already asked if I am bringing the good pie. I told her yes.

If your husband has found a reason he can live with and moved down the hall.

If somebody has started opening a window in your car and telling you it is the heat.

If you have already tried the thing that was supposed to work, and stopped, and quietly decided the problem is you.

You do not need to be fixed.

You need to find out what you actually bought.

Get the soap. Take the shower. Turn the box over first.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

It was never me.

It was never going to be me.

Your move.

body.text:
My husband divorced me for a pregnant 37-year-old.
Then I heard my daughter say "she has her dog."
I wish somebody had told me how to get out of a kitchen like that.

Rick and I were married 32 years.

I kept the books for a dentist on Water Street. He sold farm equipment, so he was gone Tuesday to Thursday.

Thursday nights were the good ones. We ate late. We had the same 6 people over for New Year's, 20 years running.

People assume you miss the big things.

What I miss is having somebody to tell a small thing to. The dentist's wife had her hip done. A raccoon got in the Nolans' trash. Nothing you would pick up a phone for.

He went the February before last. The house sold in the spring, so I bought the little brick one on Fairmount with my half.

I got Sadie that summer because the house was too quiet to sit in.

The first time the whole family was in one room after all of it was Nora's birthday in May.

I got there at 3 to do the potatoes.

Meg had 14 people. Tom's parents. 2 women from her street.

I stayed at the counter with the peeler. There is a lot to do for 14.

We sat down at 6. I was between Nora and the end of the table.

It went along nicely a while. Then one of the women from Meg's street turned to me. Sharon. Her boy is in Nora's class.

She was being kind. She meant nothing by it.

"So are you seeing anyone yet?"

I had my fork halfway up.

15 months I had had to think of an answer to that question. A year and a half on my own in a small house with nothing but time, and I never once worked out what I was going to say.

Meg got there before I did.

"Mom. Do you want more potatoes."

She said it too loud, so it went across 2 people. Every single person at that table heard exactly what she was doing.

Then Nora looked up at me with her fork.

"Who are you seeing?"

She is 6. She had caught a word, so she wanted the rest of it.

Nobody answered her. Somebody laughed at something down the other end.

"Nobody, sweetheart," I said.

That was the first time I ever said that word out loud about myself.

I said yes to potatoes I did not want. I put them on my plate. I ate them.

Later I leaned in to ask Sharon about her boy. She leaned back the same amount I leaned in.

It was nothing. People do that.

When the cake came out Nora got down off her chair, went round the whole table, and climbed up on Tom's mother to watch it.

I have had that child asleep on me since the day she was born.

Then I got up and started clearing. There were plates.

Clearing is a thing you can do with your hands while your face does whatever it is doing.

I was at the sink with the water going when Sharon started up again in the dining room. She was apologising to Meg.

"I did not mean to put her on the spot."

"No, God, don't." Meg's voice went down the way it goes down when a person thinks you cannot hear them. "She is doing okay. She really is."

I turned the water off so I could hear it.

"She has her dog."

Then I turned the water straight back on so nobody would know I had ever turned it off.

15 months. That was the first time I ever heard my own daughter explain me to somebody.

There is no walking out of a kitchen like that. Not without going back in there and letting her know I had heard it.

So I stayed at that sink. I dried her plates. I put them away in cupboards that were not mine.

There is a sentence you say to yourself at a moment like that, and mine was that she is tired, she has had 14 people, she did not mean it the way it sounded.

I have used that sentence a lot since February. It has never once been true.

I did not come out until my face was doing the right thing.

Not one word of it was cruel. That is the part I could not put down.

I drove home and sat in my own driveway a while with the engine off.

She has her dog.

I am 61 years old. I know what I look like.

Rick did not leave for a mystery. He left for a woman of 37 who was 5 months pregnant when he told me. She had the baby that July.

So there it was. Rick had traded me for a woman of 37, and my own daughter had explained me to a room with a dog.

After that I stopped looking for a more complicated answer.

People know what to do with a woman of 61 whose husband has gone. Apparently so did I.

Once you have decided a thing like that, you stop deciding anything else. You just start checking.

There was a flyer at the library for a Thursday morning class at the Y, so I signed up. My first one was the 15th of May.

9 of us in the same water. 45 minutes, 8 o'clock.

They go for coffee after, at the place across the lot. I had been watching them through that glass from my car since May.

I bought a coral blouse at the outlet that June because the woman working there said the color was good on me.

The 24th of July was the 11th one.

That morning, in the water, I decided I was going to say something to them. I had it worked out by the last lap.

I might go and get a coffee myself.

That was the whole sentence. I said it the length of that pool and back.

We got out at ten to 9.

"Are you coming, Pat?"

"Two minutes."

I did the buttons on that blouse twice because I got them wrong the first time.

They went out the door in twos.

Then I did not go to my car.

I walked across that lot behind them, the way you walk behind people you are not with.

They took the big table in the window, the same one every week.

I got in the line. There were 2 people ahead of me, so I let them both go in front of me.

Then I stood at that counter with my purse in both hands for 4 minutes. 6 feet from that table.

You hear a lot in 4 minutes. Somebody's grandson had got into the college he wanted. Somebody else was having a knee done in September and was not looking forward to it.

I knew the knee. I had been in the water next to that knee since May.

I never said my sentence. There was never anywhere to put it.

I never ordered a coffee either.

Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not one of them, not one time.

That was almost the worse part. If Pat had been rude to me I could have disliked Pat.

She held the door. She smiled. Then she went back to that table.

So I did the arithmetic I had been doing since February.

Nobody had anything against me. They just did not particularly want me there.

Bev called me on a Tuesday evening at the end of July. I had one chop under the broiler.

Bev is one of the 6 who used to come to us for New Year's. In 20 years not one of us ever needed inviting. We simply knew who was coming.

This time she asked me which day I thought I might drive up.

There was nothing wrong with the question. That was the trouble. By then I could make a meaning out of anything.

I heard myself tell her I already had something that weekend.

I did not have anything that weekend. I had 3 days and a dog.

But if I stayed home, then nobody at that lake had to look relieved when I left.

After that I quit. Not all at once. You do not catch yourself quitting.

I never went back to that class after the 24th. Meg asked me about a Sunday twice, so I told her I was busy twice. After the second one she stopped asking.

My sister Joyce called every Sunday, the way she always has. I told her I was fine, honestly.

Joyce did 40 years at the county hospital. 22 of them on a geriatric floor.

She let me say it.

By the end of August I had taken myself out of every single thing a woman can take herself out of.

The one thing I could not get out of was my dog. Sadie goes out at 7 whether you are fine or not.

So the only people I saw all that summer were the ones on those 4 blocks. And that is where it stopped adding up.

Diane comes out of the yellow house at the same time with her beagle. We have walked the same 4 blocks together since last spring.

The Tuesday after Labor Day. Fairmount down to 9th. Carl was out with his hose at the end of his drive, so he turned it off.

He turned the water off to talk to Diane about the storm. He said good morning to me over her shoulder.

9th along to Bell. The girl who runs the coffee place came out onto the sidewalk in her apron with a cup in her hand. For Diane.

I told her it was going to be a warm one. I said it to be in it.

She said it certainly was, without turning round, the way you do when somebody behind you says a nice thing.

By then I had got very good at noticing who people move toward.

Diane is 62. Her husband left too, 4 years back, for a woman from his office. She lives 2 doors from me in a house bought out of the same kind of settlement.

She is not younger than me. She is not prettier. She is not happier either, and I know that because I watched her cry on the corner of Fairmount and 9th in March and walked her home.

And they still step toward her.

I had been carrying the question for 3 weeks by then. It is not a thing one woman asks another woman. You are asking her to say out loud that she has got something you have not got.

So at the light on 9th, on the way back, I asked her anyway.

"Diane. What is it that you do."

"What do you mean."

"People stop for you. They do not stop for me. We are the same woman."

She did not laugh at me. I was ready for her to laugh at me.

"I do not do anything."

"You must."

"Ruth. I put my pants on and I walk the dog."

"People come toward you."

She looked at me then, and she was working on it same as I was.

"Maybe you are watching them too hard."

"What does that mean."

"I do not know. Maybe nothing."

Then the beagle got into the Nolans' hedge, so we walked the rest of it about their roof.

I went home and put the kettle on and did not make anything with it.

Maybe you are watching them too hard.

I sat at my own table and went back through the whole spring. Sharon leaning back the same amount I leaned in. 11 Thursdays. 4 minutes at that counter with my purse in both hands.

Bev on the phone, and me saying I had something on. That one was mine. I did that one to myself.

But I did not make Sharon lean back.

I had been calling all of it being 61.

And 2 doors down there is a woman who is 62 and does not have to call it anything.

Joyce came that Saturday with a chicken, because she has decided I do not eat.

It was the first cool day we had had. The sun gets into my kitchen after 2, so it was all over the counter while we worked.

I was at the stove. She came in behind me for the salt.

She reached past me and stopped.

Not stopped exactly. She changed the angle of herself.

I had spent a whole summer watching people do that. I know that movement better than I know my own signature.

"You moved."

"I was getting the salt."

"No."

She had the salt in her hand and she did not set it down.

"Sharon did that at Nora's birthday," I said. "Pat at the Y as well. Not the same. Something like it."

"Ruthie."

"Do not Ruthie me. What is it."

All summer I watched strangers step back off me and I never once asked one of them why. It took my own sister at my own stove.

Joyce put the salt down. Then she sat, which she never does with something in the oven.

She had her bag on the chair beside her, the one she has carried since 1987. She took something out of it and set it on the table between us.

Small. Wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She did not say one word about it.

"Do you want the nurse answer or the sister answer."

"I want whichever one nobody has given me."

"Then here it is. There is something." She turned her cup around on the table. "You have been right about that since February."

"I shower twice a day."

"I know you do."

"Then what."

"Things change on a woman past a certain age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go."

"Everybody knows that."

"Your skin also starts making something it never made before."

"What does it do."

"It has got a smell to it."

I sat there with that.

"I have never heard of that in my life."

"Nobody has. People do not talk about it."

"Joyce. He left me for a woman who was 5 months pregnant."

"I know it."

"So it was not that."

"I am not telling you why your husband went. I am telling you why a room does what a room does."

"Then what are you telling me."

"That you noticed something real. And then Rick taught you to explain it in the cruelest way there is."

I had to put my cup down.

"Then I will wash more."

"That is the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap does not take it off."

"Now you are being silly."

"Chop garlic tonight. Then wash your hands twice with your good soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"Garlic."

"Garlic. Your hands are clean and it stayed on you anyway. Soap has got nothing to take hold of."

Then she said the name of it, once. Nonenal. She said it the way people say a word they have heard a hundred times but never once had to write down.

I was doing arithmetic again, only this time it came out the other way.

Nora, who is 6 and climbs on everybody, going round a whole table on her own birthday to get up on somebody else.

And Meg. Meg in that hallway, saying the kindest sentence she could think of, with her voice down.

"22 years on that floor. And you stood at my stove and moved away from me."

"I did."

"And you never said it to me."

"No." She looked at the table. "I have got a list of women I never said it to, and my own sister is on it. There is no way to say it to somebody you love that does not come out of your mouth as an accusation. So none of us says it. And every one of us thinks we are being kind."

That is when I understood what my daughter had been being.

And the other thing, which took me until that night.

I had not imagined one bit of it. Every last thing I had counted up since February had actually happened.

I had just found the cruelest possible reason for it, and then I had gone and made the reason into who I am.

"So what takes it off."

She pushed the little parcel across the table at me.

"I have been sat here 20 minutes waiting on you to ask me for it."

I got the tissue paper off it.

"It is soap."

"Persimmon. It does not cover it up. It takes it apart."

I turned it over in my hand. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

I have smelled that before. I have smelled it 4 mornings a week since last spring, on a sidewalk, on a woman standing closer to me than anybody had stood in a year and a half.

"Diane," I said.

"I would think so." Joyce did not look up from her cup. "And she will not know why either."

"And it works."

"I sent women home off that floor with one for 15 years. I have used it myself since I was 58."

She wrote it on the back of my grocery list. Kaori.

"Order 2 while they have got them. They do it in small batches, so once a batch goes you are waiting on next year's harvest."

At the door she got her coat on and said the part I have thought about every day since.

"You did not let yourself go, Ruthie. You changed your face cream at 50 and never thought twice about it. You are still washing with what you used at 30. That is the whole of it."

It is a bar of soap. That is all it is. I am 61 years old, so I expected nothing at all from a bar of soap.

What I did that night was go round my own house and think about every person who has stood in it since February. The man who read the meter. The girl who brings the pharmacy order. The fellow who came about the gutters and talked to me from the step the whole time.

You cannot do that for long. I made myself quit and I ran the bath.

I used it because it was sitting there on the edge of the tub.

The next morning I caught the Kaori on my arm at the sink. It was still there at supper.

Thursday I went past the hall mirror, and then I stopped and went back and stood in front of it.

Not for any reason. Just standing there. Taller, somehow.

I had not looked at myself on purpose since February.

On the Friday I stood in the line at the Kroger right up behind the woman in front of me, the way a person stands in a line. I did not work out first where to put myself.

I have no idea how long I had been doing that.

Nora came for the weekend in October, the way she does when Meg and Tom go to somebody's wedding.

Saturday she fell asleep against me on the couch through the back half of a movie.

She is 6, so she has opinions on everything.

"You smell like the good store," she said.

I asked her which good store.

She said she did not know the name of it. Then she went to sleep on my arm.

I sat there with a dead arm through the end of that movie and most of the news after it.

I was not going to be the one who moved.

The second Thursday in October I went back to the 8 o'clock class. I had not been in that water since July.

I do not know what I thought was going to happen.

In the same changing room, at the same locker, Pat came round the end of the row with her towel.

"What is that," she said. "That is lovely."

"It is soap," I said. "Persimmon."

She shut her eyes for a second, which is a peculiar thing to watch a woman do in a changing room.

"My grandmother's back porch," she said. "In the summer. She has been gone since I was 19."

Then she picked her bag up.

"We are going over for coffee. Come."

In July I stood 6 feet from that table for 4 minutes waiting for somebody to make room for me.

This time Pat said come. So I did not ask her whether she meant it.

Meg had a Sunday at the end of October. Sharon was there.

She asked me how the swimming was.

I looked at Meg. She was cutting bread, so she did not look up.

She did not say one word about potatoes.

So I answered it myself.

I stayed until 9. I did not touch one plate.

At the door Meg held on to my arm a second longer than she needed to. I did not step back off her.

"You seem like yourself," she said.

That was 6 weeks ago.

I go Tuesdays and Thursdays now. Pat and I have got our own end of that table.

Bev called about New Year's and I got in first. 6 people. 20 years. My house.

Nora is coming to me for the whole week at Christmas, and Meg is the one who asked.

Somebody will ask me again whether I am seeing anyone. They always do.

I know what I am going to say this time. No.

Just the no. Nothing hung on the end of it.

Joyce texted me Thursday. Kaori is back on the website. Diane ordered 2. Pat from the pool ordered one.

Meg does a Sunday every other week now. The next one is this Sunday.

Nora has already asked if I will still smell like the good store at Christmas. I told her yes.

If everybody has been kind to you since the day your husband left.

If somebody in your family has ever explained you to a stranger while you were standing right there.

If you have started telling people you already have something on.

You do not need a man to want you.

You need to be underestimated one more time. So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the soap. Put the blouse on. Go on the Thursday.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

Every one of them was being kind to me.

Not one of them was right.

Your move.

body.text:
I was renewing my license and the woman behind the counter held my old photo up next to my face and told me she couldn't take it. She said the woman in that picture is fifty-five and you're not.

I told her I am fifty-five. She said look at the lines around the mouth in this photo, they're not on your face. I said that's because I fixed them.

It got loud enough that an officer walked over. She looked at the photo, looked at me, and told the other woman it's her, look at the eyes. Then she asked me what I'd done. Surgery. B0t0x. Fillers. A laser. No, no, no, no. So she asked if it was a cream. The La M3r? The Estée Iauder everybody buys at the mall?

I told her I've owned all of it. Twenty-three products. I counted them once and then stopped, because counting them was making me feel insane. Not one of them did a thing.

Then I put a plain white tube on the counter and said that one. She said that's just foundation. And that's the whole trick, because it was never my skin. It was every foundation I ever put on it. Every one of them is one fixed color, mixed in a factory for somebody else's face, so it can't really match you. It just sits on top, turns orange by noon, and sinks into every line you've got. For nine years I was painting myself older every morning and calling it my age.

She didn't believe me, so I swiped it down one side of her face right there. She looked in the little mirror on the counter and went quiet. One side glowing. The other side exactly how she walked in.

Then she turned around and told them to stamp my paper.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.

Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.

My name is Dr. Margaret Ellis. I'm a geriatrician and I've been doing this for 22 years

I want to be clear about something before I say anything else. I don't recommend products. My patients will tell you that. When I finally do tell someone to buy something, it's because I've watched it work, over and over, for years.

Which is why what happened last year bothered me so much. But let me start from the beginning.

I did part of my training at a geriatric hospital in Japan.

Part of the reason why I went to Japan was to find out why they live so long.

What I found was, a big part of that is that they are extremely comfortable and confident with aging, you would love to see how most of them go so confidently into their 90's

And this isn't just a feeling. There's real research behind this.

How you feel about aging changes how you age.

In the most famous study, people with a positive view of getting older outlived the people who feared it by around seven and a half years.

Which is exactly why the next thing I learned in Japan stuck with me. Because there is one thing that can quietly take all that confidence away

That's where I first heard a word we don't have in English.

Kareishu.

Aging odor.

In Japan, nobody pretends it isn't real, it's common sense there, the way gray hair is common sense.

Everyone knows that around sixty, your skin starts making a compound called 2-nonenal. Everyone knows what it smells like. And everyone knows what to do about it.

Because they've been dealing with it for centuries.

The answer there has always been the same.

A soap made from fermented persimmon. They call it kakishibu.

Unripe persimmons, pressed, then left to ferment for months, until they're full of tannins.

And tannins are one of the only things that actually grab onto nonenal

At the hospital, nurses handed those bars to patients the way we hand out blood pressure pamphlets.

Then I finished my training, came home, and learned something strange. Here, none of this existed.

No word for it. No pamphlet. In 20 years of practice, not one patient has ever brought it up with me first.

But I would watch what it did every single week.

One of my patients taught second grade for 41 years. Then one September the school gave her class to a teacher half her age and called it restructuring.

It took her months to get the real reason out of her principal. Parents had complained about a smell.

Patients noticing their grandson's hugs getting shorter.

Family becoming more and more distant.

So I did the only thing I could.

Quietly, in my office, I started telling people about persimmon soap. I've been doing it since the year I opened my practice.

Back then my patients had to order it from tiny importers and wait weeks for it. But it worked, over and over, right in front of me.

For twenty years it was the one product I broke my own rule for.

Then, about a year ago, everything changed. Persimmon soap was suddenly everywhere.

Suddenly, patients were asking me about it.

People walked into my office holding their phones, showing me ads.

After twenty years of explaining kakishibu from scratch, I didn't have to convince anyone anymore.

You have to understand what that means in my office. Telling a patient about aging odor is the most delicate conversation I have.

I am telling someone they carry a smell they cannot smell.

So when patients started bringing it up themselves, it honestly felt like a relief.

Last year alone, sixty-one of my patients bought a bar on my recommendation. I know the exact number, because I keep track of everything I recommend.

Then the calls started.

"Be honest with me, doctor. Was this supposed to do anything at all?"

By the end of the year, nineteen of those sixty-one patients had left my clinic. A few told my receptionist why. Most just stopped booking.

One woman had been with me for eleven years. On her way out she said she didn't need "this old people smell nonsense." Eleven years, gone.

And I had no answer.

Same soap, as far as I knew. Same instructions I'd given for two decades. It had never failed like this.

So I did something I've never done in my career. I started calling the ones who would still take my call, and I asked them to bring me what they had bought.

The first bar arrived on a Monday morning. A patient named Ruth set it on my desk, still in its box.

And the moment I put my eyes on that bar I knew something was wrong.

That bar was bright orange, looked like a block of cheddar

The Kakishibu I knew from Japan was nothing like that.

So I did the test the nurses in Japan taught me.

I carried her bar to my office window and held it up against the light. The light hit it and stopped. Nothing came through.

Real kakishibu is translucent. Hold it to a window and the light passes straight through it, and it glows amber, like honey held up to a lamp.

The next day I brought my own bar from home and held them side by side at the same window and sent her a photo.

Mine glowed. Hers might as well have been a brick.

Two more patients brought theirs in that week. Different brands, different boxes.

Same brick.

Not one of them had ever touched the thing I was recommending.

Here's what they'd actually bought. Juice soap. Ripe persimmons pressed for juice, stirred into an ordinary soap base, dyed orange.

And juice has none of the tannins.

The tannins come from fermenting the unripe fruit for months. Skip the fermentation and you have a bar that smells nice, looks the part, and does absolutely nothing about nonenal.

That glow isn't a color anyone can add. It's the material itself. Which is why no dyed bar can fake it.

My patients had been washing with orange dye for months. And here is the part that made me genuinely angry. It's completely legal.

Juice, dye, a persimmon on the label, and the box gets to say persimmon soap.

Nineteen people trusted me, scrubbed every day with colored soap base, smelled exactly the same, and decided I was a fool. And honestly, they were half right.

Because I'd been saying "persimmon soap" for twenty years, when I should have been telling them exactly what to look for.

So I started doing the research I should have done a year earlier.

Out of everything sold online, there were only two brands that looked like they produced real kakishibu.

One of them is the famous one, The girl that owns it has been on shark tank.

It looked like something I could actually trust, but I'd already lost nineteen patients to a label. I wasn't going to risk a twentieth.

So I dug deeper.

On that Shark Tank episode, the founder said each bar costs about a 1.85$ to make.

AND they sell it on a subscription, every month, all year round. And it has never, as far as I can tell, been out of stock.

Not once.

Now remember what kakishibu is. Persimmons ripen once a year. The unripe fruit gets pressed and then ferments for months. There is only ever as much real kakishibu as the last harvest gave.

A dollar eighty-five, unlimited supply, forever, from a once-a-year fruit. I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I'm telling you I cannot make that math work.

That was enough for me to keep looking.

So I ordered a bar from the other brand, shipped to my clinic. This time I was going to test it myself before it went anywhere near a patient.

The bar arrived two days later, from a small brand called Kakiyu.

I took it straight to the same window where Ruth's orange bar had failed, and held it up.

The light went straight through it. That deep amber glow, exactly like the bars the nurses handed out in Japan.

My receptionist asked me why I was smiling at a bar of soap.

It looked like a scene coming out of a Indiana Jones movie

Then I took it home and used it for two weeks, because a glow isn't a result.

It was the first bar I'd held in a year where everything matched: the color, the light, the one-harvest story, even the fact that it kept selling out while I was researching it.

And it held up.

So I went back to their site and ordered nineteen more.

All nineteen bars went out the same week, to their homes, each with a handwritten note.

I kept the note short. The soap was real. The bar you bought was not. Hold this one up to a window and you'll see the difference for yourself. Then call me.

The first call came nine days later.

It was Ruth. She didn't say hello. She said, "My daughter hugged me goodbye yesterday, and she didn't rush it."

Then she went quiet, and we stayed on the phone like that for a moment, and I didn't mind one bit.

Within two weeks, my front desk had heard from fourteen of the nineteen.

One man told me his wife had started sitting on his side of the couch again.

Another patient said her grandkids stayed the whole sunday afternoon, and nobody found a reason to leave early.

Here's the thing about this problem.

Nobody ever announces the change, in either direction. Nothing gets said when people drift away, and nothing gets said when they drift back. They just lean in again.

But you can see it. My patients walk into my waiting room differently now. Straighter. They linger at the front desk to chat.

That confidence I saw everywhere in Japan, the one the research says is worth seven and a half years, I watch it come back one appointment at a time.

I now tell every patient the same thing.

If you're going to try persimmon soap, you have exactly one job. Make sure it's real kakishibu. Hold the bar up to a window.

If the light passes through and it glows amber, it's real. If the light stops, you're holding dye.

Kakiyu is the only bar I've found that passes every test I know how to run. I don't get a cent for saying that, and they have no idea I'm writing this

There's a sixty day guarantee, so the test costs you nothing. Use it for two months. If nobody around you moves closer, send it back. I only wish the nineteen orange bars had come with those terms.

So this is me, asking you the same thing I asked at the start. Please don't buy persimmon soap. Buy the real thing once, or don't buy anything at all.

Twenty-two years, and this is the first time I've ever written something like this about a product. But I watched nineteen people spend months getting quietly written off by the people they love, over a bar of dyed soap.

If this reaches even one person before they buy another orange bar, it was worth writing.

PS. A few people asked me to put the link here. I didn't include one when I first wrote this, I was writing a warning, not an advertisement. But you're right that it saves you searching, so here it is: https://kakiyucare.com/products/kakiyu-persimmon-soap

PPS. Since posting this, I've had people tell me they went looking for Kakiyu on Amazon. Please don't. Kakiyu doesn't sell there, and what comes up when you search the name is exactly the orange soap this whole letter is about. The real bar exists in one place, their official website. Use the link above and nowhere else.

body.text:
We sold the house. Bought a ranch three streets from our son. And for a year, my husband walked over to Saturday breakfast without me.

I stayed home and made coffee for one.

I'm 64. Dennis is 66.

Forty years of working. Forty years of saving. Forty years of saying that when we retired we'd go wherever the grandchildren were.

He was a lineman for the power company. I did payroll for the school district, thirty-one years in the same office.

Michael is our only one. He and Ali are in Charlotte. Hannah is ten, Ben is seven.

Eighteen months ago we sold the house we raised him in. Four hundred miles south, in April, in a U-Haul Dennis insisted on driving himself.

The night we decided I stood in the kitchen in Dayton with the realtor's card propped against the sugar bowl and said it out loud to nobody.

"I just had a moment where I thought about all I give up. Now it's my turn."

Saturday breakfast at Michael's started the second weekend we were there.

There's no invitation. There never has been. The back door is open from about seven thirty, Ali puts a pan of something in the oven, the radio is on, and whoever turns up turns up. Michael's friend Tony turns up. The man with the beagle turns up.

That was the thing. That was the whole four hundred miles.

Those first months I was there every week. Dennis and I would walk over at ten after eight and be the first two in the kitchen.

The first Saturday in July I left at nine because the man was coming to look at the air conditioning between ten and twelve.

That's it. That's the whole of it. A real reason, and I had it.

I said I'd see them next week.

I went the next week.

I want to be careful here, because nothing I'm about to tell you was anybody being unkind.

Michael hugs me at the door every single time. He has never once not hugged me. But he lets go first, and he's already half a step back when he does it. I could not tell you when that started.

That kitchen is loud. You can hear it from the driveway.

"Tony, you want the end piece or not?"

"I'll take the end piece."

"Mom, coffee?"

"I'm all right."

When I came through the door the volume would drop about a quarter, the way it does when a song changes, then come back up.

Dennis sat across from me instead of beside me. He'd sit beside me a while, get up for the coffee pot, come back around the other side.

There's a chair at the end of that table that's mine. Nobody put me in it. I sat down there the first week and I've sat there ever since. Some Saturdays there'd be nine people in that kitchen with that chair still the one nobody fought me for.

The end of the table.

No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

So I left at nine again. By August I was going every other week.

In September Michael came by on a Wednesday to look at our water heater. He washed his hands at my sink afterwards and said it with his back to me.

"Mom, you don't have to come every Saturday. It's a lot of noise over there, and you've still got half this house in boxes."

He meant it. That's the part I keep landing on. He meant it kindly, he said it to the faucet, and he had no idea what he'd just done.

"It's no trouble," I said.

"I know. I'm only saying."

By the end of that month I had stopped going.

Nobody called to ask where I was. I want to be fair about that too. Nobody called because nobody has ever called. It's an open house. There's nothing to be invited to, so there's nothing anybody could have failed to do.

In October Dennis started bringing something back for me. A cinnamon roll from Hanley's in a white bag, still warm, every Saturday without fail. He'd set it on the counter and say the same thing every time.

"Still warm. You'd have liked the eggs this morning."

Then he'd go change out of his boots.

He is a kind man, it was a kind thing, and I need you to know that I know that.

It was also the week I understood that Saturday had turned into something he did for me instead of something we did together.

I said it out loud in my own kitchen more than once that winter.

"They're just busy. It's not about me."

Here's the one that got me.

For twenty-odd years, when Michael couldn't come at Thanksgiving, I'd say to whoever was in the room, "They're busy. It's a long way."

That was the sentence. That was the sentence we sold the house to be rid of.

I caught myself saying it in March. Three streets.

Eighteen months in their town and I'd become the stop on the way home.

A year of Saturdays, three streets away.

Saturday the thirteenth of June. Eight forty in the morning. Dennis had been gone twenty minutes. I was at my own sink with my hands in the water.

The window over that sink looks straight down the street. You can see their roof from it. That's how close I had moved.

If anybody had asked me what was wrong I'd have had one sentence for them. I just didn't feel seen anymore.

Underneath that was the thing I never said to a living soul, including him.

We sold that house. Twenty-six years of the two of us paying it down, and a kitchen Michael learned to walk in, and I got us here and I'm the one who cannot settle.

Whatever this is, I did it.

Dot lives four doors down and has done since 1992. She's seventy-one. She sits out on her porch with a coffee from about seven thirty every day of the year that isn't raining, with a blanket over her knees when it's cold. She is not a nurse. She is not anybody's expert. She sits there and she sees things.

The Saturday after, I walked down with a card for her birthday. She said sit down a minute.

She had a cup already poured for me, which should have told me something.

"When did Michael stop calling you on a Saturday?"

"I don't know what you mean."

"Joan."

"A while," I said. "How would you know a thing like that?"

"I'm out here at eight. Nine months I've watched your husband go past on his own."

I didn't say anything to that.

"And not one of those Saturdays did anybody come down and get you."

"It's an open house," I said. "Nobody comes and gets anybody."

"I know. That's what makes it so easy."

She let that sit there a while.

"You've got the right fact and the wrong reason," she said. "Those two aren't the same thing."

"The right fact being what?"

"That something changed. The wrong reason being that it's you not settling." She had both hands around her cup. "Something came off you, Joan. It isn't the move and it isn't your boy."

"I shower every day."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"Thirty-four years I've watched the women on this street get to our age. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin dries out on you."

"Nobody's fault," I said. "You color it. You get glasses."

"That's right. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a nice one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

She took something out of her cardigan pocket and set it on the rail between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon-orange, with writing on the front I couldn't read.

She didn't say one word about it.

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She put her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed on them anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that the soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat on Dot's porch and did the arithmetic. It came out somewhere I could not go.

"Then Michael has known for a year," I said.

"No."

"He would have had to."

"He hasn't got a word for it. Neither had I, until somebody gave me one." She looked off down the street. "You don't think, there's something the matter with my mother. You just don't call on a Saturday. Then the Saturday after that you can't remember why you didn't call the week before."

I thought about Dennis.

We were in the car coming back from his sister's a long time ago. I said to him, half joking, "If I start to smell like an old person, you need to let me know."

He laughed. "I'll make a note."

"Dennis would have told me," I said.

"Dennis would have told you if he had the faintest idea what he was smelling. He hasn't. Men don't."

"He's walked over there every Saturday for nine months."

"Same as you did for twenty years in Ohio. Nobody told you either."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the rail.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"Soap."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And that works."

"Four years I've used it. My sister-in-law Marilyn sent me the first one." She wrapped her hands back around the cup. "Christmas before last I noticed my daughter-in-law had started sitting next to me again. I never said one word to that woman. She just started sitting next to me again."

"It's called Kaori. Get more than the one while you can. They make it in small batches, and when a batch is gone you wait months."

"Where do you buy it?"

"I'm not selling you anything," she said. "I'll write it down for you."

She went inside and came back out with the back of an envelope.

I walked home with it in my cardigan pocket. It's a bar of soap. I did not expect a thing from it.

I used it that night.

On the Tuesday I was at the register in the Harris Teeter and caught the lemon off my own wrist. I'd washed with the Kaori at seven that morning.

That Saturday I walked over with Dennis at ten after eight.

I am not going to tell you anybody said anything, because nobody did.

The kitchen was loud from the driveway. We came in the back door. It stayed loud.

Ali had a bag of peppers and about four minutes, so she put the bag in my hands.

"Can you do those thin?"

I stood at the counter next to the stove and cut peppers while she did the eggs.

Michael came around to get at the coffee. Then he didn't go anywhere. He stood on the other side of me and told me a long story about Hannah's soccer coach that didn't have an ending to it.

"The man has a laminated card, Mom. Laminated."

I never sat down.

An hour and a half in that kitchen and I never once got to the end of the table.

Dennis stayed on the stool by the door with his coffee, watching the room.

On the walk home he said, "You didn't sit down once."

That was all he said. He said it the way you read something off a receipt.

He didn't stop at Hanley's. There was no reason to.

That was June. There have been thirteen Saturdays since.

Last Saturday I was at their back door at ten after seven. Ben has been up at six since the day he was born, so I knew the door would be open. He was on the floor in the front room with the iPad and didn't look up.

I had the pot going before anybody else came down.

Ali came in at seven thirty in her robe, stopped behind me, and said, "What is that? That's lovely."

"It's a soap."

"It's lemons." She got two mugs down and stayed where she was. She told me her own mother was always up before everybody, and that out of all of it that's the one she misses. Then Ben came through for more milk and that was the end of that.

Dennis arrived at eight. Hung his coat on the back of the door. Looked at me at the counter with the pot in my hand.

"I can stop going by Hanley's, then."

That's all he said. He didn't explain it and I didn't ask him to.

Eighteen months, and that was the first Saturday that felt like the reason we came.

Dot knocked on Tuesday. There's a new batch up. Marilyn has ordered two.

Saturday comes around again the day after tomorrow.

Ben wants to know if I'm bringing the lemon soap. I told him yes.

If you moved for them and you're the one who isn't in the room.

If everybody is lovely to you and you walk home from it feeling like a guest.

If you have started saying they're busy out loud to people who didn't ask.

You don't need to move again.

You need one Saturday where you get there before anybody else does.

Get the soap. Wash with it. Walk over.

It's called Kaori. The link is below. A bar is $19.95 and it lasts me about a month. If it doesn't make you feel fresher they give you your money back, sixty days.

They make it in small batches. When a batch goes you wait months on the next one.

It is your morning.

It was always your morning.

Go and get there first.

snapshot.caption: try-kaori.com

body.text:
I got scammed by a criminal for $500 because she called me Grammy.
It was my rent money.
I almost gave up until a dermatologist helped me get my money back.

I'm putting this on here even though it embarrasses me.

If you're a widow, if you're a grandmother, or if your family calls less than it used to, please read this to the end.

It's long. I know you're busy.

I'm 70. My husband Roger passed four years ago.

I rent a one bedroom on the second floor. Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

My check comes once a month. The rent goes first.

My son Kevin and his wife Dana live 25 minutes away. Three kids.

Kayla, the oldest, is 18. She started college in August, two hours west.

She calls me Grammy. Nobody else does.

My phone sits by me on the kitchen table. It doesn't ring much.

The last Tuesday in January, at 9:34 at night, it rang. A number I didn't know.

I almost let it go. But it could have been one of the kids, so I picked up.

"Is this Kayla's Grammy?"

A woman. Talking fast.

"Yes. I'm her grandmother."

"I'm the doctor in the emergency room. Kayla was in a car accident tonight. She's awake. Her phone got smashed, so she gave us your number."

She said her name. I didn't catch it. Then the name of a hospital near Kayla's school.

I sat down.

She knew her birthday. She even knew about the penicillin. Kayla has been allergic since she was four.

"She has a cut on her chin. We want to do a scan. Grammy, here's the problem."

Kayla's card had been declined, she said. She couldn't make the payment for the ER. They needed $500 before they went any further.

"Right now," she said.

"How do I pay it?"

She read me an account number. I wrote it on my notepad.

Kayla had put the credit union app on my phone last summer. I had only used it a few times.

The $500 in there was my rent. It was due Sunday.

I didn't think twice. That's my baby.

My thumb shook so hard I got the number wrong the first time. She stayed on the line until it went through.

Then she said, "She really loves you, you were the only one to call."

The only one.

Not her father. Not her mother. Me.

"Tell her Grammy's right here," I said.

"I will. I have to get back to her."

Then she was gone.

I called Kevin straight away. He could be out there in two hours.

It rang and rang. I didn't leave a message. I wanted to tell him myself.

I walked the kitchen. I put the kettle on, then forgot it.

I didn't sleep.

At seven I called Kevin again. Nothing.

At a quarter past, nothing.

On the third try he picked up. I could hear his turn signal.

"What is it?"

"Kevin, how is Kayla? Is she all right? Where is she? Did somebody go to her? The doctor said..."

"Mom, what are you talking about, she's at college."

"But last night the doctor..."

"I have to go to work now. I'll call you later, Mom."

He was gone before I finished.

The phone was still in my hand.

She's at college.

She was never in any emergency room.

It hit me like a, you know a ton of rocks.

At nine I called the credit union. A man took it all down. The time. The account number off my notepad.

"How are you holding up, ma'am?"

"I just feel sick," I said.

He couldn't promise me anything.

I texted Kayla. Are you all right, sweetheart?

A thumbs up came back at four.

At least she was safe.

So I sat for a couple hours just thinking through it. Just thinking that I had to reveal my gullibility.

I could have called Kevin back. I didn't.

He didn't call later either. Not that day. Not the next.

Saturday was Owen's tenth birthday. He's their youngest.

I put a twenty in a card. I didn't have it to spare. I drove it out anyway.

Dana opened the door halfway.

"Janet! You should have called first. We're just heading out."

She took the card. She stayed in the doorway.

Owen said thank you from the bottom of the stairs. Then he went back up.

Kevin waved at me from the kitchen with his phone at his ear. He held up one finger.

He never came to the door. Nobody asked me in.

In the car I sat a while before I turned the key. The front curtain didn't move.

Driving home I counted. Two years since anybody sat at my table.

Sunday went to the diner out on the pike, once a month. Christmas went to Dana's.

They're busy, I always said. It's not about me.

I could call them and would if I needed to. That's what I told people.

Well, I had needed to.

A stranger got through to me in five minutes. My own son couldn't give me one.

By the time I parked, I had it figured out. They don't want me.

What's wrong with me?

Sunday the rent was due. I slipped a note under the manager's door. It would be late. I didn't say why.

I put the electric bill off. I waited on payday.

At night I did the numbers with a pencil. My next check could cover one rent, not two.

At my age, I didn't know where I would go.

The credit union had nothing new. I stopped calling them.

I stopped texting Kayla first. I stopped waiting on Kevin's later.

I was ready to give up. On the $500, and on all of them.

The second Friday in February I nearly cancelled my skin appointment. I'd booked it in the fall, for the itching I get every winter.

It was the only thing on my calendar. I went.

Dr. Marsh has been my dermatologist for eleven years. She's about my age.

She looked at my arms. Then she looked at my face.

"Janet. What happened?"

Any other year I'd have said I was fine.

This time I told her. The call. Grammy. The $500. Kevin's "What is it?" Dana in the doorway. All of it but the rent.

Then I said the thing I hadn't said to anybody.

"I am crushed that they don't even care about me."

She rolled her stool closer.

"First, the call. They do this all day long, Janet. It works on smart women. It worked on you because you love that girl."

"I should have known better."

"Just because we're older, it doesn't mean we're stupid."

Then she asked, "When did Kevin and them stop coming to your place?"

"The spring before last. Dana said the boys had gotten too big for my kitchen."

"How old are the boys?"

"Ten and twelve."

She didn't say anything to that.

"I know they are busy and I also know they love us," I said.

"They are busy. Busy just isn't the whole of it."

"Then what is? I haven't done anything."

"I know you haven't."

She took her glasses off.

"Janet, skin changes with age. It gets thinner. Drier. That's why you're here."

"The itching."

"The itching. It also starts making something it didn't make before. Researchers in Japan found it rises as we get older. It has a smell to it."

I put my hands in my lap.

"I'm clean."

"I know you are. That's what's so unfair about it. Your nose tunes out a smell that never leaves you."

"So I couldn't tell on myself."

"No. And hardly anybody will say it. People wouldn't mention it even to a close friend."

"You're telling me that's the reason everybody keeps me at arm's length now?"

What is this fuss about?

"Then I'll just shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong. Ordinary soap can't wash it away for good."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"It's called nonenal. It doesn't dissolve in water. It sticks to the oil on your skin. Think of burned grease in a pan."

"Hot water won't touch that."

"No. You need a special dish soap to cut through it and lift it off. It's the same here."

She let that sit.

"People take it for the smell of the place. Even a little of it, and they want to visit less."

I sat very still.

Dana in the doorway. Owen at the bottom of the stairs. Two years of my table with nobody at it.

Nobody had said one word. Nobody ever would have.

It didn't explain that woman. She would have called me no matter what. It didn't explain Kevin's "What is it?" either. He couldn't have smelled a thing over the phone.

But the doorway. And my table.

"So they never stopped loving me," I said.

"Not for a minute. It isn't you, Janet. It comes with age, same as the itching. It happens to me too."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She reached into her own purse. She set a small box in my hand.

"I was hoping you'd ask before I had to offer."

"It's soap," she said. "In a lab test, persimmon tannin took off all of it."

I opened it. An orange bar. It smelled fresh and floral.

The box said Kaori.

"I've used it since New Year's," she said.

"Dr. Marsh, I live on my Social Security alone, it's really hard to spend it on expensive stuff."

"It's not expensive, and it's money well spent. But that one's mine. Take it."

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

Then every morning after.

At the pharmacy, a woman my age asked me what I had on. She liked the fragrance.

I had to write Kaori down for her.

Whatever had been standing between me and people was gone.

I walked home the long way with my shoulders back. I felt like myself.

When I got in, I called Kevin. He picked up on the first ring.

"Kevin, I want all of you here Sunday. At my table. Kayla too. I have something to tell you."

He was quiet.

"Mom, your kitchen's kind of small for..."

"Bring two chairs."

Another quiet. Then, "What time?"

"One o'clock."

I had never once said it to him without making it a question.

They came. All of them.

Kevin carried two folding chairs up the stairs. Dana hugged me at the door. She didn't let go first.

Kayla got a ride home from school for it. She sat right next to me. Not across. Next to me.

When everybody was sitting, I told them all of it. The call at 9:34. Grammy. The woman who said she was a doctor. Every time I'd called Kevin.

Then the part nobody knew.

"That $500 was my rent."

Kevin took out his phone. He scrolled back to that night.

"You called four times," he said. He didn't say anything else for a while.

Nobody said how could you.

Kayla had her hand over her mouth. "They used ME," she said. "My name. To take from you."

Then we went after it. All of us.

I got out my notepad. Kevin dialed the credit union's fraud line. Then he handed me the phone. "It's your account, Mom."

I did the talking. I told them I had reported it the very next morning.

Dana filed the police report online while I read her the numbers.

The lady from the credit union asked if anybody in the family could have made that call.

Kayla leaned over the phone. "It wasn't me. I was at college. I'll sign whatever you need."

They still couldn't promise anything.

We also established a code sentence, Kayla and I. Only the two of us know it.

They stayed until almost six. Owen fell asleep on my couch with his head on my arm.

At the door Kevin said, "I should have let you finish, Mom."

"You're here now," I said.

Dana put me in the family group chat that night.

On Thursday the credit union called. The $500 was back in my account. Every penny.

I paid my rent that afternoon.

I ordered my own Kaori that same week. I took my chances.

I nearly skipped that skin appointment. If I had, I never would have picked up the phone to ask them. Without that Sunday at my table, the $500 would still be gone.

Sunday is at my place again. Kevin keeps the two folding chairs in my hall closet.

Last Tuesday Kayla called. No reason. She wanted to tell me about a girl on her floor.

I never said a word to any of them about the two years. There's nothing to say.

If your family meets you everywhere but your own home.

If you are always the one who texts first.

If nobody has sat at your table in a long time, but nobody will tell you why.

You didn't do anything wrong. You don't have to sit by the phone, either.

You need to feel like yourself. Then you need to ask them.

It's called Kaori. It's made only for women over sixty. The link is below.

One bar is $19.95. Six bars are $60.

If it doesn't make you feel fresher and more confident, you get your money back.

Get the bar. Use it every day. Then pick up the phone.

It's your table.

It was always your table.

Ask them to come.

P.S. My mother lived alone her last nine years. We took her out to eat, but we almost never went to her house. I figured she liked her quiet. Nobody ever told her. I would have, if I had known. I think about her kitchen a lot now. Don't let yours go that quiet.

P.P.S. I'm writing this at 10:20 on a Sunday night, alone at my kitchen table, because on Friday the lady across the hall mentioned her son hasn't been by since the fall. "They're busy," she said. I used to say it the same way. I didn't know how to tell her.

Please share this with anyone you love whose family has stopped coming to her place. Even just lately. Even if they still call on her birthday. Even if she says it's fine. I promise you busy isn't the whole of it.

We only do this once a year.

The fruit is picked green, once a year, and the fermenting takes months. When a batch is gone it's gone until next autumn.
