body.text:
We sold the house. Bought a ranch three streets from our son. And for a year, my husband walked over to Saturday breakfast without me.

I stayed home and made coffee for one.

I'm 64. Dennis is 66.

Forty years of working. Forty years of saving. Forty years of saying that when we retired we'd go wherever the grandchildren were.

He was a lineman for the power company. I did payroll for the school district, thirty-one years in the same office.

Michael is our only one. He and Ali are in Charlotte. Hannah is ten, Ben is seven.

Eighteen months ago we sold the house we raised him in. Four hundred miles south, in April, in a U-Haul Dennis insisted on driving himself.

The night we decided I stood in the kitchen in Dayton with the realtor's card propped against the sugar bowl and said it out loud to nobody.

"I just had a moment where I thought about all I give up. Now it's my turn."

Saturday breakfast at Michael's started the second weekend we were there.

There's no invitation. There never has been. The back door is open from about seven thirty, Ali puts a pan of something in the oven, the radio is on, and whoever turns up turns up. Michael's friend Tony turns up. The man with the beagle turns up.

That was the thing. That was the whole four hundred miles.

Those first months I was there every week. Dennis and I would walk over at ten after eight and be the first two in the kitchen.

The first Saturday in July I left at nine because the man was coming to look at the air conditioning between ten and twelve.

That's it. That's the whole of it. A real reason, and I had it.

I said I'd see them next week.

I went the next week.

I want to be careful here, because nothing I'm about to tell you was anybody being unkind.

Michael hugs me at the door every single time. He has never once not hugged me. But he lets go first, and he's already half a step back when he does it. I could not tell you when that started.

That kitchen is loud. You can hear it from the driveway.

"Tony, you want the end piece or not?"

"I'll take the end piece."

"Mom, coffee?"

"I'm all right."

When I came through the door the volume would drop about a quarter, the way it does when a song changes, then come back up.

Dennis sat across from me instead of beside me. He'd sit beside me a while, get up for the coffee pot, come back around the other side.

There's a chair at the end of that table that's mine. Nobody put me in it. I sat down there the first week and I've sat there ever since. Some Saturdays there'd be nine people in that kitchen with that chair still the one nobody fought me for.

The end of the table.

No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

So I left at nine again. By August I was going every other week.

In September Michael came by on a Wednesday to look at our water heater. He washed his hands at my sink afterwards and said it with his back to me.

"Mom, you don't have to come every Saturday. It's a lot of noise over there, and you've still got half this house in boxes."

He meant it. That's the part I keep landing on. He meant it kindly, he said it to the faucet, and he had no idea what he'd just done.

"It's no trouble," I said.

"I know. I'm only saying."

By the end of that month I had stopped going.

Nobody called to ask where I was. I want to be fair about that too. Nobody called because nobody has ever called. It's an open house. There's nothing to be invited to, so there's nothing anybody could have failed to do.

In October Dennis started bringing something back for me. A cinnamon roll from Hanley's in a white bag, still warm, every Saturday without fail. He'd set it on the counter and say the same thing every time.

"Still warm. You'd have liked the eggs this morning."

Then he'd go change out of his boots.

He is a kind man, it was a kind thing, and I need you to know that I know that.

It was also the week I understood that Saturday had turned into something he did for me instead of something we did together.

I said it out loud in my own kitchen more than once that winter.

"They're just busy. It's not about me."

Here's the one that got me.

For twenty-odd years, when Michael couldn't come at Thanksgiving, I'd say to whoever was in the room, "They're busy. It's a long way."

That was the sentence. That was the sentence we sold the house to be rid of.

I caught myself saying it in March. Three streets.

Eighteen months in their town and I'd become the stop on the way home.

A year of Saturdays, three streets away.

Saturday the thirteenth of June. Eight forty in the morning. Dennis had been gone twenty minutes. I was at my own sink with my hands in the water.

The window over that sink looks straight down the street. You can see their roof from it. That's how close I had moved.

If anybody had asked me what was wrong I'd have had one sentence for them. I just didn't feel seen anymore.

Underneath that was the thing I never said to a living soul, including him.

We sold that house. Twenty-six years of the two of us paying it down, and a kitchen Michael learned to walk in, and I got us here and I'm the one who cannot settle.

Whatever this is, I did it.

Dot lives four doors down and has done since 1992. She's seventy-one. She sits out on her porch with a coffee from about seven thirty every day of the year that isn't raining, with a blanket over her knees when it's cold. She is not a nurse. She is not anybody's expert. She sits there and she sees things.

The Saturday after, I walked down with a card for her birthday. She said sit down a minute.

She had a cup already poured for me, which should have told me something.

"When did Michael stop calling you on a Saturday?"

"I don't know what you mean."

"Joan."

"A while," I said. "How would you know a thing like that?"

"I'm out here at eight. Nine months I've watched your husband go past on his own."

I didn't say anything to that.

"And not one of those Saturdays did anybody come down and get you."

"It's an open house," I said. "Nobody comes and gets anybody."

"I know. That's what makes it so easy."

She let that sit there a while.

"You've got the right fact and the wrong reason," she said. "Those two aren't the same thing."

"The right fact being what?"

"That something changed. The wrong reason being that it's you not settling." She had both hands around her cup. "Something came off you, Joan. It isn't the move and it isn't your boy."

"I shower every day."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"Thirty-four years I've watched the women on this street get to our age. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin dries out on you."

"Nobody's fault," I said. "You color it. You get glasses."

"That's right. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a nice one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

She took something out of her cardigan pocket and set it on the rail between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon-orange, with writing on the front I couldn't read.

She didn't say one word about it.

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She put her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed on them anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that the soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat on Dot's porch and did the arithmetic. It came out somewhere I could not go.

"Then Michael has known for a year," I said.

"No."

"He would have had to."

"He hasn't got a word for it. Neither had I, until somebody gave me one." She looked off down the street. "You don't think, there's something the matter with my mother. You just don't call on a Saturday. Then the Saturday after that you can't remember why you didn't call the week before."

I thought about Dennis.

We were in the car coming back from his sister's a long time ago. I said to him, half joking, "If I start to smell like an old person, you need to let me know."

He laughed. "I'll make a note."

"Dennis would have told me," I said.

"Dennis would have told you if he had the faintest idea what he was smelling. He hasn't. Men don't."

"He's walked over there every Saturday for nine months."

"Same as you did for twenty years in Ohio. Nobody told you either."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the rail.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"Soap."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And that works."

"Four years I've used it. My sister-in-law Marilyn sent me the first one." She wrapped her hands back around the cup. "Christmas before last I noticed my daughter-in-law had started sitting next to me again. I never said one word to that woman. She just started sitting next to me again."

"It's called Kaori. Get more than the one while you can. They make it in small batches, and when a batch is gone you wait months."

"Where do you buy it?"

"I'm not selling you anything," she said. "I'll write it down for you."

She went inside and came back out with the back of an envelope.

I walked home with it in my cardigan pocket. It's a bar of soap. I did not expect a thing from it.

I used it that night.

On the Tuesday I was at the register in the Harris Teeter and caught the lemon off my own wrist. I'd washed with the Kaori at seven that morning.

That Saturday I walked over with Dennis at ten after eight.

I am not going to tell you anybody said anything, because nobody did.

The kitchen was loud from the driveway. We came in the back door. It stayed loud.

Ali had a bag of peppers and about four minutes, so she put the bag in my hands.

"Can you do those thin?"

I stood at the counter next to the stove and cut peppers while she did the eggs.

Michael came around to get at the coffee. Then he didn't go anywhere. He stood on the other side of me and told me a long story about Hannah's soccer coach that didn't have an ending to it.

"The man has a laminated card, Mom. Laminated."

I never sat down.

An hour and a half in that kitchen and I never once got to the end of the table.

Dennis stayed on the stool by the door with his coffee, watching the room.

On the walk home he said, "You didn't sit down once."

That was all he said. He said it the way you read something off a receipt.

He didn't stop at Hanley's. There was no reason to.

That was June. There have been thirteen Saturdays since.

Last Saturday I was at their back door at ten after seven. Ben has been up at six since the day he was born, so I knew the door would be open. He was on the floor in the front room with the iPad and didn't look up.

I had the pot going before anybody else came down.

Ali came in at seven thirty in her robe, stopped behind me, and said, "What is that? That's lovely."

"It's a soap."

"It's lemons." She got two mugs down and stayed where she was. She told me her own mother was always up before everybody, and that out of all of it that's the one she misses. Then Ben came through for more milk and that was the end of that.

Dennis arrived at eight. Hung his coat on the back of the door. Looked at me at the counter with the pot in my hand.

"I can stop going by Hanley's, then."

That's all he said. He didn't explain it and I didn't ask him to.

Eighteen months, and that was the first Saturday that felt like the reason we came.

Dot knocked on Tuesday. There's a new batch up. Marilyn has ordered two.

Saturday comes around again the day after tomorrow.

Ben wants to know if I'm bringing the lemon soap. I told him yes.

If you moved for them and you're the one who isn't in the room.

If everybody is lovely to you and you walk home from it feeling like a guest.

If you have started saying they're busy out loud to people who didn't ask.

You don't need to move again.

You need one Saturday where you get there before anybody else does.

Get the soap. Wash with it. Walk over.

It's called Kaori. The link is below. A bar is $19.95 and it lasts me about a month. If it doesn't make you feel fresher they give you your money back, sixty days.

They make it in small batches. When a batch goes you wait months on the next one.

It is your morning.

It was always your morning.

Go and get there first.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.
Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.
One bar of it cost me my doctor of eleven years.

I have never told anybody what I paid for that bar.

Now I'm putting it on Facebook.

If you already bought a persimmon soap but got nothing out of it, this is for you. Please read the whole thing.

It's long. You're busy. I know.

It started in September.

I'm 67. Dr. Mercer knew my knees, my blood pressure, the year my mother died.

At the end of my checkup she put her pen down.

"One more thing, Diane. Our skin changes as we get older. It can carry a smell it didn't used to, and nobody ever mentions it."

Then two words. "Persimmon soap."

She said it kindly. She said it once. It wasn't on any of the papers she gave me.

Doctors never said anything. Mine did.

I'd been seeing those ads for weeks. I scrolled past every one. But they made me kind of doubt myself.

For about a year, my daughter Sarah's Sunday visits had been ending a little quicker at the door. No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

I'd asked her once, straight out, because I couldn't tell on myself. "Do I smell like an old lady to you?"

"Mom. You're fine."

My daughter's real frank about things and outspoken. I would've thought she would have told me if I needed it. But you never know.

An ad is one thing. Eleven years of Dr. Mercer is another.

I decided to buy it and not tell my husband the price.

That night I ordered the first one that came up on my phone. $18.99, plus $5.99 to ship it.

It came in a small box with a persimmon printed on it.

The box didn't say much. So I used it like any soap. Every morning, in the shower, down to a sliver I could barely hold.

It was nice but I wasn't sure if that solved the problem.

After, I'd put my nose to the collar of my robe anyway. The sniff test.

Every morning it told me the same thing. Nothing.

The first Sunday, Sarah hugged me at the door with her car keys already in her hand.

The second Sunday, the same.

The third Sunday I said it before she could. "Go on. Beat the dark." She was on her feet before I'd finished.

Fourth Sunday. Keys.

Fifth Sunday, I'd used the last of the bar that morning. Keys.

I wondered if it was just another soap.

My husband Don found the empty box in the bathroom cabinet. "That the fancy stuff?"

"It seems like voodoo," I said. "Not a clue if it is effective."

I didn't tell him what I'd thought every one of those mornings. What Dr. Mercer smelled on me in that exam room. For nothing.

My blood pressure check was a Thursday in October.

Dr. Mercer wrapped the cuff around my arm. "How did you get on with the soap, Diane?"

I waited until I had my coat back on.

Then I said, "Next time, keep your two words to yourself."

At the front desk I asked Patty for the form to have my records sent somewhere else.

"Are you sure, Diane?"

Dr. Mercer stood in the hall with my chart. She didn't say a thing.

I signed it.

That Sunday Sarah got up at a quarter to four.

"You okay, Mom? You're quiet."

"Just tired," I said.

At the door I got the side hug. The back arched and the behind hanging out creating distance between the hugger and the hugged. Her keys were already in her hand.

I knew that hug. I used to give it.

My mother lived alone her last six years, forty minutes from me. Every other Sunday I drove over. Every other Sunday I hugged her at her door exactly like that, with my keys in my hand.

I remember the smell of my mother and my grandmother and just thought it was old people smell.

"Leaving already?" she'd say.

"Traffic, Mom."

I never said a word to her.

That night I lay next to Don with the clock on 11:40.

Five weeks. $24.98. Eleven years.

"Why didn't it work?" I said. Out loud.

Don said, "Hmm?" He rolled over.

Nobody answered.

My hugs had started declining. I noticed but figured it is what it is.

I was an idiot paying so much for soap.

So I stopped. No more sniff test, no more asking Sarah. I didn't go looking for another bar.

Ten days later the phone rang at suppertime.

"Diane, it's Dr. Mercer." A pause. "Not the office. Me."

I nearly hung up.

"I'm not calling to get you back," she said. "I'd like to see what you bought. The box, if you still have it."

"Why?"

"Because I'm the one who sent you to buy it."

I figured she'd be nice to me right up until I bought something.

But she was asking me to bring her the proof she was wrong.

I put the empty box in my handbag. I went to be proved right.

She saw me after her last patient, in her own office.

There were six boxes on her desk. Different names. A persimmon printed on every one.

I wasn't the only one she'd rung.

I set mine down with the others. She looked at them a long time.

"Twenty years I've been saying those two words to women," she said. "I never once told anybody how to choose one."

"So it's a fad."

"How do you know?"

"I really didn't notice a difference."

"When you come home from a week away, what do you smell?"

"The house. Coffee, and Don's old jacket by the door."

"And the next morning?"

"Nothing. It's just the house."

"Where did it go?"

I didn't answer. She waited.

"Nowhere," I said. "I stopped noticing it."

"The brain tunes out a smell that never leaves you. Mine does too."

"Every morning for five weeks I smelled my own collar," I said. "I probably wouldn't be aware of any difference. Either way."

"You weren't a fool, Diane."

"Then who would know?"

"Who did you ask?"

"Sarah. She said I was fine."

"Would she tell you?"

I thought about my mother's front door.

"No," I said. "I never told mine."

"Then how was I supposed to choose one?"

"Now I'm telling women to find a maker who says who it's made for," she said. "One who tells you where to wash with it. Behind your ears, around your neck, your chest, across your back."

"Mine never said."

"Neither did I. You didn't do one thing wrong."

She touched the nearest one. "But that's still only a box talking. It can't tell you whether it works."

"Only Sarah can," I said. "At the door."

"Which one do you use?"

She opened her desk drawer. A bar, still in its paper.

"This isn't a prescription," she said. "It's made only for women over sixty. I'm 64, and it's what I wash with."

The paper said Kaori.

I held it to my nose. "Citrusy."

"Don't ask me if it works. I'd be the last to know."

I knew how I looked. A woman my age, being handed soap across a desk.

Not sure if I was investing in another scam. Always thinking it would be one more thing I'm wasting money on.

"Why that one?" I said. "Any of these would do."

"Maybe. I can't tell them apart, and I've tried. So I take the one where somebody else pays if it does nothing for me."

"I'm not buying another one."

"I'm not selling you anything." She pushed it over to me. "Ring me. Whatever happens."

I drove home with it on the passenger seat. I put it in the shower where the last one had been. I didn't tell Sarah. I didn't tell anybody.

I washed where Dr. Mercer had said, every morning. I didn't do the sniff test once.

The first Sunday on her bar, Sarah hugged me at the door with her keys in her hand. Same as always.

Voodoo, I thought. Again.

That night I nearly put it back in its paper.

The second Sunday it was dark by five. The porch light came on when we stepped out. There were wet leaves all over the step.

Sarah had her coat on. Her keys were still in her bag.

She hugged me with both arms. Her chin on my shoulder, the way she did when she came home from college.

She stood there long enough for the porch light to click off.

I don't know which of us let go first.

Neither of us mentioned it. I didn't ask her. I'm not going to.

Nobody said a word when Sarah started leaving early. Nobody said a word on Sunday either.

My mother never found out. I nearly didn't.

On Monday I rang Dr. Mercer. My turn. She answered on the first ring.

"Well?" she said.

"She didn't get her keys out till she was at the car."

The line went quiet for a second.

"Can you put me back on your list?"

"I never took you off it."

Dr. Mercer can't put any of this on Facebook. I can.

So please. Don't buy persimmon soap to find out with your own nose. Mine told me nothing for five weeks.

Don't ask your daughter either. She'll tell you you're fine.

If you buy one more bar, give it two weeks. Then watch how the people you love say goodbye.

I'm just Dr. Mercer's patient. Nobody pays me a cent for any of this.

The one she gave me is Kaori. One bar is $19.95. Six bars are $60.

If it does nothing for you, they give you your money back.

Sarah's coming Sunday.

Diane

P.S. Don read this over my shoulder. He says he never knew what I paid for that first bar. He also says I can't write all this without saying where to get the other one.

I left it out on purpose. I didn't sit down to sell anybody soap. But he's right, it saves you looking.

body.text:
I bought the persimmon soap the internet keeps telling women my age to buy.
I used it every day for 3 weeks, morning and night, the whole bar.
My husband is still sleeping in the spare room.

I am 61. Ron and I have been married 34 years. He retired last September after 38 years at the county.

He was still in our room at Christmas. I want to be accurate about that, because I have gone over the order of it more times than I can tell you.

This is what happened in between, and what it cost me to find out.

By January he had stopped coming into our bedroom.

He would stand in the doorway with his coffee and tell me about the gutters from there. Not crossing in. Talking to me from the threshold like a man delivering something.

In March he moved his pillow into the spare room. He said it was his back, and that the mattress in there was firmer, and that he was sorry, and he was sorry the way you are sorry when you have already decided.

I bought him a mattress topper in April. The expensive one, the one the man in the store said was for people with backs.

In June I went in there for the window fan and I found it behind the door. Still in the plastic. The tape had not been broken.

I stood there holding a mattress topper for a long time.

He had not been sleeping badly. He had been sleeping somewhere else, and he had found a reason for it that I could not argue with, because you cannot argue with a man's back.

Kate is our daughter. She is 33 and she is 40 minutes away, and she is the kind of daughter who calls on the drive home.

She had been putting the window down in my car since about February. Two inches. Then she would say something about the heat, in February, in Ohio.

In May she drove us both to my sister's and she had the air on the whole way with the windows cracked, and when I asked her she said she gets carsick if it is stuffy. She has never been carsick in her life.

In April, at my own table, she suggested we eat out on the porch. It was 48 degrees. We ate out on the porch, all of us, in coats, and everybody said what a lovely idea.

I want to be fair to them. Nobody was ever unkind to me. Not once. Not one word.

They just kept finding reasons, and the reasons were all good ones, and there were a lot of them.

The night I found the topper I sat up until 2 in the morning with my phone, typing things into it I would not have said out loud in an empty house.

I will not write out what I typed. Any woman my age who has done it knows what I typed.

I found women saying the same 3 words to each other on a page I will not name. Persimmon soap. That was all of it. Nobody said why it was persimmon and I did not care why.

I ordered a persimmon soap that night. 9 dollars, an orange bar, persimmons all over the box, a bit of Japanese on the front. It came on the Thursday.

I used it every day for 3 weeks.

I want to tell you exactly how careful I was, because I need you to understand what it did to me when nothing happened. Every morning. Every night. The whole bar.

Ron stayed in the spare room.

Kate put the window down in July.

And I stopped, because there is only one thing left to think when the answer does not work. It is not the answer that is wrong. It is you. And you are not fixable.

I put the wrapper in the bin and I did not tell one living person I had bought it.

In August I went into the pharmacy on Harrison for Ron's back. That is the part I still cannot get over. I was in there buying a heat patch for the back he does not have a problem with.

Maggie has been behind that counter 17 years. She did my mother's blister packs for the last 2 years of her life and she never once made me feel like I was asking too much.

She rang up the heat patches and she said, "How is he doing?"

And I said, "He's fine," and then I stood there and did not move away from the counter.

There was nobody behind me. She waited.

"Maggie, can I ask you something that isn't about him."

She put the patches in the bag and left the bag on the counter.

"Is there something about me. A smell. I have thought about it every day since March and I cannot ask anybody in my own house."

She did not look surprised, which was the first kind thing that happened to me all year.

"There's something," she said. "You're not imagining it. But it isn't what you think it is."

"I shower every day. I have showered every day of my life."

"I know you do."

"Then what?"

"I've stood here 17 years. Things change for women our age. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then I'll shower twice a day."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She leaned on the counter.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"That can't be right."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I did not answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway."

"Garlic leaves a molecule behind that soap doesn't react with. Still there."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I put my hand on the counter.

"Then what gets rid of it?"

"Persimmon. The tannins take it apart. It doesn't cover it."

And I heard myself say it out loud in a pharmacy at 20 past 4 in the afternoon.

"I bought that. I bought a persimmon soap in June. I used it for 3 weeks and nothing happened, so I stopped."

She did not say anything for a second.

Then she said, "Have you still got the box?"

I said it was in the bin in June.

"Then buy another one and bring me the box before you use it. Any of them. Whichever one you like the look of."

I did. I brought it in the following Tuesday in my purse.

She turned it over on the counter and put her finger on the list on the back and read it to me out loud, the way she reads a label to somebody's mother.

Water. Palm oil. Glycerin. Fragrance. A color, with a number on it.

She got to the bottom of the list and stopped.

"Now find me the persimmon."

It was on the front of the box 4 times. It was in the name of the product. There was a photograph of one on it.

It was not in the list at all.

"That's what you bought in June," she said. "You didn't try persimmon soap. You tried an orange soap that had been told to look like one."

I stood in that pharmacy and my eyes went, which I had not done in front of anybody all year, including in the spare room doorway in March.

"So it was never me."

"It was never you. And it wasn't even your judgment. It was one line on a label that nobody has ever told you to read."

She reached under the counter for her handbag, which is a thing I had never seen her do, and she took out a small parcel wrapped in tissue paper. Persimmon orange. Characters on the front I could not read.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"I can't take yours."

"I buy 3 at a time. They make it in small batches and this one's nearly gone, so I've learned."

"Does it work?"

"I've used it 6 years. One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped standing a bit back from people. I never knew I'd been doing it."

"It's called Kaori. I can't sell it to you. That is more or less the point of it."

I used it that night. It is a bar of soap. I did not expect anything, because I had already been here in June.

The first week I could not tell.

The second week Kate drove me to my sister's again and we had the windows up the whole way and she talked about her job the entire time and I do not think she noticed she was doing it.

At the end of August, Ron came into our bedroom to get a book off his own shelf, which he had been doing from the doorway since January.

He came in. He sat on the end of the bed while he found his place in it. He stayed about 20 minutes.

He did not say anything and neither did I. I have learned something about what does not get said in that house.

In September a woman waiting for her prescription behind me at Maggie's counter said, "I'm sorry, what is that? It's citrus. It's lovely."

I said it was a bar of soap.

Maggie did not look up from her computer. She said, "Isn't it."

Ron came back into our room on the 4th of October. He carried his own pillow in and put it down and said, "I've been sleeping badly in there."

I said, "Have you."

That is as close as either of us is going to get, and after 34 years I find I do not need the rest of it.

Here is the part I keep coming back to.

I was right in June. I had the right idea in the middle of the night on my own phone, and I paid 9 dollars for it, and it did nothing, and I decided that meant there was something wrong with me that could not be fixed.

It was the bar. It was only ever the bar.

Maggie texted me last week. Kaori is back on the website. She has ordered 3, because that is what she does.

Kate is driving us both to my sister's for her birthday on the 2nd.

She has already asked if I am bringing the good pie. I told her yes.

If your husband has found a reason he can live with and moved down the hall.

If somebody has started opening a window in your car and telling you it is the heat.

If you have already tried the thing that was supposed to work, and stopped, and quietly decided the problem is you.

You do not need to be fixed.

You need to find out what you actually bought.

Get the soap. Take the shower. Turn the box over first.

They only harvest the persimmon once a year. This batch is almost gone. If you wait, you wait a long time.

It was never me.

It was never going to be me.

Your move.

body.text:
Please DON'T buy persimmon soap. I'm begging you.
Not one more bar. Not until you've read this.
One bar of it cost me my doctor of eleven years.

I have never told anybody what I paid for that bar.

Now I'm putting it on Facebook.

If you already bought a persimmon soap but got nothing out of it, this is for you. Please read the whole thing.

It's long. You're busy. I know.

It started in September.

I'm 67. Dr. Mercer knew my knees, my blood pressure, the year my mother died.

At the end of my checkup she put her pen down.

"One more thing, Diane. Our skin changes as we get older. It can carry a smell it didn't used to, and nobody ever mentions it."

Then two words. "Persimmon soap."

She said it kindly. She said it once. It wasn't on any of the papers she gave me.

Doctors never said anything. Mine did.

I'd been seeing those ads for weeks. I scrolled past every one. But they made me kind of doubt myself.

For about a year, my daughter Sarah's Sunday visits had been ending a little quicker at the door. No one said anything, family or friends. But you know when you know.

I'd asked her once, straight out, because I couldn't tell on myself. "Do I smell like an old lady to you?"

"Mom. You're fine."

She said it at the door, with her car keys already in her hand.

An ad is one thing. A suggestion from Dr. Mercer is different.

I decided to buy it.

That night I looked at every one of them on my phone. One said handmade in Japan. If I was going to do this, I was going to buy the good stuff.

They only sold them in twos. $59.99.

I'd never paid sixty dollars for soap in my life. My thumb sat over that button a long time before I pressed it.

I didn't tell my husband the price.

They came in two small boxes with a persimmon printed on each. I opened one and used it like any soap. Every morning, in the shower, down to a sliver I could barely hold.

It was nice but I wasn't sure if that solved the problem.

I wondered if it was just another soap.

My husband Don found the empty box in the bathroom cabinet. "That the fancy stuff?"

"It seems like voodoo," I said. "Not a clue if it is effective."

My blood pressure check was a Thursday in October.

Dr. Mercer wrapped the cuff around my arm and leaned in close to read it.

Then she sat back. "Diane, it's about time you got yourself that persimmon soap."

I had. Three weeks of it, down to the last sliver.

She could still smell it on me.

I smiled at her. "I'll look into it."

I didn't tell her what I'd spent. Sixty dollars on soap, and she was sitting there telling me to go and buy some.

I had my coat on before she'd written the numbers down.

At the front desk I asked Patty for the form to have my records sent somewhere else.

"Are you sure, Diane?"

"I already bought her soap," I said. Loud enough for the hall.

Dr. Mercer stood in the hall with my chart. She didn't say a thing.

I signed it.

That Sunday Sarah got up at a quarter to four.

"You okay, Mom? You're quiet."

"Just tired," I said.

At the door she hugged me from the side. Her keys were already in her hand.

I knew that hug. I used to give it.

My mother lived alone her last six years, forty minutes from me. Every other Sunday I drove over. Every other Sunday I hugged her at her door exactly like that, with my keys in my hand.

I remember the smell of my mother and my grandmother and just thought it was old people smell.

"Leaving already?" she'd say.

"Traffic, Mom."

I never said a word to her.

That night I lay next to Don with the clock on 11:40.

Three weeks. $59.99.

"Why didn't it work?" I said. Out loud.

Don said, "Hmm?" He rolled over.

Nobody answered.

I thought I was an idiot paying so much for soap.

So I stopped. I never opened the second bar. It sat in its box at the back of the bathroom cabinet.

Ten days later the phone rang at suppertime.

"Diane, it's Dr. Mercer." A pause. "Not the office. Me."

I nearly hung up.

"I'm not calling to get you back," she said. "I'd like to see what you bought. The box, if you still have it."

"Why?"

"Because I'm the one who sent you to buy it."

I got the second bar out of the cabinet, still in its box, and put it in my handbag.

Fine. She could see for herself what $59.99 buys you.

She saw me after her last patient, in her own office.

There were six boxes on her desk. Different names. A persimmon printed on every one.

I wasn't the only one she'd rung.

I set mine down with the others. She looked at them a long time.

"Twenty years I've been saying those two words to women," she said. "I never once told anybody how to choose one."

"So it's a fad."

"You know it's the tannin in the persimmon that does the work?"

"Yes."

"Mine was the good one," I said. "Thirty dollars a bar. Handmade in Japan."

"Then turn it over and find the tannin."

I turned it over. At the very bottom, in the smallest print on the box, were three words.

"Huh," I said. "Made in China."

"It was a marketing lie," she said. "The industry is full of them. But they can't fake the ingredient list."

"Their website has a woman who grew up with this soap in a little Japanese village."

"I looked her up. Read the small print at the bottom of that page. She's a brand persona. They made her up."

"They sell you the story," she said. "So you never question what's actually in the bar."

I went down the list with my finger. Persimmon was tenth. The persimmon tannin was the very last thing on it.

"I went through all of these last week." She touched the six. "No wonder they don't work. The one thing that does the work is down at the bottom of every list."

"I paid $59.99 for that," I said. "And washed with everything ahead of it."

"You didn't do one thing wrong," she said. "I did."

"The tannin is in the green fruit," she said. "It's what makes an unripe persimmon pucker your whole mouth. Let it ripen and the pucker is gone. It's just sweet."

"So which one is in mine?"

"Yours says fruit extract. That's all it has to say. The green fruit, or the sweet juice of a ripe one. The box doesn't tell you."

"Which one do you use?"

She took a box out of her desk drawer. She turned it over before she held it out, her finger on the first line.

Persimmon Extract.

"First on the list," she said. "Pressed from the green fruit, before it ever turns sweet."

The front said Kaori. No village. No grandmother.

"This one doesn't need a story to sell."

"This isn't a prescription," she said. "I'm 64, and it's what I wash with now."

I held it to my nose. "Citrusy."

She took another box out of the drawer, still sealed, and pushed it across the desk to me.

"That one's yours."

Whatever you do, don't wait for your daughter to say something. She won't.

She'll just leave a little earlier. Half an hour this year. An hour next year. Then every other Sunday. Then a phone call instead.

It's already started, or you wouldn't still be reading.

And you don't get those Sundays back. Not one of them.

One day you'll be the one at the door, saying "Leaving already?"

body.text:
I just did an eight-day wellness retreat in Kyoto. Three thousand four hundred pounds plus the flights. And the thing that actually changed was sitting on the shelf in the bathroom the whole time.

I need to back up, because this is going to sound ridiculous.

I have been dealing with something for nearly three years that I have never said out loud to anybody. Not the kind of thing you mention. The kind where you strip the bed on a Sunday and put your face in the pillowcase before it goes in the machine, every single week, and never tell one living person you do it. The kind where you have a rule about which side of people you stand on and you have never once written that rule down.

My mother had it. She died at eighty-one, and for the last decade of her life she stopped going to things and told everybody it was her hip.

I am 61. And I have spent every morning of the last three years checking myself for it.

I have done everything. Two showers a day, three on a bad one. Antibacterial wash. A charcoal bar. Two "all day" sprays, one for the handbag and one for the car. A perfume I do not like, chosen because it was the loudest tester on the counter. I have washed cardigans after one wear for two years.

And I have bought three persimmon soaps. Nine pounds, fifteen, twenty-two. Every one of them did precisely nothing, which is why I had decided the whole idea was rubbish.

I have spent close to six hundred pounds on this without ever naming it to a single person.

And the afternoon never changed. Not once in three years. I would be fine at nine in the morning and by three it was back, on the collar, and I would go and stand somewhere on my own for a minute.

My friend Marsha told me about this retreat in Kyoto. Eight days. Run by a Japanese doctor who works with women after the menopause. They blend Kampo — Japan's traditional plant medicine — with Western practice. Marsha said her sister came back a different woman.

I thought, why not. I had already thrown money at everything else.

Day one was lovely. Quiet gardens. Somebody speaking softly. Morning walks. Tea.

Day two something shifted, and it took me until the fourth day to work out what.

Nobody moved.

That sounds like nothing. But if you have spent three years watching for the small adjustments people make — the half step back, the chair that goes an inch the wrong way, the way somebody turns their head very slightly as they lean in — then you know precisely what I mean. You stop noticing you are watching for it until a day comes when there is nothing to watch.

That was day two.

Day four at lunch I sat next to a woman called Eleanor. Sixty-two. A retired teacher from Bristol.

She leaned over and said, "Forgive me, but I have to ask. Are you finding something here that has nothing to do with the meditation?"

I laughed, because I had been thinking exactly the same thing.

She said, "My mother had this. I have had it since I was fifty-five. I have not taken my coat off indoors since 2022. I have taken it off every day since I arrived here."

We started comparing notes.

Both of us had stopped checking. Both of us had stopped doing the standing-on-the-right-side thing. Both of us had spent years on sprays and washes and both of us had bought at least two persimmon soaps that did nothing at all.

I thought, maybe it is the air, or the food, or being somewhere nobody knows me.

But then I noticed something.

In the bathroom of every room in that place there was one bar of soap. Dark. Nearly black in the middle, amber where the light came through the edge. It looked like something out of a shed. It did not look like a product.

I had been using it for four days without once thinking about it. It was just what was there.

On day five I asked the woman who did the rooms what it was.

She said, "That is kakishibu. Sensei has it in every bathroom. She says it is the most important thing in the whole programme, but most guests do not believe her until they have been here a week."

I nearly dropped my tea.

I said, "Wait. Persimmon soap? I have persimmon soap. I have bought three and none of them did anything."

She smiled like she had heard it several hundred times.

She said, "Sensei says everybody says that. She says when you get home, look at the box you have been buying. If persimmon is on the front and not in the ingredients, you have been buying orange soap."

That night I could not stop thinking about it.

I went to my room and pulled up the listing for the bar I had been buying off Amazon for two years. Good reviews. Nice box. "Japanese Persimmon Soap" on the front in big letters, with persimmons all over it.

I zoomed in on the ingredients.

There it was.

CI 15985.

That is an orange food colouring. That was the entire reason the bar was orange.

Persimmon was printed on the front of that box four times and did not appear once, anywhere, in the ingredient list.

Two years.

I had been buying that bar for two years telling myself persimmon soap does not work for me, when in fact I had never once used persimmon soap. I had been washing with dyed glycerin and a good photograph.

On day seven I asked to speak to the doctor directly.

She was exactly what I expected. Sixty-something. Direct. Warm, but not soft. She has been practising in Kyoto for twenty-six years.

She said, "Here is what nobody tells women in the West. After about forty, your skin begins producing an oil it did not produce before. It is not sweat. It is not bacteria. It has a name and it was identified in 2001."

"Your soap is a detergent. It is built for sweat and dirt. Oil and water do not mix. So you wash, and you are clean, and by the afternoon it is back, and you decide the problem is you."

"In the West they tell you it is the menopause and send you home. They sell you a stronger deodorant, which works where you sweat, and this is not sweat. They sell you perfume, which does not cancel it — it sits on top of it, and what comes back at three o'clock is both."

"What lifts it is a tannin. And it has to come from the unripe fruit."

She was very clear about this part.

"The persimmon you know — the orange one, soft, sweet — has almost none of the tannin left in it. The tannin is in the green fruit, when it is hard and it shuts your mouth. Picked green, pressed, then left to ferment for months until it is dark. That is kakishibu. We have used it for four hundred years."

"Both can legally be called persimmon soap. There is no standard behind those two words. That is why the ones you bought did nothing, and that is why most Western women try this once and give up on the only thing that was going to help them."

I asked her the question I had been carrying for three years, which was why my own GP had never mentioned any of it.

She was not unkind about it.

She said that in Japan this has an ordinary name — karēshū — and that it is printed on packaging, advertised on trains, and sold in an aisle in the chemist with a sign over it, and that men buy the product for themselves in the shop without embarrassment.

She said that in the West there is no word for it. And that where there is no word, there is no conversation, and where there is no conversation there is no leaflet, no training and no aisle. Just a woman in a surgery trying to describe something in two rehearsed sentences to a doctor who has never been taught it.

"Your doctor is not hiding it from you," she said. "She has never been told either."

Then she said the thing I have repeated to about nine people since.

"You have not been failing to get clean. You have been trying to wash off an oil with a detergent. Every woman knows you cannot do that with a frying pan. Nobody thinks of it in the shower."

I sat there thinking about the three thousand four hundred pounds I had just spent, and the fact that the most useful thing in the entire eight days was the bar of soap in my own bathroom that I had walked past for four days.

When I got home I threw away everything on my shelf. Six things. The two sprays. The charcoal bar. The antibacterial wash. The perfume. And the three orange persimmon soaps, which was the one that actually annoyed me.

Then I went looking for the one thing she had described.

It is harder than it should be. Almost everything sold here is the ripe fruit, or a fragrance, or a dye. The word is on the front of all of them.

The one I found that is actually the fermented extract from the unripe fruit is made by a Japanese woman who grew up with it, in Mino in Gifu — the town where the stuff has been made for centuries. Diospyros Kaki, named on the ingredient panel, third down, where anybody can check it in ten seconds.

That was nine weeks ago.

The afternoon is gone. Not reduced. Gone.

The checking is gone. I could not tell you the last time I put my face in a pillowcase.

The rest came back in stages. The first fortnight, honestly, nothing — and I want to say that plainly, because it is exactly where I would have stopped if Eleanor had not been emailing me. Week three it was the pillowcase. Week five I wore the wool coat. Week eight my granddaughter fell asleep against my arm on the sofa and stayed there.

My daughter rang me a fortnight ago and we talked for forty minutes and afterwards she said, "You sound like yourself again."

I nearly went completely to pieces on the phone.

I told Eleanor. She ordered the same day she got back to Bristol.

She emailed me a week later and the subject line was "I am furious."

She said, "I have spent eleven thousand pounds on this over four years. Consultants. Sprays. Three of the same orange bars. This is what I needed? Twenty-five pounds and a fruit picked while it's still green?"

Yes. Same.

I am writing this for the woman who is where I was nine weeks ago. The one who checks the pillowcase and has never told anybody. The one whose mother had it and stopped going out. The one who has already bought a persimmon soap and decided the whole thing was nonsense.

You do not need to fly to Kyoto.

But you do need to check the box before you buy another one, because six out of every ten sold here will do nothing at all and you will conclude, again, that it is you.

My mother never found out, because nobody told her. I am telling you.

👉 The woman who makes the one I use grew up with it in Japan and has written down exactly what she checks, and why what is sold here under that name is usually not the same thing.

Read that before you buy another bar — from her or from anybody.

P.S. — Turn your bar over. Read the back, not the front. The front lies. The two words you want are Diospyros Kaki. If you only see "persimmon fruit extract", or if persimmon appears on the front and nowhere in the ingredients, that is exactly what I was washing with for two years. Send this to your sister. She is probably using the same one.

P.P.S. — I genuinely do not mind which brand you buy. Fermented. Unripe fruit. Named on the panel. The brand is not the point — starting is. But I will tell you what the doctor in Kyoto said when I asked her whether I could find the real thing at home. She said one or two have it right and the rest are selling dyed glycerin. I checked her description against the bar on my shelf and it matched. That is the only reason I am pointing anywhere at all.

"Huh," I said. "Made in China."

"It was a marketing lie," she said. "The industry is full of them. But they can't fake the ingredient list."

"Their website has a woman who grew up with this soap in a little Japanese village."

"I looked her up. Read the small print at the bottom of that page. She's a brand persona. They made her up."

"They sell you the story," she said. "So you never question what's actually in the bar."

I went down the list with my finger. Persimmon was tenth. The persimmon tannin was the very last thing on it.

"I went through all of these last week." She touched the six. "No wonder they don't work. The one thing that does the work is down at the bottom of every list."

"I paid $59.99 for that," I said. "And washed with everything ahead of it."

"You didn't do one thing wrong," she said. "I did."

"The tannin is in the green fruit," she said. "It's what makes an unripe persimmon pucker your whole mouth. Let it ripen and the pucker is gone. It's just sweet."

"So which one is in mine?"

"Yours says fruit extract. That's all it has to say. The green fruit, or the sweet juice of a ripe one. The box doesn't tell you."

"Which one do you use?"

She took a box out of her desk drawer. She turned it over before she held it out, her finger on the first line.

Persimmon Extract.

"First on the list," she said. "Pressed from the green fruit, before it ever turns sweet."

The front said Kaori. No village. No grandmother.

"This one doesn't need a story to sell."

"This isn't a prescription," she said. "I'm 64, and it's what I wash with now."

I held it to my nose. "Citrusy."

She took another box out of the drawer, still sealed, and pushed it across the desk to me.

"That one's yours."

I drove home with it on the passenger seat. I put it in the shower where the last one had been. I didn't tell Sarah. I didn't tell anybody.

The next Sunday Sarah came in, hugged me, and stopped.

"Oh, Mom. Is that a new perfume? It's nice."

I told her it was the Kaori bar I'd been using.

"Well, it smells really good," she said.

Dr. Mercer can't put any of this on Facebook. I can.

If she hadn't rung, I'd have quit for good. The second bar would still be in the cabinet.

My mother had six years of Sundays left when I started leaving early. Half an hour off every visit. I worked it out once. More than three whole days I could have sat with her, and I'll never get one minute of it back. She never found out why. I nearly didn't.

So please. Don't buy the next persimmon soap. Not one more bar until you've turned the box over. If persimmon isn't first, it isn't the one Dr. Mercer suggests.

Don't ask your daughter either. She'll tell you you're fine.

We made a soap that pulls odor out of your skin instead of covering it with fragrance.

It sounds almost too simple — until you learn why nothing else has worked.

Let me explain.

We didn't set out to make another "clean" soap. We set out to solve a problem most people don't even have a name for.

Around your mid-forties, your skin starts producing more of a compound called nonenal. It's what causes that faint musty smell on collars, pillowcases, jackets. It isn't sweat. It isn't hygiene. It's chemistry.

And here's the part nobody tells you: nonenal isn't water-soluble. Soap and water slide right past it. Deodorant lays perfume on top and hopes.

So for years, people over 40 dealt with the same frustrating loop:

Showering twice a day and still noticing it on a pillowcase. Washing a jacket that came back smelling the same. Buying stronger deodorant, then stronger perfume. Quietly wondering whether other people notice — and knowing nobody would ever say anything.

They'd try premium body washes. Same result. Because the problem was never how hard they scrubbed. It was that ordinary soap can't dissolve an oil-based compound.

The answer wasn't a stronger cleanser. It was a different ingredient entirely.

Persimmon tannin doesn't cover nonenal — it binds to it. Japan has used persimmon this way for centuries. It was never a secret. It's just not a business model, because you only need one bar.

body.text:
My husband said I was "getting too stale" at 55.
Four months later I walked into our grandson's birthday on another man's arm.
He choked on it. Still doesn't know how.

It started the night Greg came home from his buddy Dale's, three beers in, bragging about Dale's new girlfriend.

Half his age, he said. And the way she smelled. Like a woman who still bothered to take care of herself.

He told me that from his recliner, eyes already drifting back to the TV.

"You've gone a little stale, hon. That's all I'm saying."

Then he turned the volume up.

For ten years our evenings had looked exactly like that. Two recliners, two TV trays, the blue light of the television, and not one word between us.

The kids were grown and gone, and the house had gotten so quiet I left the kitchen radio on just for the sound of another voice.

And still, every morning, I made his coffee. Two sugars, by his chair.

I worked, I paid the bills, I ironed the shirts he wore to the bar without me, I cleared the plates he never carried to the sink.

Somewhere in those years he'd stopped seeing me. Stopped saying thank you. Stopped saying my name.

He hadn't always been like that. Somewhere under the recliner was the man who'd once driven through a snowstorm to bring me soup at the office. I'd just stopped being able to find him.

I told myself it was a rough patch. I'd been telling myself that for ten years.

I almost laughed. Stale. From the man who hadn't hauled himself off that recliner in two years. The man whose shirts I still ironed.

But the word crawled under my skin and stayed.

That comment wasn't really the reason. We'd drifted apart so slow I never saw the day it finished.

Two strangers under one roof. And I was tired. Bone tired of being the only one still trying.

It was my daughter Katie who finally said it out loud, both hands around a coffee mug at my kitchen table.

"Mom. You should have done this years ago. And I'll be right here."

So at fifty-five, I signed the papers on a Tuesday and walked out into a parking lot that smelled like rain, lighter than I'd felt in a decade.

I left Greg. He never left me.

The first weeks on my own were a strange kind of wonderful.

Biscuit asleep on the side of the bed that used to be off-limits. The kitchen painted the yellow Greg had vetoed for twenty years. Cereal for dinner, and nobody to answer to.

I called it freedom.

Freedom held up fine until about two in the morning. That's when I'd reach across the bed, find nothing but a cold sheet, and lie there in a house so quiet I could hear the clock in the hall.

I didn't want to grow old as the woman nobody reached for. I didn't want to die in that little house alone.

Greg didn't take it like a man.

He couldn't stand that I'd been the one to walk out, so he got on the phone before I could and poisoned every friend we had.

Poor Greg. Have you heard? She's falling apart. Couldn't last a month on her own.

Thirty years I kept his house and covered for him, and his parting gift was a whisper campaign. He made sure every word got back to me. That was the whole point.

For a while, God help me, I half believed him.

Then I got angry. Good and angry, for the first time in years.

I'd find a man who actually saw me. And I wanted Greg to choke on it.

Watch me, I thought.

Wanting it turned out to be the easy part.

Katie talked me into online dating, built the profile, hit save before I could lose my nerve.

I bought a new blouse for the first date and redid my lipstick at the mirror like a girl. I hadn't sat across a table from a strange man in thirty years.

He showed up twenty minutes late in a stained golf shirt, ordered for both of us without asking, and spent the whole dinner explaining his ex-wife was "clinically insane."

His photos had been fifteen years and forty pounds optimistic. I was home by eight.

The next one was better. Kind, funny, read actual books, asked questions and waited for the answers.

Three hours over coffee, and I caught myself thinking, maybe.

Then he mentioned, light as anything, that he still kept a key to his ex's place. "Just in case."

And just like that, the maybe was gone.

By the fifth date I stopped opening the app.

Some women just don't get a second act, I decided. I'd had mine.

The one person I finally told all of it to was my friend Sue.

Thirty years a nurse, sharp as a tack, seen everything twice.

We sat on her porch with iced tea, and I gave her the whole thing. The weird ones. The red flags. And finally, the word.

"Stale," I said. "Who says that to his own wife?"

Sue didn't laugh, and she didn't pity me. She just nodded, slow, like she already knew what I was about to say.

"Can I tell you something, and you won't take it wrong?"

"Go on."

"He was being cruel. But the smell part. He wasn't entirely wrong."

"Excuse me?"

"Hear me out. It matters more than anyone admits, with a man. And it shifts on all of us as we get older. Hormones."

"Sue. Are you telling me I stink?"

She laughed. "I'm telling you it's normal, and you'd never catch it on yourself. There's a name for it, even. Nonenal. We used to smell it on the older patients all the time."

"That is horrifying."

"It's chemistry, hon. Not character. Greg made it a verdict. It isn't one. It's about the only thing on your whole list you can actually fix."

"So I shower more."

"Regular soap doesn't touch it. It isn't made for that." She went inside and came back with a small wrapped bar called Kaori. "Here. We used to swear by this one on the ward. Persimmon. Do it for you, not for him."

I felt ridiculous even taking it. A bar of soap against thirty years of a man who'd stopped looking.

But that same night I looked it up. Glasses on, reading like I was buying a car. Turns out it's a real thing, properly studied. Persimmon is one of the only things that actually binds it, where regular soap just sits on top. That little Kaori bar is built on an old Japanese way of making it.

So I tried it. Not for Greg, not for anyone. Just for me. Ten quiet minutes at the sink every morning, a small ritual that was only mine. Taking care of myself, for once.

And after a while, I caught myself standing taller in the mirror. Shoulders back. Looking myself in the eye for the first time in years.

I didn't feel fixed. I felt like me, the one from before.

A week later Sue called. "Get dressed. Girls' night. There's a bar across town with a bluegrass band, and I'm not taking no for an answer."

She picked me up, took one look, and leaned in. "Well, look at you. You smell good." She grinned.

I went for the music. I'll have that on the record. I was finished with men.

The place was half empty, string lights over the bar, a trio tuning up in the corner.

And there was a man sitting right down on the floor by the fiddle player, eyes shut, grinning like it was the best thing that had happened to him all year.

When he came up for a beer he ended up on the stool beside me, and we talked clean through the second set.

Ray. Gardener's hands, dirt under one nail, a laugh that came easy.

At some point I realized an hour had gone by and I hadn't once braced for the catch. He just listened, laughed in the right places, and looked at me like the conversation was the best thing in the room.

Thirty years, and I'd forgotten what that did to a person.

The warmth up the neck. The little kick under the ribs. Butterflies, at fifty-five, in a half-empty bar.

He walked me to my car and didn't try a thing. Just asked, hands in his pockets, if he could call.

He was a kind man. The plain, real kind. Not pushy. Not playing games. I'd forgotten men like that were even out there.

So three days later, before I could talk myself out of it, I texted first.

We started slow. Long walks with my old dog. Suppers he cooked badly and proudly at my kitchen table.

On about the third one he stopped chopping, looked over, and said it like it was nothing. "You smell like citrus. I like that."

I had to turn back to the stove so he wouldn't see my face.

And slowly, the house began to change.

Muddy boots by my door now. Two coffee cups in the sink instead of one. My old dog losing her mind the second his truck turned into the drive.

The radio stayed off, because the quiet wasn't so heavy anymore. And the two-in-the-morning dread, the one I'd carried for years, just stopped coming.

I was a little bit in love. At my age, I'd long stopped believing that could happen again.

Then, four months after Greg told me I'd gone "stale," our grandson turned five.

The whole family came to my son's backyard for the party. Greg too, in a lawn chair by the cooler.

This time I didn't walk in alone. I walked in on Ray's arm, in a red dress I'd bought myself that morning.

Our grandson spotted him first and came tearing across the grass, and Ray scooped him up like he'd done it a hundred times.

The boy had taken to calling him "Bumpa," and he hollered it now so the whole yard could hear.

"BUMPA, come see the frogs!"

My son watched them go, then put a hand on my shoulder.

"I like him, Mom," he said. "And you. You seem happy. Properly happy."

Across the patio, Katie caught my eye and didn't say a word. She didn't need to.

The same friends Greg had told I was falling apart watched me come in glowing, a good man's hand at the small of my back.

Nobody was using the soft, careful voice now.

And Greg looked up from his chair, saw the man, saw my face, and the hello died in his throat.

He never got the word out.

That was the choke. The one I'd wished on him, alone on the cold side of that bed. He still doesn't know how I did it.

I didn't go over and smooth it for him. I'd done that my whole marriage. Not this time.

He'd called me stale, four months and a whole life ago. He had it exactly backwards.

Ray and I are driving up to a little cabin this weekend. Just the two of us.

Sue called this morning.

"Well?" was all she said. She could already hear the answer.

"I'm going to need more of that bar," I told her.

"Order a few while you're at it," she said. "They sell out fast. And tell the other women."

So that's what I'm doing.

Those ten quiet minutes at the sink became the first kind thing I do for myself all day. I can't start a morning without them now.

So I left the link below. It's a little persimmon bar called Kaori.

If you wake up tired, half sure the best part's behind you, it's a good place to start.

And if someone you love has gone quiet, and you can't work out why.

Maybe you don't need to prove anyone wrong. Maybe you just need a better bar.

❌ Orange colourant, CI 15985, doing the work the fruit was supposed to do
❌ "Persimmon extract" on the front, nothing named on the back
❌ Real persimmon, but unfermented, which skips the step that creates the tannin

body.text:
After my divorce my best friends lied about excluding me from Italy. But they missed my ex-husband more. So I booked the flight and took care of that.

Cassie and I have been best friends for 20 years.

She and Greg. Mike and Pam. Dave and Rachel. Three couples, plus Mark and me.

Every September for 16 years, the 8 of us traveled together.

I researched the towns. I found the excursions. I booked the restaurants. Mark handled the logistics.

For 16 years this was the best week of my year.

Then Mark and I divorced. 14 months ago. He'd been having an affair with a woman from his gym. She was 34.

After the papers were signed, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off wine.

Everyone saying "we're here for you, whatever you need."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning. And there they are. All six of them.

At a café in Florence. Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning. The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan." That voice. The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to make things awkward. It was sort of last-minute. And honestly, sweetheart, we thought you needed a little time for yourself. After everything you've been going through."

Everything I've been going through.

She kept going.

"And it's close quarters over there. One apartment, six of us, the heat in August. Ever since the divorce you just haven't been yourself, Susan."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good. We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back. Tanned. Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news. We're doing Amalfi in September. And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary. You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about. You're so good at organizing."

I said, "Sure, Cassie. I'll put something together."

Then I hung up. I sat in the kitchen for an hour.

Why did I say yes.

That's the part I kept going back to. She left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. And I said sure. Like it was nothing.

Maybe I was being unfair to her. It really could have been last minute. Cassie has not been cruel to me one day in 20 years.

Or maybe I said yes because it was the only thing they still wanted me for.

I sat there a while longer. Then I got the laptop.

I started planning it. Spent weeks on it.

Found a private lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through the terraces that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE. You're amazing. This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house. "Just a little get-together," she said. "Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out. Candles lit. All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in. The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about September."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Mark and Brittany took your spot this year."

Mark.

And Brittany.

The woman he left me for. She was 34. She'd been in his life for two years, one of them while he was still married to me.

"Mark reached out," Cassie continued. "He and Brittany just got engaged. And honestly, we've all known Mark for 20 years. It felt wrong to exclude him forever."

Exclude him.

The man who cheated on me for a year. Who left me for a woman half my age. Who kept the house in the settlement because I couldn't afford to fight him for it.

He's the one they were worried about excluding.

"Susan, we love you. You know that. But nothing has changed since we talked on the phone."

Close quarters. The heat. I just hadn't been myself.

She looked around the table. Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way. You have to understand."

You have to understand.

I looked at Cassie. At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get. Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass. Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry. I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

She wasn't wrong. That was the part I couldn't put down.

The next morning I drove over to Nora's. My sister. 28 years a nurse, most of it on a geriatric floor. She lives 20 minutes away and has never once pretended not to notice something.

I told her everything. The photos from Florence. The "you're so good at organizing" call. The dinner. Cassie's voice. "Ever since the divorce."

And the part I could barely say out loud: that Mark and Brittany were taking my spot. On the trip I planned.

She let me finish. Then she poured the coffee.

She put something on the table between us. Small, wrapped in tissue paper. Orange.

She didn't say a word about it.

"They're right that there's something," she said. "They're wrong about what it is. Those two aren't the same thing."

"Nora, what is this about?"

"28 years I looked after women our age and older. Things change. Your hair goes. Your eyes go. Your skin gets drier."

"Nobody's fault. You color it, you get glasses."

"Well. It also starts making something it never made before. A compound. It has a smell to it. Not a pleasant one."

"I've never heard of that."

"Nobody has. People don't talk about it."

"Then that's not me. I'm a clean person, Nora. I always have been. I buy the good body wash."

"That's the part everybody gets wrong."

She set her cup down.

"Ordinary soap doesn't take it off."

"Now you're being ridiculous."

"Think about garlic. You chop it, then you wash your hands. Twice, with soap. And?"

I didn't answer her.

"And?"

"They still smell."

"They still smell. Your hands are clean and it stayed anyway. Garlic leaves something behind that soap doesn't touch."

"What our skin starts making is called nonenal. Works exactly the same way."

I sat there with that.

"And people notice it," she said. "Not that they know what they're noticing. They couldn't tell you. They just start standing a little further back, and they make up a reason for it afterward."

"Nora."

"You didn't do anything, Susan. Nobody did this to you. Your skin changed at 60 the same way your eyes changed at 45, and nobody sent you a letter about either one."

"So it was never me."

"It was never you."

"Then what gets rid of it?"

She pushed the little parcel across the table.

"I was hoping you'd ask me before I had to offer."

"It's soap. Made from persimmon."

"It doesn't cover it. The tannins take it apart."

"And it works?"

"I sent half my floor home with one. I've used it for years."

"One morning it occurred to me I'd stopped bracing every time somebody hugged me. I never knew I'd been doing it."

I picked it up and held it to my face. Citrus. Warm, though. Not the sharp kind.

"It's called Kaori. I'm down to two bars myself."

I was at the door when she said the other thing.

"Book the flight, Susan. Go on your own."

"Cassie isn't going to un-invite Brittany."

"I'm not talking about Cassie. You found that grove because you wanted to see a grove. You got that table because you wanted to sit at it."

She held the door open.

"So go sit at it."

I drove home with it in my purse.

I used it that night. It's a bar of soap. I didn't expect anything.

The next morning I caught myself standing at the mirror longer than usual. Not for any reason. Just standing. Looking taller, somehow. Skin felt different. Lighter.

I had not stood like that in over a year.

That afternoon I ordered two more. Then I booked the trip.

Same week. Same coast.

Their hotel. One floor up.

Paid for with the money from my half of the retirement account. The only thing I got in the divorce that was actually mine.

And I told no one.

September on the Amalfi Coast is hotter than people think.

I was on the hotel terrace with a glass of prosecco when I saw them come up from the road below. Cassie fanning herself with a folded map. Brittany walking ten feet behind Mark, not talking.

Twenty minutes later Cassie appeared on the terrace. Flushed. Hair coming undone.

She froze.

"Susan? What are you doing here?"

"Same week. Same coast."

She stared a second too long. Then she went to her room without saying anything else.

I didn't move. I had nowhere to be. And a very good glass of prosecco.

Day three. The lemon grove.

Twelve spots. I'd booked one for myself. The group had the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I got there first. Signora Rossi walked me up through the terraces and showed me how they wrap the lemons in cloth for the winter.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi looked up and waved at me across the terrace.

"Susan. You are the one who wrote to me. In Italian."

The whole group turned around.

Mark saw me. He stopped.

"Susan? You're on this tour?"

"I found this tour, Mark."

He opened his mouth. Closed it. Looked at Brittany.

Brittany adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

There was a woman on the tour with her daughter. About my age. She ended up next to me at the wall while Signora Rossi was talking.

She leaned in slightly. Then leaned back.

"I'm sorry," she said. "Are you wearing something? I've been trying to place it since the van."

"It's a soap."

"It smells so good. Like citrus. Fresh." She laughed at herself. "Sorry. I've been behind you for twenty minutes trying to work out what it was."

"It's called Kaori."

She typed it into her phone right there against the wall.

Cassie was three feet away with her hand cupped over her eyes against the sun.

She didn't say anything.

I thought about that on the walk back down.

We've been talking, all of us. That is what Cassie said at the table.

All of them. Talking. And not one of them ever talked to me.

I think I understood now.

That evening the group was at the bar on the hotel terrace. I was two tables away with a book.

Dave came over. The quietest of the husbands. He sat on the edge of the chair next to mine.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip," he said. "And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar. Then he got up and went back to it.

I didn't read another page.

Night four. The dinner Cassie had booked for the group.

I came down at eight.

Cassie was already seated, fanning herself with the menu. Brittany's shoulders were burned across the top. She kept shifting in her chair.

Mark looked up when I walked in.

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-50s. Elegant. Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But I have to ask what you're wearing."

"It's a soap."

"A soap." She put her hand on her chest. "I write for a travel magazine. I've been trying to place that since you sat down. It isn't perfume. It's citrus, and it's fresh. It's lovely."

"Kaori. My sister gave it to me."

"Can I get it here?"

"They only make it when the persimmons come in," I said. "Once a year."

She wrote it in the journal anyway.

Brittany leaned over and said something to Mark. He didn't answer her.

Cassie watched all of it.

The woman with the journal. The pen.

She picked up her wine glass. Took a long sip. Set it down. Looked straight ahead.

Brittany had stopped shifting in her chair.

Mark was watching me. Not Brittany. Me.

Day seven I ate alone at the cliffside table in Positano. The one I'd booked three months earlier, for them.

They had tried for it that morning. Fully booked, the restaurant told them.

Last night. Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the terrace afterward. Water black. Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Greg hasn't left the room with the air conditioning since Tuesday," she said.

"That's a shame."

"Brittany's shoulders are blistering. She had to wear a shawl to dinner."

"I noticed."

She looked at me.

"People keep asking about you."

"They do."

"The woman with the journal. The girl at the front desk asked me what my friend uses."

Silence.

"Where did you get it?"

I looked at her.

"Kaori," I said. "But they only make it when the persimmons come in. That batch is gone."

She looked down.

"Of course it is."

"They restock when the fruit comes in. If you wait, you wait a long time."

She nodded.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my room without looking back.

Here's what I keep coming back to.

They left me off a trip, then called me to plan the next one. Apparently I'm capable enough to find a restaurant with a three-month waitlist. Just not capable enough to sit at one.

"We thought you needed a little time for yourself."

"Ever since the divorce, you just haven't been yourself."

Not one of them ever told me what they actually meant.

My sister did. In her kitchen, in about ten minutes.

Nora called last week. Kaori has a new batch up. It's already most of the way gone.

They're doing September again next year. Sicily, someone said.

Nora has already asked whether Sicily has lemon groves.

I told her yes.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost yourself.

You don't need to be replaced.

You need to be underestimated one more time.

So you can show them exactly who they were wrong about.

Get the Kaori. Run the bath. Go anyway.

It costs less than fifty cents a day. Less than the coffee I drink while I plan other people's trips.

They only make it when the persimmons come in. Once a batch goes, you wait months.

Cassie asked where I got it. I told her it was sold out.

She's waiting until next year.

I was already home.

Your move.
